~~~text
\chapter{Continuous temporal uncertainty and an informative intervention}
\label{exec13:temporal-region}

\hypertarget{the-banking-question-and-the-observation-law}{%
\section{The banking question and the observation
law}\label{the-banking-question-and-the-observation-law}}

A bank can observe a stable association between an offer and a
subsequent outcome yet remain unable to price the effect of changing the
offer. The missing information can persist even with an exactly known
observational distribution. This chapter develops a restricted temporal
confidence construction and shows what an additional direct intervention
would contribute. The mathematical construction and exact calculations
are project derivations, not a fitted bank result.
\cite{exec13_temporal_argument,exec13_temporal_exact}

In the preserved temporal graph study, all valid cells covered and
retained their declared true graph in 512 of 512 requests. Weak
relevance and unrestricted latent observation each produced 512
whole-line sets. The persistent cell produced 507 finite sets and five
whole-line sets. Under false exclusion, the true graph was retained zero
times despite numerical effect coverage. These findings distinguish
numerical coverage from informative effects and from a valid causal
restriction. \cite{exec13_temporal_predecessor}

Let \(X_t=(Z_t,A_t,Y_t)'\) satisfy \[
 X_t=\rho X_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,\quad
 \varepsilon_t\mathrel{\mathop\sim^{\rm iid}}N_3(0,\Sigma),\quad
 \Sigma\succ0,\quad \rho\in I\subset(-1,1).
\] Here \(I\) is a declared closed interval, not an estimated selected
lag. Initial observations have the invariant distribution
\(N_3(0,\Sigma/(1-\rho^2))\), independently of future innovations. We
observe \(X_0,\ldots,X_n\), with \(n\ge2\). The scalar lag common to all
coordinates and the Gaussian independent innovations are substantive
restrictions. A general lag matrix, unknown lag order, nonstationarity,
hidden temporal state, selection and measurement errors are outside this
law.

A structural innovation model is \[
 \varepsilon_Z=E_Z,\qquad
 \varepsilon_A=k\varepsilon_Z+U,\qquad
 \varepsilon_Y=\tau\varepsilon_A+c\varepsilon_Z+V,
\] where \(E_Z\) is independent of the jointly Gaussian pair \((U,V)\).
Dependence between \(U\) and \(V\) represents latent action/outcome
confounding. The target \(\tau\) is the contemporaneous response to
changing \(A_t\) while holding the past fixed. In observed-coordinate
structural equations, the lag matrix is \(\rho(I-B)\), where \(B\)
contains the contemporaneous coefficients. It is not permissible to
change that lag matrix to \(\rho I\) in the structural equations and
claim the same target/law.

The declared graph family may include the exclusion model \(c=0\) and a
broad latent model with unrestricted \(c\). In the former,
\(\Sigma_{ZY}=\tau\Sigma_{ZA}\). In the latter that equality need not
hold. An exclusion is a scientific restriction, not a conclusion from
fitting a favorable covariance. The construction below accommodates a
finite declared family through a union over graph/parameter pairs; it
does not claim an exhaustive search over unrestricted causal structures.

\hypertarget{a-feasible-region-with-continuous-unknown-lag}{%
\section{A feasible region with continuous unknown
lag}\label{a-feasible-region-with-continuous-unknown-lag}}

For every candidate \(r\in I\), form residuals \(E_t(r)=X_t-rX_{t-1}\).
Use the nine fixed directions \[
 \mathcal V=\{e_1,e_2,e_3,e_1+e_2,e_1-e_2,
 e_1+e_3,e_1-e_3,e_2+e_3,e_2-e_3\},\quad K=9.
\] For each direction, let \(S_v(r)\) be the ordinary sample variance of
\(v'E_t(r)\), with divisor \(\nu=n-1\). At the true lag only,
\(\nu S_v(\rho)/(v'\Sigma v)\) is the sum of squares of \(\nu\)
independent standard normal variables. To see this, scale the vector of
independent normal residuals by its population standard deviation and
apply an orthogonal matrix whose first row is the normalized all-ones
vector. The remaining \(\nu\) coordinates are independent standard
normals, and their squared norm is the centered sum of squares.
Consequently \[
 E[S_v(\rho)]=v'\Sigma v,\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(S_v(\rho))=2(v'\Sigma v)^2/\nu.
\] For a declared rational tolerance \(0<t<1\), Markov's inequality
applied to the squared relative error gives \[
 P\{|S_v(\rho)/(v'\Sigma v)-1|>t\}\le\frac{2}{\nu t^2}.
\] If \(2K/(\nu t^2)\le\alpha_O\), the union bound supplies simultaneous
coverage at least \(1-\alpha_O\) for \[
 L_v(r)=\frac{S_v(r)}{1+t}\le v'\Sigma v
 \le \frac{S_v(r)}{1-t}=U_v(r),\qquad v\in\mathcal V,
\] evaluated at \(r=\rho\). Dependence between the nine directions is
harmless for this bound. Residuals at an incorrect lag need not be
independent.

Define \(\mathcal C_O\) to contain every tuple \((r,G,\lambda,\Sigma)\)
for which \(r\in I\), \(G\) is in the declared family, its parameters
\(\lambda\) generate \(\Sigma\succ0\) under the stated innovation law,
and all nine inequalities hold. All nuisance coefficients and the
continuous lag remain in the region. Let \[
 \mathcal S_O=\{\tau(G,\lambda):(r,G,\lambda,\Sigma)\in\mathcal C_O\}.
\] On simultaneous variance inclusion, the true tuple belongs to
\(\mathcal C_O\); hence its effect belongs to \(\mathcal S_O\). Thus
\(P(\tau_0\in\mathcal S_O)\ge1-\alpha_O\), provided the declared family
contains the true structural model. No multiple-testing penalty over the
continuum of candidate lags is required: this proof uses a single
coverage event at the fixed true lag, and the union includes that lag.
It does not declare every wrong-lag confidence calculation valid or
justify discarding the true lag by a separate selector.

The construction is deliberately conservative. With \(t=1/4\), \(K=9\)
and \(\alpha_O=.02\), it needs \(\nu\ge14{,}400\). The predecessor used
240 transitions; this particular finite bound cannot give it the
displayed two-sided relative band. At smaller sample size this profile
returns the whole line and a bound-insufficient disposition, rather than
inserting an invalid finite interval. The exact chi-square pivot above
offers a sharper candidate using suitably certified quantiles, but its
numerical implementation would need separate validation. No improvement
in cost or useful width is claimed from replacing a lag grid with this
conservative continuum argument.

\hypertarget{numerical-outer-bounds-that-cannot-lose-a-lag-or-a-component}{%
\section{Numerical outer bounds that cannot lose a lag or a
component}\label{numerical-outer-bounds-that-cannot-lose-a-lag-or-a-component}}

Let \(u_t=v'X_t\) and \(w_t=v'X_{t-1}\). Center each series over the
same \(n\) transitions. Direct expansion gives \[
 \begin{aligned}
 S_v(r)&=a_vr^2+b_vr+d_v,\\
 a_v&=\nu^{-1}\sum_t(w_t-\bar w)^2,\\
 b_v&=-2\nu^{-1}\sum_t(u_t-\bar u)(w_t-\bar w),\\
 d_v&=\nu^{-1}\sum_t(u_t-\bar u)^2.
 \end{aligned}
\] For a closed lag cell \(J=[r_L,r_U]\), its maximum is at an endpoint
because \(a_v\ge0\); its minimum is at an endpoint or at \(-b_v/(2a_v)\)
if that vertex lies in the cell. The constant case is handled
separately. Rational coefficients and cell endpoints therefore give
exact bounds \([s^-_v(J),s^+_v(J)]\). A finite partition covering all of
\(I\), with shared endpoints retained, is a continuum enclosure, not an
evaluation grid. Refining cells can reduce excess width; stopping early
preserves validity.

For exact supplied numbers, a conservative directional variance interval
over the cell is \([s^-_v/(1+t),s^+_v/(1-t)]\). Polarization gives an
entrywise covariance box. For \(i\ne j\), use \[
 \Sigma_{ij}\in\frac14
 [L_{e_i+e_j}(J)-U_{e_i-e_j}(J),
  U_{e_i+e_j}(J)-L_{e_i-e_j}(J)].
\] Dropping positive-definiteness and shared-parameter consistency
enlarges this box. It can make results much wider, but cannot remove the
true covariance. Positive-definiteness or graph constraints may narrow a
later implementation only through certified feasibility exclusion, not
by failure of an optimizer.

Exact arithmetic on decimal data alone does not enclose unknown
rounding. Suppose every coordinate of the ideal input is enclosed within
absolute error \(\eta\) of the supplied value, and let
\(h=\|v\|_1\eta(1+\max_{r\in J}|r|)\). Residual error is at most \(h\)
and its centered error at most \(2h\). Cauchy--Schwarz then bounds the
change in sample variance by \[
 B_v(J)=4h\sqrt{n/\nu}\sqrt{s^+_v(J)}+4nh^2/\nu.
\] Use rational upward bounds for the square roots and replace the
variance enclosure by \([\max(0,s^-_v-B_v),s^+_v+B_v]\) before dividing
by \(1\pm t\). This is an input-conversion certificate conditional on a
valid input enclosure. Undocumented measurement error, noisy proxies or
incorrect entity matches are changes to the observation law, not
floating-point errors that this formula repairs.

In an exclusion cell, write the resulting intervals as \(N_J\) for
\(\Sigma_{ZY}\) and \(D_J\) for \(\Sigma_{ZA}\). Retain the full set \[
 \mathcal T_J=\{\theta:\exists (N,D)\in N_J\times D_J,
                      \ N-\theta D=0\}.
\] When \(0\notin D_J\), its endpoints are the extreme corner ratios.
When the denominator straddles zero and the numerator excludes zero, two
rays can result. For \(N_J=[1,2]\) and \(D_J=[-1,1]\), the set is
\(( -\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\). When both intervals include zero, their
rectangle contains \((0,0)\), so every \(\theta\) is feasible. When
\(D_J=\{0\}\) and \(0\notin N_J\), the moment set is empty. That is a
constraint inconsistency, not evidence for a zero effect.

Union these components over every lag cell and every retained graph. The
broad latent graph below contributes the whole line whenever its
observational law is admitted. Keep disconnected components unless they
overlap; never replace a pair of rays by a finite interval. The exact
reference checks ratio sets against the independent criterion that
\(N_J\) intersects \(\theta D_J\), including zero denominators and exact
endpoints. Bounds include every continuous lag by the quadratic proof;
sampled checks alone are not the certificate. The reference is not a
general graph feasibility solver and supplies no bank-data result.

\hypertarget{an-equal-law-witness-and-what-an-exclusion-actually-buys}{%
\section{An equal-law witness and what an exclusion actually
buys}\label{an-equal-law-witness-and-what-an-exclusion-actually-buys}}

Let \(Z,U,E\) be independent standard Gaussian innovations and set \[
 \varepsilon_Z=Z,\quad \varepsilon_A=Z+U,\quad
 \varepsilon_Y=\tau\varepsilon_A+(2-\tau)Z+(1-\tau)U+E.
\] For every real \(\tau\), the observed innovation is exactly
\((Z,Z+U,2Z+U+E)'\), with covariance \[
 \Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&2\\1&2&3\\2&3&6\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad\det\Sigma=1.
\] The confounded disturbance has variance \(1+(1-\tau)^2\) and
covariance \(1-\tau\) with \(U\); its conditional noise variance is
always one. Every world is a coherent positive-definite Gaussian law.
Attaching the same scalar lag and invariant initialization makes the
entire observed temporal law identical for every \(\tau\), while a
contemporaneous intervention on \(A\) changes \(Y\) at slope \(\tau\).
The equality is algebraic for all real effects, not merely an equality
across the finite checked examples.

The restriction \(c=0\) reduces this family to \(\tau=2\); strong
observed relevance \(\Sigma_{ZA}=1\) then gives the familiar ratio. But
relevance alone does not establish exclusion: all other worlds have the
same strong observed correlation with \(Z\). Merely observing more of
this law, using a different discovery optimizer or asking an LLM to
orient an edge cannot choose among these effects. No theorem here rules
out all additional measurements; it states exactly what the declared
observational law omits.

At zero relevance, even exclusion can leave every effect feasible. Take
\(\varepsilon_A=U\) and
\(\varepsilon_Y=\tau\varepsilon_A+(1-\tau)U+E=U+E\), with \(Z\)
independent. Now \(c=0\), \(\Sigma_{ZA}=\Sigma_{ZY}=0\), and the effect
is still arbitrary. A weak-instrument ratio that quietly deletes zero
cannot solve this information problem.

\hypertarget{a-direct-intervention-that-separates-effects-without-identifying-every-edge}{%
\section{A direct intervention that separates effects without
identifying every
edge}\label{a-direct-intervention-that-separates-effects-without-identifying-every-edge}}

Consider independent experimental episodes at a common fixed pre-action
history. Replace the action equation by \(A=a_0+\delta R\), where
\(\delta>0\) is known and \(R\in\{-1,1\}\) is assigned with \(m\)
episodes per arm independently of innovation roots. Keep the other
structural equations unchanged. Under the restricted linear Gaussian
model and an invariant \(\tau\), the outcome has the form \[
 Y=\mu+\tau\delta R+\xi,\quad
 \xi\mathrel{\mathop\sim^{\rm iid}}N(0,\sigma_I^2),\qquad \sigma_I^2>0.
\] The unknown \(\mu\) absorbs the fixed history and baseline action;
the unknown variance absorbs the remaining contemporaneous causes. The
episodes must be independent; taking adjacent dates from one continuing
customer trajectory does not satisfy this experiment. Identical variance
in the two arms and a common transported effect are additional model
assumptions.

Let \(\widehat\tau_I=(\bar Y_+-\bar Y_-)/(2\delta)\), and let \(S_p^2\)
be the usual pooled within-arm variance with \(\nu_I=2m-2\) degrees of
freedom. Orthogonal Gaussian projections within each arm make its sample
mean independent of its centered residuals. Hence \[
 T=\frac{\widehat\tau_I-\tau}{S_p/(\delta\sqrt{2m})}
   =\frac{Z_0}{\sqrt{Q/\nu_I}},\qquad
 Z_0\sim N(0,1),\quad Q\sim\chi^2_{\nu_I},\quad Z_0\perp Q.
\] For \(m>2\), integrating the chi-square density gives
\(E[Q^{-1}]=1/(\nu_I-2)\), so \(E[T^2]=\nu_I/(\nu_I-2)\). Choose any
rational \(b^2\ge\nu_I/((\nu_I-2)\alpha_I)\). Markov's inequality proves
finite coverage at least \(1-\alpha_I\) for \[
 \mathcal S_I=\left[\widehat\tau_I-
  \sqrt{\frac{b^2S_p^2}{2m\delta^2}},\quad
  \widehat\tau_I+\sqrt{\frac{b^2S_p^2}{2m\delta^2}}\right].
\] This conservative alternative avoids unverified numerical tail
quantiles. A sharper Student pivot interval is possible with certified
quantiles. Nonpositive pooled variance or insufficient degrees of
freedom produces a refusal/whole-line result under the declared
algorithm, never zero-width certainty. A nonnormal outcome model needs
another uncertainty argument. If input numbers are enclosed rather than
exact, enclose the arm means and pooled variance as well before
projecting these endpoints.

Under a common effect parameter, report
\(\mathcal S=\mathcal S_O\cap\mathcal S_I\). The two component coverage
events need not be independent: the union bound gives at least
\(1-\alpha_O-\alpha_I\). Using outer numerical supersets preserves this
inclusion proof. An empty intersection is a retained
inconsistency/failure event, not an invitation to change the error
budget or delete a graph after seeing the result. If no observational
restriction is defensible, use \(\mathcal S_I\) alone under its own
experiment and target assumptions.

In the equal-law family, intervention changes the arm mean difference to
\(2\delta\tau\). Distinct effects are now distinguishable, although
several graphs can remain compatible. Identifying the decision-relevant
effect does not require identifying every edge. Randomizing a variable
that merely encourages the action is a different experiment: exclusion,
compliance and relevance then need their own argument.

\hypertarget{precision-costs-and-the-exact-remaining-scope}{%
\section{Precision, costs and the exact remaining
scope}\label{precision-costs-and-the-exact-remaining-scope}}

For a binary offer, take \(a_0=\delta=1/2\). A planning illustration
with \(m=200\) per arm, \(\alpha_I=.03\), a reported effect of twenty
dollars and \(S_p^2=100\) dollars squared gives \(b^2=9950/297\) and
half-width \(\sqrt{9950/297}\), approximately 5.788 dollars. The exact
reference uses a rational upward square-root enclosure. These are
supplied planning summaries, not observations from a completed trial.

For 3,000 eligible customers and fifteen dollars incremental
implementation cost per offer, the point scenario has fifteen thousand
dollars net benefit. Its conservative interval still includes a small
loss. Scaling an effect by population does not remove uncertainty, and
changing the intervention or customer population may invalidate
transport. A genuine next-experiment proposal should ask whether
resolving this decision is worth the experiment's cost, compare a
cheaper operational alternative, and include delayed outcomes,
noncompliance and treatment costs in the estimand. No measured bank ROI
is inferred from this illustration.

What is resolved is the mathematical route for one continuous scalar-lag
Gaussian family, a certified enclosure strategy, exact information
counterexamples and a separating intervention with an explicit finite
bound. What remains is a resource-profiled implementation and
prospectively registered study, tighter useful uncertainty, justified
input and model assumptions, actual interventions/measurements if the
proposal advances, and the general
unknown-lag-matrix/latent-state/non-Gaussian/heterogeneous-effect
problem. This argument establishes no general temporal-graph capability,
bank validation or independent acceptance. The computational and
information routes are concrete enough to design the next bounded
public/generated experiment. The following design analysis tests whether the displayed bounds could be informative at the predecessor's sample size and whether its qualification screen has adequate power. It keeps theorem validity, finite availability and a useful financial comparison as separate requirements.

\label{exec13:temporal-region-end}
~~~

~~~text
preserves validity.

For exact supplied numbers, a conservative directional variance interval
over the cell is \([s^-_v/(1+t),s^+_v/(1-t)]\). Polarization gives an
entrywise covariance box. For \(i\ne j\), use \[
 \Sigma_{ij}\in\frac14
 [L_{e_i+e_j}(J)-U_{e_i-e_j}(J),
  U_{e_i+e_j}(J)-L_{e_i-e_j}(J)].
\] Dropping positive-definiteness and shared-parameter consistency
enlarges this box. It can make results much wider, but cannot remove the
true covariance. Positive-definiteness or graph constraints may narrow a
later implementation only through certified feasibility exclusion, not
by failure of an optimizer.

Exact arithmetic on decimal data alone does not enclose unknown
rounding. Suppose every coordinate of the ideal input is enclosed within
absolute error \(\eta\) of the supplied value, and let
\(h=\|v\|_1\eta(1+\max_{r\in J}|r|)\). Residual error is at most \(h\)
and its centered error at most \(2h\). Cauchy--Schwarz then bounds the
change in sample variance by \[
 B_v(J)=4h\sqrt{n/\nu}\sqrt{s^+_v(J)}+4nh^2/\nu.
\] Use rational upward bounds for the square roots and replace the
variance enclosure by \([\max(0,s^-_v-B_v),s^+_v+B_v]\) before dividing
by \(1\pm t\). This is an input-conversion certificate conditional on a
valid input enclosure. Undocumented measurement error, noisy proxies or
incorrect entity matches are changes to the observation law, not
floating-point errors that this formula repairs.

In an exclusion cell, write the resulting intervals as \(N_J\) for
\(\Sigma_{ZY}\) and \(D_J\) for \(\Sigma_{ZA}\). Retain the full set \[
 \mathcal T_J=\{\theta:\exists (N,D)\in N_J\times D_J,
                      \ N-\theta D=0\}.
\] When \(0\notin D_J\), its endpoints are the extreme corner ratios.
When the denominator straddles zero and the numerator excludes zero, two
rays can result. For \(N_J=[1,2]\) and \(D_J=[-1,1]\), the set is
\(( -\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\). When both intervals include zero, their
rectangle contains \((0,0)\), so every \(\theta\) is feasible. When
\(D_J=\{0\}\) and \(0\notin N_J\), the moment set is empty. That is a
constraint inconsistency, not evidence for a zero effect.

Union these components over every lag cell and every retained graph. The
broad latent graph below contributes the whole line whenever its
observational law is admitted. Keep disconnected components unless they
overlap; never replace a pair of rays by a finite interval. The exact
reference checks ratio sets against the independent criterion that
\(N_J\) intersects \(\theta D_J\), including zero denominators and exact
endpoints. Bounds include every continuous lag by the quadratic proof;
sampled checks alone are not the certificate. The reference is not a
general graph feasibility solver and supplies no bank-data result.

\hypertarget{an-equal-law-witness-and-what-an-exclusion-actually-buys}{%
\section{An equal-law witness and what an exclusion actually
buys}\label{an-equal-law-witness-and-what-an-exclusion-actually-buys}}

Let \(Z,U,E\) be independent standard Gaussian innovations and set \[
 \varepsilon_Z=Z,\quad \varepsilon_A=Z+U,\quad
 \varepsilon_Y=\tau\varepsilon_A+(2-\tau)Z+(1-\tau)U+E.
\] For every real \(\tau\), the observed innovation is exactly
\((Z,Z+U,2Z+U+E)'\), with covariance \[
 \Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&2\\1&2&3\\2&3&6\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad\det\Sigma=1.
\] The confounded disturbance has variance \(1+(1-\tau)^2\) and
covariance \(1-\tau\) with \(U\); its conditional noise variance is
always one. Every world is a coherent positive-definite Gaussian law.
Attaching the same scalar lag and invariant initialization makes the
entire observed temporal law identical for every \(\tau\), while a
contemporaneous intervention on \(A\) changes \(Y\) at slope \(\tau\).
The equality is algebraic for all real effects, not merely an equality
across the finite checked examples.

The restriction \(c=0\) reduces this family to \(\tau=2\); strong
observed relevance \(\Sigma_{ZA}=1\) then gives the familiar ratio. But
relevance alone does not establish exclusion: all other worlds have the
same strong observed correlation with \(Z\). Merely observing more of
this law, using a different discovery optimizer or asking an LLM to
orient an edge cannot choose among these effects. No theorem here rules
out all additional measurements; it states exactly what the declared
observational law omits.

At zero relevance, even exclusion can leave every effect feasible. Take
\(\varepsilon_A=U\) and
\(\varepsilon_Y=\tau\varepsilon_A+(1-\tau)U+E=U+E\), with \(Z\)
independent. Now \(c=0\), \(\Sigma_{ZA}=\Sigma_{ZY}=0\), and the effect
is still arbitrary. A weak-instrument ratio that quietly deletes zero
cannot solve this information problem.

\hypertarget{a-direct-intervention-that-separates-effects-without-identifying-every-edge}{%
\section{A direct intervention that separates effects without
identifying every
edge}\label{a-direct-intervention-that-separates-effects-without-identifying-every-edge}}

Consider independent experimental episodes at a common fixed pre-action
history. Replace the action equation by \(A=a_0+\delta R\), where
\(\delta>0\) is known and \(R\in\{-1,1\}\) is assigned with \(m\)
episodes per arm independently of innovation roots. Keep the other
structural equations unchanged. Under the restricted linear Gaussian
model and an invariant \(\tau\), the outcome has the form \[
 Y=\mu+\tau\delta R+\xi,\quad
 \xi\mathrel{\mathop\sim^{\rm iid}}N(0,\sigma_I^2),\qquad \sigma_I^2>0.
\] The unknown \(\mu\) absorbs the fixed history and baseline action;
the unknown variance absorbs the remaining contemporaneous causes. The
episodes must be independent; taking adjacent dates from one continuing
customer trajectory does not satisfy this experiment. Identical variance
in the two arms and a common transported effect are additional model
assumptions.

Let \(\widehat\tau_I=(\bar Y_+-\bar Y_-)/(2\delta)\), and let \(S_p^2\)
be the usual pooled within-arm variance with \(\nu_I=2m-2\) degrees of
freedom. Orthogonal Gaussian projections within each arm make its sample
mean independent of its centered residuals. Hence \[
 T=\frac{\widehat\tau_I-\tau}{S_p/(\delta\sqrt{2m})}
   =\frac{Z_0}{\sqrt{Q/\nu_I}},\qquad
 Z_0\sim N(0,1),\quad Q\sim\chi^2_{\nu_I},\quad Z_0\perp Q.
\] For \(m>2\), integrating the chi-square density gives
\(E[Q^{-1}]=1/(\nu_I-2)\), so \(E[T^2]=\nu_I/(\nu_I-2)\). Choose any
rational \(b^2\ge\nu_I/((\nu_I-2)\alpha_I)\). Markov's inequality proves
finite coverage at least \(1-\alpha_I\) for \[
 \mathcal S_I=\left[\widehat\tau_I-
  \sqrt{\frac{b^2S_p^2}{2m\delta^2}},\quad
  \widehat\tau_I+\sqrt{\frac{b^2S_p^2}{2m\delta^2}}\right].
\] This conservative alternative avoids unverified numerical tail
quantiles. A sharper Student pivot interval is possible with certified
quantiles. Nonpositive pooled variance or insufficient degrees of
freedom produces a refusal/whole-line result under the declared
algorithm, never zero-width certainty. A nonnormal outcome model needs
another uncertainty argument. If input numbers are enclosed rather than
exact, enclose the arm means and pooled variance as well before
projecting these endpoints.

Under a common effect parameter, report
\(\mathcal S=\mathcal S_O\cap\mathcal S_I\). The two component coverage
events need not be independent: the union bound gives at least
\(1-\alpha_O-\alpha_I\). Using outer numerical supersets preserves this
inclusion proof. An empty intersection is a retained
inconsistency/failure event, not an invitation to change the error
budget or delete a graph after seeing the result. If no observational
restriction is defensible, use \(\mathcal S_I\) alone under its own
experiment and target assumptions.

In the equal-law family, intervention changes the arm mean difference to
\(2\delta\tau\). Distinct effects are now distinguishable, although
several graphs can remain compatible. Identifying the decision-relevant
effect does not require identifying every edge. Randomizing a variable
that merely encourages the action is a different experiment: exclusion,
compliance and relevance then need their own argument.

\hypertarget{precision-costs-and-the-exact-remaining-scope}{%
\section{Precision, costs and the exact remaining
scope}\label{precision-costs-and-the-exact-remaining-scope}}

For a binary offer, take \(a_0=\delta=1/2\). A planning illustration
with \(m=200\) per arm, \(\alpha_I=.03\), a reported effect of twenty
dollars and \(S_p^2=100\) dollars squared gives \(b^2=9950/297\) and
half-width \(\sqrt{9950/297}\), approximately 5.788 dollars. The exact
reference uses a rational upward square-root enclosure. These are
supplied planning summaries, not observations from a completed trial.

For 3,000 eligible customers and fifteen dollars incremental
implementation cost per offer, the point scenario has fifteen thousand
dollars net benefit. Its conservative interval still includes a small
loss. Scaling an effect by population does not remove uncertainty, and
changing the intervention or customer population may invalidate
transport. A genuine next-experiment proposal should ask whether
resolving this decision is worth the experiment's cost, compare a
cheaper operational alternative, and include delayed outcomes,
noncompliance and treatment costs in the estimand. No measured bank ROI
is inferred from this illustration.

What is resolved is the mathematical route for one continuous scalar-lag
Gaussian family, a certified enclosure strategy, exact information
counterexamples and a separating intervention with an explicit finite
bound. What remains is a resource-profiled implementation and
prospectively registered study, tighter useful uncertainty, justified
input and model assumptions, actual interventions/measurements if the
proposal advances, and the general
unknown-lag-matrix/latent-state/non-Gaussian/heterogeneous-effect
problem. This argument establishes no general temporal-graph capability,
bank validation or independent acceptance. The computational and
information routes are concrete enough to design the next bounded
public/generated experiment. The following design analysis tests whether the displayed bounds could be informative at the predecessor's sample size and whether its qualification screen has adequate power. It keeps theorem validity, finite availability and a useful financial comparison as separate requirements.

\label{exec13:temporal-region-end}
~~~

~~~text
\section{When a valid temporal region is still an unsuitable study design}
\label{exec13:temporal-design-review}

The restricted continuous-lag argument separates mathematical coverage
from decision-useful precision. At the true common scalar lag, invariant
Gaussian initialization and independent innovations justify the projected
variance argument. A union over candidate lags need only retain the true
lag on that event; incorrect lags need not themselves produce independent
residuals. This is a useful restricted result. It does not establish a
confidence procedure for an arbitrary lag matrix, unknown order,
nonstationary hidden histories or a general learned partial ancestral
graph. These differences also determine whether a proposed numerical
study is worth conducting \cite{exec13_temporal_design}.

Consider the displayed Chebyshev construction with nine variance
directions, relative tolerance $t=1/4$ and observational error allocation
$\alpha_O=.02$. For a Gaussian sample variance with $\nu$ residual
degrees of freedom, the relative variance is $2/\nu$. Chebyshev and a
union bound therefore give
\[
 \Pr(\hbox{at least one relative deviation exceeds }t)
 \leq \frac{18}{\nu t^2}.
\]
To make this bound at most $.02$ requires $\nu\geq14{,}400$, or
$14{,}401$ transitions under the stated residual convention. With $240$
transitions and $239$ degrees of freedom, the untruncated expression is
approximately $1.20502$ and gives no useful coverage bound. The specified
whole-line fallback is honest about this limitation. Increasing the number
of Monte Carlo replications cannot make that per-request fallback
decision-useful \cite{exec13_temporal_design}.

A sharper pivot is a concrete development route. At the restricted true
lag, an exact chi-square variance pivot can replace the Chebyshev band
while preserving the continuous union. Ordinary development quantiles
at $239$ degrees of freedom and the nine-way $.02$ allocation give
variance multipliers approximately $[.76731,1.34533]$. These values
indicate potential improvement; they are not certified release endpoints.
The implementation must enclose the tail quantiles, observable inputs
and propagated covariance constraints, preserve conservative fallback
under timeout, and profile the continuous-lag calculation. Sampling a
lag grid or accepting a point optimizer's failure does not certify the
whole continuum \cite{exec13_temporal_design}.

The preserved finite-lag study also requires a precise reading. Its
persistent cell returned $507$ finite sets among $512$ requests, so
$507/512=.990234375$ passes the original raw finite-fraction threshold
of $.99$. The five whole-line answers remain visible, but do not justify
declaring that particular threshold failed. Weak relevance and the
unrestricted latent observational cell each returned zero finite sets
and still fail it. False exclusion retained the true graph in zero
requests, despite wide effect sets covering the numerical effect.
These findings concern different obligations: availability, effect
coverage, and scientific validity of the graph class
\cite{exec13_temporal_design}.

A lower confidence-bound rule for availability would be a different
criterion. At family error $.05$ across sixteen comparisons, the
one-sided lower bound for $507/512$ is about $.97130$; even $512/512$
gives about $.98880$. The historical study used a lower-bound screen
for coverage, but a raw fraction for finite availability. They should
not be interchanged retrospectively. A prospective successor may
justify different criteria, provided it states them before final data
and keeps the predecessor's outcomes under their original definitions
\cite{exec13_temporal_design}.

The coverage screen has its own design-power issue. With $512$
independent final requests per cell and error $.05/16$, at least $500$
successes are required for the exact one-sided lower bound to exceed
or equal $.95$. Exact binomial-tail calculations give per-cell passing
probabilities approximately $.001849$, $.234929$, $.770054$ and
$.997670$ when true coverage is respectively $.95$, $.97$, $.98$ and
$.99$. Thus a nominal $.95$ method is very unlikely to certify a
lower bound of $.95$ using this screen. More replications improve
discrimination above the boundary; they do not create high power at
the boundary while retaining the same error control. No product of
these per-cell powers is a joint power calculation without an
across-cell dependence argument \cite{exec13_temporal_design}.

Useful precision also requires an information distinction. In the
unrestricted equal-law latent family, every real effect can produce
the same observed temporal law. No numerical improvement can create
a uniformly finite informative effect set from those unchanged
observations. A direct assigned-action experiment changes the
information available. The proposed Gaussian episode argument assumes
independent episodes, a common transported effect and equal arm
variances. Adjacent records from one trajectory or encouragement in
place of the action require different assumptions and derivations
\cite{exec13_temporal_design}.

The supplied-summary example makes the planning distinction concrete.
At $200$ episodes per arm, reported effect $20$ dollars, reported
pooled variance $100$ dollars squared and the specified conservative
bound, the half-width is about $5.78806$ dollars. For $3{,}000$
eligible customers and an incremental cost of $15$ dollars per offer,
the net-benefit lower endpoint is approximately $-2{,}364.19$ dollars.
Holding the same reported variance and effect fixed, $268$ episodes
per arm first reduce the half-width below $5$ dollars, while $400$
give about $4.08761$. In a future experiment both the estimated effect
and pooled variance would vary. These are conditional arithmetic
screens, not prospective power or recommended bank sample sizes
\cite{exec13_temporal_design}.

The next restricted study therefore needs a certified executable and
input-enclosure policy, measured resource limits, a fixed final grid
of observational and added-information regimes, and an explicit
useful-width or loss criterion. A generated experiment can develop
these elements now. It should preserve strong, weak and zero relevance,
false exclusion, latent equal-law cases and all interval topologies.
Final seeds, replication budgets and stopping rules must follow the
design review. General hidden-state, non-Gaussian, selection and
heterogeneous-transport questions remain unresolved beyond the
restricted claim; public observations alone cannot decide among
observationally equivalent causal worlds
\cite{exec13_temporal_design}. The next chapter adds fitted prediction to the information budget. Its pilot certificates can control specified nuisance errors, but the same questions about weak identification, dependence and useful width still determine whether a larger experiment is justified.
\label{exec13:temporal-design-review-end}
~~~

~~~text
\section{From a frontier result to a banking capability}
\label{exec13:frontier-synthesis}

The inspected literature gives reasons to invest in better assistance, but it
does not yield a single ranking of causal systems. A system that extracts
relations from documents, a system that answers a supplied structural-model
question and a system that chooses a treatment policy may all receive a score
called causal accuracy. Their inputs, permissible assumptions and correct
outputs differ. A product proposal must recover these differences before it
uses an experimental result to select software or allocate development effort.

For this purpose, describe an evaluation claim by
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal E=(\mathcal T,\mathcal I,\mathcal A,\mathcal O,\mathcal B,\mathcal L),
 \label{exec13:frontier-claim}
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal T$ is the task distribution, $\mathcal I$ the information
supplied to the system, $\mathcal A$ its scientific assumptions, $\mathcal O$
the oracle or adjudication rule, $\mathcal B$ the tool, repair and human budget,
and $\mathcal L$ the loss used to score its output. This is a proposed
comparison vocabulary, not a theorem that these quantities are observed without
error. It asks a practical question: which parts of the published experiment
would remain the same in the proposed banking use? A change in any component
requires an argument or a new experiment before the original score can carry
the same interpretation.

For example, a graph provided in the prompt belongs to $\mathcal I$. Correctly
calculating a back-door formula from it tests conditional reasoning. Inferring
that graph from account and contact records is a different task with different
assumptions. Likewise, a human who repairs a mistaken join changes the combined
workflow's information and cost. The repaired answer can be valuable, but
attributing its correctness entirely to the model would misdescribe the product
being evaluated. This motivates an explicit comparison of the strongest
available alternatives rather than an agent-only leaderboard.

\subsection{Favorable and adverse results locate different opportunities}

The earliest broad frontier analysis treats language models as a channel for
domain knowledge and a possible aid to graph construction, critique and
robustness analysis. It also probes memorization and prompt sensitivity. These
observations motivate assistance with familiar concepts while warning that a
recognizable public dataset can supply information absent from a fresh bank
problem. Neither renaming a variable nor recalling a benchmark answer
establishes a new identification result \cite{v12_la_2305_00050}.

CLadder gives a more controlled formal task: generated questions from specified
causal structures with alternative verbalizations. That design isolates
important distinctions among association, intervention and counterfactual
reasoning. The supplied structure and generator, however, are part of the
experimental information. A bank workflow must also determine whether its
variable, treatment and population definitions support that structure. The
paper's remaining language-to-formal-tool problem is therefore central to the
proposed product, not an incidental user-interface issue
\cite{v12_la_2312_04350}.

Two comparisons show why the proposal should retain nonagent and smaller-model
baselines. In CausalEval, adding function calls improves the reported GPT-4o
CLADDER point score from 69 to 76 relative to ordinary chain-of-thought, but
reduces its e-CARE score from 90 to 73. These are outcomes from the named
historical configurations and samples. They demonstrate variation across tasks,
not a general tool penalty or benefit. In the inspected relation-extraction
study, the DDI F1 values for Single-Prompt C and PubMedBERT are 67.4 and 87.9.
The task concerns binary pairwise relations and the fine-tuned system receives
labeled training examples. The result supports considering supervised
extraction where the document domain and annotation budget are suitable; it
does not compare whole causal pipelines at equal total cost
\cite{exec13_census_causaleval,exec13_census_graph_validation}.

Retrieval has similarly mixed consequences. LACR combines background knowledge,
documents and optional numerical information. Its ASIA skeleton F1 falls from 1
to approximately .73 when documents are added, while other reported cases
benefit. Documents can add an applicable mechanism, introduce a conflicting
definition or repeat the same unsupported assertion. The scientific question
is which information changed and why it was relevant, rather than how many
documents entered the prompt \cite{v12_la_2402_15301}.

Auditing assumptions is another promising but restricted task. ARGUS assesses
the reported support for difference-in-differences assumptions, uses injected
flaws as local ground truth and explicitly avoids adjudicating causal truth.
Its five-paper human-label pilot and in-sample calibration do not establish
the error rate on a new collection of studies. A bank can use such an assistant
to find missing discussion or contradictory passages while keeping assignment,
parallel trends and measurement facts open to scientific assessment
\cite{v12_la_2609_30867}.

CausalCollab makes the longitudinal issue concrete. It defines an incremental
stylistic effect in sequential human--model interactions under explicit
positivity and sequential exchangeability premises. Its intervention mixes
text versions through a specified functional construction. A proposed
collections-message rewriting policy is not automatically that intervention:
it must define which actual messages are delivered, to whom, and after which
history. Model-generated counterfactual edits or outcome labels in an
evaluation remain generated evidence. The theorem's premises, the estimator's
approximation and the operational rewriting policy must be reviewed separately
\cite{exec13_census_collaboration}.

These results favor a portfolio of bounded roles. Template-driven formalization,
supervised extraction, retrieved evidence, formal graph algorithms and numerical
causal estimators can each be a baseline or component. A language model is
valuable where it reduces a measured bottleneck while preserving the meaning
of the task. Its presence is not a requirement for every component. The
architecture chapter develops how to enforce those boundaries in handoffs;
the question here is what evidence can justify selecting them.

\subsection{Task composition can reverse a published ranking}

Let $s_{ak}$ be method $a$'s success probability on task stratum $k$ and $w_k$
the proportion of eligible requests in that stratum, with $\sum_k w_k=1$.
Under a common success definition, the overall probability is
\begin{equation}
 S_a(w)=\sum_k w_k s_{ak}.
 \label{exec13:frontier-mixture}
\end{equation}
Even when every $s_{ak}$ is known, ranking methods requires $w$. A pooled score
from one benchmark mixture is not a mixture-free property of a system. When
the strata use incompatible outcomes, they should first remain separate rather
than be forced into this formula.

As an arithmetic illustration, use the two reported CausalEval point-score
pairs just discussed. Give CLADDER weight $w$ and e-CARE weight $1-w$. The
FunctionCall-minus-chain-of-thought difference is
\begin{equation}

mechanism-level dependence would be needed for an uncertainty calculation

an observed confounder set, the experiment cannot establish performance on

support and weights of the intended workload are unknown, report stratum-level

retries and report uncertainty at the level where the evaluation law supplies
independence. No variance estimate can be recovered from a published average
alone.

Suppose a request passes five stages: correct formulation $E_1$, observation
construction $E_2$, identification $E_3$, numerical execution $E_4$ and
reporting $E_5$. By the chain rule,
\begin{equation}
 P\!\left(\bigcap_{j=1}^5 E_j\right)
 =P(E_1)\prod_{j=2}^5P\!\left(E_j\mid\bigcap_{k<j}E_k\right).
 \label{exec13:frontier-chain}
\end{equation}
This identity does not require independent stages. It does require that each
factor refer to the same workflow and condition on all relevant preceding
successes. Marginal accuracies reported in five unrelated papers are not those
conditional probabilities. They may concern different data, expert information
and definitions of success. Multiplying them would manufacture an end-to-end
claim from incompatible experiments.

$(.96,.95,.90,.97,.98)$ yield $.78025248$. If these numbers are instead only
marginal success probabilities in a common request population, the joint
success is bounded by
\begin{equation}
 \max\!\left(0,1-\sum_{j=1}^5P(E_j^c)\right)
 \leq P\!\left(\bigcap_{j=1}^5 E_j\right)
 \leq\min_jP(E_j),
 \label{exec13:frontier-frechet}
\end{equation}
giving $.76$ to $.90$. The lower bound follows from the union bound for
failures; the upper follows because joint success implies every individual
success. Two authored populations of 100 requests attain the endpoints. In
one, failure sets of sizes 4, 5, 10, 3 and 2 are disjoint, leaving 76 complete
successes. In the other the failure sets are nested inside the ten largest
failures, leaving 90. Both have exactly the same stage marginals
\cite{exec13_frontier_exact}.

For the proposal, this means stage tests diagnose where to improve, while a
separate composition test measures the completed request. A syntactically
valid graph can propagate a wrong population through every later stage. A
correct estimator may precisely calculate the wrong target. Conversely,
several stages can fail on the same small subset, so adding their failure
counts overstates the number of affected requests. Record per-request
transitions and preserve the joint history needed to distinguish these cases.

\subsection{An answer key is another measured object}

Let $Z$ be a benchmark's recorded label, $T$ the scientifically intended answer
and $\widehat T$ the system output. For exact-match correctness,
\begin{equation}
 \left|1\{\widehat T=T\}-1\{\widehat T=Z\}\right|
 \leq1\{T\ne Z\}.
 \label{exec13:frontier-oracle}
\end{equation}
Whenever the label is correct, both correctness indicators are equal;
otherwise their difference is at most one. Taking expectations therefore
bounds the difference between scientific accuracy and label agreement by the
answer-key error probability. If a defensible upper bound is $\epsilon$,
reported agreement $a$ implies only
$\max(0,a-\epsilon)\leq P(\widehat T=T)\leq\min(1,a+\epsilon)$.
This statement assumes a meaningful common answer space; set-valued and
ambiguous tasks require an explicitly defined acceptance relation.

With agreement $.9$ and a stipulated label error $.1$, truth accuracy can be
$.8$ or 1 in two simple 100-case constructions. Errors in the key can either
conceal wrong outputs or penalize correct ones. This is an exact example, not
an allegation that any inspected benchmark has a ten-percent error rate

label rule and edge cases before using a score as product evidence. An
incorrect IV-to-population-ATE oracle cannot be repaired by making an agent
match that oracle more reliably. Likewise, model-generated labels and
model-generated answers can share errors even when their agreement is high.

is actually available: variable definitions, temporal admissibility, numerical
reproduction, sensitivity to assumptions and agreement with a justified design.

truth. For generated mechanisms, keep generator truth outside the analysis
interface and verify the reference calculation independently. An intentional
nonidentified case must accept appropriate refusal or a valid set, rather than
reward a precise but unjustified number.

\subsection{Causal uncertainty matters through the decision}

Return to a bank choosing an action $a\in\{0,1\}$. Let $V(a,M)$ be its net
value under causal model $M$. When the evidence retains class $\mathcal M$,
one way to display the decision consequence is regret
\begin{equation}
 R(a,M)=\max_{b\in\{0,1\}}V(b,M)-V(a,M).
 \label{exec13:frontier-regret}
\end{equation}
A model's graph accuracy and its decision regret can order systems differently.
An edge irrelevant to the intervention query may contribute graph loss without
changing the decision; a single uncertain edge on the treatment-outcome path
can reverse the preferred action. A credible evaluation reports both the
scientific object and the loss appropriate to the decision.

The architecture chapter gives two Gaussian worlds with an identical observed
distribution but effects of 0 and $1/2$. Rescale the effect to dollars so that
the two candidate gains from acting are 0 and 500, and set action cost to 250.
Not acting has value zero in both worlds. Acting has value $-250$ or 250.
Because the available information has the same law in both worlds, any
randomized rule acts with the same marginal probability $p$. Its expected
regrets are $250p$ and $250(1-p)$, so
\begin{equation}
 \inf_{0\leq p\leq1}\max\{250p,250(1-p)\}=125.
 \label{exec13:frontier-minimax}
\end{equation}
Equality holds at $p=1/2$; either deterministic rule has worst regret 250.
This restricted two-world calculation illustrates the cost of unresolved
information. It is not a recommendation to randomize real banking actions,
and the world class and loss are authored. It explains why a request for an
informative experiment can be more valuable than another confident narrative
\cite{exec13_architecture_exact,exec13_frontier_exact}.

The next experiment should target information capable of distinguishing models
with different preferred actions. A public simulator can check that the
proposed procedure chooses such an experiment under known truth. Public
observations can establish feasibility of a data pipeline or stress an
assumption. Neither proves that the same model class, costs or experiment
availability holds at a particular bank. Those transport questions belong to
a later study justified by the prototype's findings.

\subsection{A public-evidence portfolio with explicit transfer limits}

An affordable portfolio follows the four banking journeys already developed.
For funding, public panel and macro records support data-clock, aggregation
and reproducibility checks, while declared generated laws supply causal truth
for uncertainty tests. For servicing, a controlled history/action generator
tests positivity failures, feedback, policy definitions and the effect of
withheld state information. For discovery, known mechanisms should include
observationally equivalent graphs whose effects differ, so a confident single
graph is not always rewarded. For observation construction, public or generated
documents can test extraction and linkage while preserving the difference
between a faithfully extracted assertion and a true causal statement.

Each journey should compare a deterministic reference, an established
statistical route and the proposed assistance where its role is relevant.
Give all arms the same admissible information and account separately for
training labels, retrieval, tool use and human repair. Freeze mechanisms,
splits, budgets and scoring before final evaluation. A fixed held-out set can
be used for that registered comparison; repeated development against its
answers creates a new dependence and requires a new final evaluation design.
An unavailable or malformed answer remains in the assigned-request denominator.

The interpretation should stay attached to the actual evidence. A document
review can justify an integration candidate. A local exact example can expose
a failure mechanism. A controlled prototype study can compare methods under
its declared law. A live-model study adds evidence about a particular model
revision and task distribution. A bank study adds evidence about the target
process and its decision consequences. These are useful, different claims;
their separation allows the proposal to advance now without purchasing an
expensive experiment merely to satisfy a deployment gate.

The current research frontier therefore supports a concrete proposal: build
typed formulation and evidence assistance around an auditable causal core;
retain supervised, deterministic and formal alternatives; measure composition
and review costs; and direct new information acquisition toward consequential
ambiguity. It leaves open the reliability of language-mediated assumptions,
performance outside benchmark support, annotation validity and the economics
of sustained human review. Those are falsifiable next questions. A count of
papers, agents or completed reports does not answer them.
\label{exec13:frontier-synthesis-end}
~~~

~~~text
\section{From a frontier result to a banking capability}
\label{exec13:frontier-synthesis}

The inspected literature gives reasons to invest in better assistance, but it
does not yield a single ranking of causal systems. A system that extracts
relations from documents, a system that answers a supplied structural-model
question and a system that chooses a treatment policy may all receive a score
called causal accuracy. Their inputs, permissible assumptions and correct
outputs differ. A product proposal must recover these differences before it
uses an experimental result to select software or allocate development effort.

For this purpose, describe an evaluation claim by
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal E=(\mathcal T,\mathcal I,\mathcal A,\mathcal O,\mathcal B,\mathcal L),
 \label{exec13:frontier-claim}
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal T$ is the task distribution, $\mathcal I$ the information
supplied to the system, $\mathcal A$ its scientific assumptions, $\mathcal O$
the oracle or adjudication rule, $\mathcal B$ the tool, repair and human budget,
and $\mathcal L$ the loss used to score its output. This is a proposed
comparison vocabulary, not a theorem that these quantities are observed without
error. It asks a practical question: which parts of the published experiment
would remain the same in the proposed banking use? A change in any component
requires an argument or a new experiment before the original score can carry
the same interpretation.

For example, a graph provided in the prompt belongs to $\mathcal I$. Correctly
calculating a back-door formula from it tests conditional reasoning. Inferring
that graph from account and contact records is a different task with different
assumptions. Likewise, a human who repairs a mistaken join changes the combined
workflow's information and cost. The repaired answer can be valuable, but
attributing its correctness entirely to the model would misdescribe the product
being evaluated. This motivates an explicit comparison of the strongest
available alternatives rather than an agent-only leaderboard.

\subsection{Favorable and adverse results locate different opportunities}

The earliest broad frontier analysis treats language models as a channel for
domain knowledge and a possible aid to graph construction, critique and
robustness analysis. It also probes memorization and prompt sensitivity. These
observations motivate assistance with familiar concepts while warning that a
recognizable public dataset can supply information absent from a fresh bank
problem. Neither renaming a variable nor recalling a benchmark answer
establishes a new identification result \citep{v12_la_2305_00050}.

CLadder gives a more controlled formal task: generated questions from specified
causal structures with alternative verbalizations. That design isolates
important distinctions among association, intervention and counterfactual
reasoning. The supplied structure and generator, however, are part of the
experimental information. A bank workflow must also determine whether its
variable, treatment and population definitions support that structure. The
paper's remaining language-to-formal-tool problem is therefore central to the
proposed product, not an incidental user-interface issue
\citep{v12_la_2312_04350}.

Two comparisons show why the proposal should retain nonagent and smaller-model
baselines. In CausalEval, adding function calls improves the reported GPT-4o
CLADDER point score from 69 to 76 relative to ordinary chain-of-thought, but
reduces its e-CARE score from 90 to 73. These are outcomes from the named

study, the DDI F1 values for Single-Prompt C and PubMedBERT are 67.4 and 87.9.

extraction where the document domain and annotation budget are suitable; it
does not compare whole causal pipelines at equal total cost
\citep{exec13_census_causaleval,exec13_census_graph_validation}.

Retrieval has similarly mixed consequences. LACR combines background knowledge,

definition or repeat the same unsupported assertion. The scientific question
~~~

~~~text
\chapter{Using shared information to narrow uncertainty}
\label{integrated:weak_audit_sharpening}

\begin{quote}\small
Separate response bands retain uncertainty about customer identity but can
produce broad funding-value sets. Shared information in the two observed
candidate responses can narrow those sets by forming average and difference
scores before covariance estimation. A repaired 3,600-request study finds narrower transformed sets in
all 2,937 paired finite cases of six selected designs, without a general
dominance theorem. Weak audit information remains the limiting factor: 558/600
near-rank outputs are whole-line; even with eight times as many audit labels,
105/600 are whole-line and the finite transformed median width is about
USD 15.4 million. A pathwise observational-equivalence construction shows that
false exogeneity cannot be solved by interval algebra alone. The study uses synthetic populations; performance for a particular bank
requires evidence about its assignment and observation processes.
\end{quote}

\section{A sharper primitive region, with the same target}

The financial target, independent fourfold nuisance pilot, fixed monetary
weights, exact independent-binomial audit inversion and two-candidate origin
mixture are those in Chapter~\ref{integrated:weak_audit_projection}. Write the two observable
candidate monetary responses in stratum $s$ as $\mu_{s1},\mu_{s2}$, the
correct-assignment probability as $p_s$, and the focal/companion responses as
$\theta_s,\delta_s$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{integrated:weak_audit_sharpening:eq:transform}
 A_s=\tfrac12(\mu_{s1}+\mu_{s2})=\tfrac12(\theta_s+\delta_s),\quad
 D_s=\tfrac12(\mu_{s1}-\mu_{s2})=
     \tfrac12(2p_s-1)(\theta_s-\delta_s),\quad
 \theta_s=A_s+\frac{D_s}{2p_s-1}.
\end{equation}
The value remains $V=(\theta_0+\theta_1)/2-C$. At $p_s=1/2$, $D_s=0$ in
the observational law but the focal response is not identified separately
from its companion. Projecting a region for $(A_s,D_s,p_s)$ must retain this
structural ambiguity; no transformation creates audit truth.

The separate-band method constructed four bands for the candidate
responses. Those bands can discard shared candidate noise. The alternative transforms the two financially weighted residual outcomes to their half-sum
and half-difference \emph{before} estimating the four corresponding action
slopes and fixed-horizon calendar score variances. Equivalently, if
$\widehat\phi_{s1},\widehat\phi_{s2}$ are the observable influence scores,
the new scores are $(\widehat\phi_{s1}\pm\widehat\phi_{s2})/2$. Their marginal
variances therefore include the candidate cross-covariance. Four two-sided
normal bands share response error .025 by Bonferroni; two exact equal-tail
binomial audit intervals share audit error .025. The reported set is the exact
image of the resulting $(A_s,D_s,p_s)$ rectangles under
\eqref{integrated:weak_audit_sharpening:eq:transform}, combined with fixed half-stratum weights and direct
repricing cost. A valid joint primitive region still contains $V$ after
projection, but the new rectangle is not nested in the old candidate
rectangle. Neither finite-sample response coverage nor pointwise width
dominance is a theorem.

The covariance gain and its limit can be seen directly. If the candidate
slope covariance in one stratum has diagonal entries $v_1,v_2$ and
off-diagonal entry $c$, the transformed variances are
\begin{equation}\label{rel80:transformed-covariance}
 \operatorname{Var}(\widehat A_s)=\frac{v_1+v_2+2c}{4},\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(\widehat D_s)=\frac{v_1+v_2-2c}{4}.
\end{equation}
Positive shared noise therefore increases uncertainty about the average but
reduces uncertainty about the difference. Near rank zero the inverse magnifies
the difference, so that reduction can matter greatly. Negative covariance
reverses this allocation. Separate marginal bands do not retain all the
information in a joint confidence region even after transformation.

A dimensionless covariance illustration makes the lack of width dominance
explicit. Suppose the two candidate variances are one, their correlation is
$c=0.9$, and the audit probability is known to be $p_s=3/4$. These are
stipulated values for an algebraic comparison, not estimates from the funding
experiment. With the same normal critical value $z$, candidate-coordinate
bands give a projected half-width $2z$. Transformed bands give
$z(\sqrt{0.95}+2\sqrt{0.05})\simeq1.422z$, since the focal response is the
average plus twice the difference. If the correlation is instead $c=-0.9$,
the transformed half-width is
$z(\sqrt{0.05}+2\sqrt{0.95})\simeq2.173z$, wider than the candidate result.
Both covariance matrices are positive definite. The observed narrowing in
the registered study is consequently a property of those paired requests,
not a consequence of the coordinate change alone. Audit uncertainty adds
another projection step and cannot restore a universal width ordering.

The normal/dependent-calendar bands use the conditional growing-pilot rate
and score assumptions developed in Sections~\ref{v9:pilot} and~\ref{v9:covariance}. The inspected
primary DML paper establishes the orthogonal-score/rate premise in its own
iid setting, not this project's dependent result \cite{dml2018}. The
inspected Newey--West 1986 working paper supports a Bartlett covariance
alternative, not finite-sample validity of this untapered fixed-horizon
scalar score \cite{newey1986}. Exactness applies only to the binomial audit
component. Numerical qualification refuses nonpositive/nonfinite response
variance and a difference-score variance at most
$(8\epsilon_{\rm machine})^2$ times its positive average-score variance.
That last guard prevents floating-point roundoff from turning a deterministic
zero difference into a falsely precise normal band.

\section{Registration, preserved failure and fresh comparison}

The original set's large widths motivated this separate plan, which was
registered before the follow-up's final draws. Its first 3,600 requests are
retained as \emph{exploratory and not qualified}. An adversarial fixture with
identical candidate outcomes exposed an inadequate zero-variance guard: the
fitted difference-score variance was numerically positive, roughly
$2\times10^{-33}$ of the average-score variance. The initial check had
exercised an exactly zero accumulator but failed to require refusal for this
fitted fixture. The complete initial code, specification, check receipt,
journal and summary were archived and read back before repair. The scale-aware
guard and a strengthened refusal check were registered before a new 3,600-draw
comparison with a fresh seed. The initial results were not promoted or
quietly hash-replaced.

The qualified comparison holds each evaluation history, 4,800-date independent
pilot and audit counts fixed across two methods: the candidate-response
rectangle and the transformed average/difference rectangle. Five 1,200-date
stress laws are inherited; a sixth keeps the near-rank law but uses 12,800
instead of 1,600 representative audit labels \emph{per stratum}. All have
600 fresh requests, no early stopping, the same fourfold pilot training and
the same error allocation. Numerical checks compare transformed slopes and
lag covariance with an independent dense four-coordinate calculation; its
maximum scaled variance difference was $1.65\times10^{-15}$. Whole-line,
disconnected and empty rank-one geometry, the repaired degenerate fixture and
a pathwise causal counterexample were checked separately. A read-only journal
reconstruction verifies all 3,600 request identities, both primitive bands,
audit intervals, financial sets, coverage counts and paired finite widths.

fell from USD 3.387 million to USD 2.889 million. All four selected valid-law
cells and the higher-audit cell showed 600/600 synthetic coverage for both
sets; six-cell simultaneous Monte Carlo intervals and individual counts are
saved. This is evidence about fixed simulators, not a bank coverage guarantee.

sets. Only 42 were finite; their respective median widths were roughly
USD 52.0 million and USD 16.2 million. Increasing audits eightfold raised
finite availability to 495/600, but 105/600 sets still spanned the whole line.
Among the 495 paired finite cases, transformed median width was about
USD 15.4 million, versus USD 47.8 million for the candidate rectangle. Audit
information can improve availability without producing an actionable bank
interval; its acquisition cost and decision threshold are unknown.

Under false exogeneity, candidate and transformed sets covered respectively
597/600 and 561/600 of the original causal target. Tightening lost coverage
in 36 paired requests and gained none. The second fraction is 0.935, but no
coverage theorem applies when the action innovation restriction is false.
The high first fraction is equally incapable of verifying that restriction.

\section{Why exogeneity is an information problem}

The failure is not merely an interval formula. Let
$m(W_t)=.5W_t+.2(W_t^2-1)$, $A_t=m(W_t)+e_t$, and let $g(W_t)$ be an
otherwise unknown baseline balance response. Consider the structural law
\begin{equation}\label{integrated:weak_audit_sharpening:eq:confounded}
 B_t=\rho B_{t-1}+\beta A_t+g(W_t)
      +\sigma\{c e_t+\sqrt{1-c^2}\,z_t\}+\xi_t,
\end{equation}
with independent centered $e_t,z_t,\xi_t$ before the displayed shared term.
Define a second law with independent structural error but
\begin{equation}
 \beta'=\beta+\sigma c,\qquad
 g'(W)=g(W)-\sigma c\,m(W),\qquad
 B'_t=\rho B'_{t-1}+\beta'A_t+g'(W_t)
       +\sigma\sqrt{1-c^2}\,z_t+\xi_t.
\end{equation}
Because $A_t-m(W_t)=e_t$, the two observed balance recursions are
identical path by path for the same initial balance and exogenous draws.
The candidate swaps, independent audit labels and any statistic of the
observed histories are therefore identical as well. Yet under a one-month
intervention on $A_t$, the first law has response $\beta\rho^h$ and the
second $(\beta+\sigma c)\rho^h$. At the registered false-law values
$\sigma=2$, $c=.5$, their one-unit response coefficients differ by 1 and
the fixed financial target differs by about USD 387,575. A direct coupled
numerical witness reproduced identical observed paths to floating precision.

This is an identification counterexample for a class permitting the adjusted
nuisance mean $g'$. An externally known $g$, randomized action variation,
valid instrument or other justified scientific restriction could separate
the laws. More audit labels about candidate identity or a narrower confidence
box alone cannot. Numeric declarations of exogeneity are assertions to be
validated by assignment and source owners, not tests performed by the API.

\section{Decision and delivery boundaries}

The transformed region is a locally reproducible way to use covariance that
the first box omitted. Its precision may still be inadequate for a financial decision: whole-line
sets and multi-million-dollar finite widths remain under weak audit rank,
even in the higher-audit cell. The observational counterexample isolates a separate identification limit that requires new causal information. Any next
statistical refinement must be derived, preregistered and tested on fresh
adverse laws, reporting all-request coverage and finite decision precision.

The bank has not supplied an acceptable value-width threshold, representative
history/audit prices, authentic assignment truth, independent reviewers,
target-platform service evidence or an adopted interface. Bank use still requires independent review and evidence that the
method applies to the institution and decision being considered. The next chapter changes the observation itself: selected audits reveal the focal outcome history rather than only whether a candidate assignment is correct. This can resolve the identity ambiguity, while the exogeneity counterexample continues to apply. Its benefit must therefore be compared with both the new label requirements and the remaining uncertainty.

\section*{Sources and reproducibility}

The transformation, repaired numerical check, observational example,
registered study and financial interpretation are project contributions.
The cited sources support only the technical results attributed to them.
The original failed run and the repaired comparison remain available with
the specification and code. The literature cutoff is 7 October 2026.
~~~
