\(E[g(Y(1))-g(Y(0))]\) is a target defined by that particular rule.
Searching over rules using the same treatment assignments and documents
later used for effect estimation can induce dependence and select
apparent effects. Their proposed separation of codebook discovery from
effect estimation addresses that problem, while their text-as-treatment
discussion imposes a further sufficiency restriction on the
representation. \citep{exec13_census_texts}

For a language-based measurement pipeline, the rule includes the model
version, prompt, retrieval corpus, preprocessing, extraction schema and
response aggregation. Freezing only a classifier filename while changing
the prompt after reading the effect estimates does not freeze \(g\). The
prototype should develop the rule on a designated development set,
record its identity, and evaluate it on held-out units. If several calls
concern one customer or conversation, those calls should remain together
in the split. This is a proposed implementation of the separation
principle, not a claim that sample splitting alone ensures valid
inference for dependent histories.

The held-out review asks whether the labels retain their intended
meaning, whether extraction errors differ by treatment and outcome, and
whether missing documents have a defensible observation model. It must
preserve negative findings. Rewriting the measurement rule to rescue a
disappointing effect requires a new evaluation set or an explicitly
exploratory analysis. Neither a fixed rule nor a held-out set supplies
unmeasured assignment information or repairs a post-treatment adjustment
error.

\hypertarget{formulate-competing-explanations-before-selecting-a-diagram}{%
\subsubsection{Formulate competing explanations before selecting a
diagram}\label{formulate-competing-explanations-before-selecting-a-diagram}}

Geraldo Bastías proposes building diagrams from the assumptions actually
used in a study, preserving several models where the assumptions do not
determine one. His workflow checks identification within each model,
derives observable implications, and distinguishes missing relationships
from missing variables. This is a methodological contribution to diagram
review, not an implemented LLM discovery algorithm. It supports an
assistant that makes assumptions inspectable rather than treating a
familiar design label as sufficient. \citep{exec13_census_credible}

For the servicing example, a short initial brief can leave open whether
distress caused the plan assignment, whether a later complaint caused a
note to be recorded, and whether the proposed outcome is arrears, loss
or customer welfare. The assistant should construct separate compatible
diagrams and show how each changes adjustment or identification. It can
check timing contradictions and derive conditional-independence
implications. Passing those checks does not establish that an omitted
common cause is absent. Where the diagrams imply different effects, the
useful output is the unresolved choice and the evidence that could
distinguish it.

These requirements permit immediate public and generated evaluation. A
public document corpus can supply realistic language, while a declared
generator supplies assignment, document timing, measurement error and
outcome truth. Simple extraction and fixed numerical workflows provide
baselines. The evaluation must vary mechanisms that are difficult for
the chosen extractor, including selective note availability and notes
written after treatment. Keith and colleagues specifically caution that
authors can choose semi-synthetic confounders their own method can
easily recover. Freezing adverse mechanisms and separating their
construction from final method selection addresses that concern more
directly than adding familiar domain vocabulary to a favorable
simulation. \citep{exec13_census_text_review_arxiv}

\label{exec13:census-measurement-end}

\section{A hidden-state planner consumes a model; it does not identify one}
\label{exec23:pomdppy-scope}
Servicing decisions may depend on financial distress that is only partially
observed through payments, calls and other signals. POMDP-Py offers useful
interfaces for describing such states, transitions, observations, rewards,
beliefs and online planners. The inspected revision, dated 28 October 2025,
declares version 1.3.5.1. Thirteen authenticated source/declaration files cover
selected histogram and particle beliefs, POUCT/POMCP planning, finite policy
trees and an alternative small-state value routine. This is a reference for
proposed architecture and numerical qualification. Supplied-model planning
does not establish that a latent banking model is identified, that its observation
law is truthful, or that the value of a learned optimal policy has a calibrated
confidence interval. \cite{exec23_pomdppy_sources}

\subsection{Belief and value require a declared information experiment}
\label{exec23:pomdppy-belief}
Let $S_t$ be the latent state, $A_t$ the chosen action, $O_{t+1}$ the subsequent
observation and $b_t(s)$ the posterior state probability given available
history. For supplied transition and observation laws $T(s'\mid s,a)$ and
$L(o\mid s',a)$, Bayes' rule gives
\[
 \widetilde b_{t+1}(s')=L(o\mid s',a)\sum_sT(s'\mid s,a)b_t(s),
 \qquad b_{t+1}(s')=\frac{\widetilde b_{t+1}(s')}
 {\sum_u\widetilde b_{t+1}(u)}.
\]
The denominator is the probability of the new observation under the supplied
model. It must be positive for this conditional update. A service cannot
replace a zero denominator with an arbitrary posterior and claim the same
information experiment. Model estimation, hidden-state identification,
distributional uncertainty and approximation error are separate from this
conditional algebra.

An exact banking example shows what is at stake. Suppose distress has prior
probability $1/4$. A diagnostic signal is positive with probability $3/4$ under
distress and $1/4$ otherwise. The positive-signal probability is $3/8$, and
posterior distress probabilities are $1/2$ after a positive signal and $1/10$
after a negative one. A rescue action pays a net $35$ dollars in distress and
loses $15$ otherwise; declining has value zero. Acting without information has
value $-5/2$. Under the supplied sensor, acting only after a positive signal
gives expected value $15/4$ before a two-dollar diagnostic cost, hence net
$7/4$. If the actual signal instead has probability $1/2$ in either state,
the same proposed rule has net $-13/4$. A more accurate search of the wrong
sensor model cannot repair this gap. All values are stipulated, exactly
enumerated project examples rather than measured bank or package results.
\cite{exec23_pomdppy_reference}

The histogram update follows the displayed transition-observation product and
allows a static-transition shortcut or a supplied next-state set. It normalizes
only when total mass is positive; an impossible observation therefore leaves
an all-zero histogram. The histogram constructor checks for a dictionary, not
a positive normalized probability law. Restricting the next-state set also
changes what is normalized: if the predicted masses are $1/5$ on distress and
$4/5$ on healthy but only healthy is enumerated, the returned normalized belief
places mass one on healthy. Such restriction is valid only if the discarded
mass is truly impossible or the changed conditioning target is intended.
The adapter must report unsupported observations and omitted support explicitly.
\cite{exec23_pomdppy_sources,exec23_pomdppy_reference}

Particle updating has different failure semantics. The explicit updater samples
a transition and observation from each current particle, retains exact
observation matches, and reinvigorates the survivors. An empty set raises
particle deprivation; otherwise resampling and an optional state transform
restore the requested count. Repeating survivors does not create new
independent evidence, and a transform changes the approximation law unless
justified. Exact observation equality also needs a declared discrete or
otherwise appropriate observation representation. The source marks the explicit
updater as untested. POMCP performs a related tree-based update and raises
deprivation when an anticipated observation child is absent. History, tree and
belief updates must be coordinated, with no double update or invented recovery
posterior. \cite{exec23_pomdppy_sources}

The weighted representation needs its own identity fixture. Its probability
query averages weights among repeated equal values before normalization,
whereas its sampling method weights every entry. For entries $(D,1),(D,1),(H,1)$,
the query gives probability $1/2$ to $D$, while entry-weighted sampling gives
$2/3$. This is a documented average-weight convention in one path and a
different sampling construction in the other; an adapter must not silently
treat them as a single empirical measure. Ordinary unweighted Particles
overrides the histogram and sampling methods and gives frequency $2/3$ in
this example. The defect must therefore not be attributed indiscriminately to
all particle classes. \cite{exec23_pomdppy_sources,exec23_pomdppy_reference}

\subsection{Planning budgets and reward clocks need native qualification}
\label{exec23:pomdppy-planning}
POUCT samples belief states, explores action-observation branches, and returns
the action with the highest current tree value. A positive simulation count
takes precedence over the time budget in the inspected stopping rule; when
both defaults are negative, a one-second planning duration is selected.
Elapsed-time and completed-simulation fields are useful observations, not
accuracy certificates. The stop test runs between simulations. It cannot
interrupt a single nonterminating model or rollout call. The adapter therefore
needs an independently enforced execution deadline and a durable refusal result.
Random sources, model delegates, action ordering, initial values and planning
history must be recorded for replay. \cite{exec23_pomdppy_sources}

A concrete progress edge appears with options that consume no primitive steps.
The model sampler returns duration zero when an option is not initiable.
The tree simulation branch explicitly handles zero duration, but the selected
rollout loop only adds duration to depth and repeats while depth is below its
limit. Repeatedly selecting such an option can leave depth unchanged forever.
This is a static control-flow witness, not an executed hang. Similarly, the
tree recursion stops at depth greater than the limit while rollout uses depth
strictly less than the limit. Horizon-zero, horizon-one, terminal and option
fixtures must establish the actual reward count rather than infer it from a
parameter name. \cite{exec23_pomdppy_sources,exec23_pomdppy_reference}

Option rewards introduce a second clock. The general sampler accepts an
internal discount argument defaulting to one; the selected POUCT calls omit
that argument, then discount the continuation by $\gamma^{\text{duration}}$.
For a two-step option with rewards two and eight dollars, continuation value
twenty and $\gamma=1/2$, the resulting expression is $2+8+(1/2)^2 20=15$.
Applying the primitive-step discount throughout gives
$2+(1/2)8+(1/2)^2 20=11$. Either a macro-action reward convention or a
primitive-step convention can be declared, but they are different targets.
The adapter must bind the chosen convention and test model delegates, rather
than silently adjusting rewards after planning.
\cite{exec23_pomdppy_sources,exec23_pomdppy_reference}

The source black-box interface documents a three-component sample, while the
general sampler's contract and selected planner unpack four components,
including duration. That boundary needs an explicit adapter and conformance
test. The reward model permits stochastic sampling; a call to its sample method
is not automatically the expected reward needed by an exact dynamic program.
The small-state value routine explicitly describes deterministic rewards, and
its qualification must preserve that restriction or supply justified reward
expectations. \cite{exec23_pomdppy_sources}

\subsection{Exact references must be checked against each other}
\label{exec23:pomdppy-decision}
The policy-tree value-iteration source warns of unpruned tree growth and is
restricted to enumerable actions, states and observations. Its recurrence uses
$\gamma^{\text{depth}}$ when multiplying a child value. At three stages with a
single state/action/observation, deterministic reward one and $\gamma=1/2$, that
expression yields $1+\gamma(1+\gamma^2)=13/8$. The ordinary one-step Bellman
recurrence yields $1+\gamma+\gamma^2=7/4$. The separate Python value routine
multiplies each next-horizon expectation by one factor of gamma and provides
a useful comparison target under its declared finite deterministic regime.
Neither routine has been executed here. Source-to-oracle tests must resolve
the recurrence and horizon semantics before either is labelled an exact
product backend. \cite{exec23_pomdppy_sources,exec23_pomdppy_reference}

The proposal disposition is \emph{reference}. Model/agent/planner separation
and the explicit supplied-model computations are valuable design examples.
An isolated original Python/Cython worker is a candidate after the named belief,
clock, horizon, timeout and protocol defects are reviewed and native fixtures
pass. Full adoption would include substantially more model and planner behavior
than this profile covers. Reimplementing the planner family in R, Java or C++
would also duplicate stochastic-state, belief and maintenance obligations with
no measured benefit yet demonstrated. Independent finite-state oracles should
remain independent, not be relabelled ports of the complete library.

The pinned artifact contains MIT license text and names its author. Its build
requires setuptools, wheel and Cython at least 3.0.8, and selected runtime
dependencies include NumPy, SciPy and tqdm. These are declarations, not a
locked compiler/ABI/runtime or transitive rights clearance. An executable worker
must bind those identities, its imported native binaries and model code. The
scientific owner must justify state, observation and intervention meaning; the
maintainer must resolve actual numerical and lifecycle contracts; the operator
must measure search, conversion, memory and recovery cost.
\cite{exec23_pomdppy_sources}

A proposed library/CLI/MCP request should bind model revision, initial belief,
state/action/observation vocabularies, decision history, reward and option clocks,
horizon, random seeds and both simulation and wall-time limits. The response
must distinguish proposed action, approximate supplied-model value, diagnostics,
deprivation or timeout, and any separately justified uncertainty statement.
An LLM can help articulate candidate states and diagrams, but a fluent
description cannot authenticate the latent observation law. Public qualification
can use exact finite models with deliberately wrong sensors, impossible signals,
missing support, duplicate particles, noninitiable options, changed histories
and hand-enumerated horizons. Those tests can motivate a prototype while leaving
bank identification, general POMDP uncertainty and institutional adoption open.

\section{SMILE and GeNIe: a commercial engine is not a causal evidence contract}
\label{sec:exec24-smile-reuse}

A banking team can use an interactive graphical-model environment to discuss
a lending or servicing decision, and later wish to run the agreed model in
a service. BayesFusion's GeNIe and SMILE address related parts of that
workflow. They should be compared as a connected offering without being
counted as two independent inference engines. The proposal makes two reuse
choices: one for the compiled SMILE engine and its wrappers, and one for the
GeNIe-centered modeling environment and its route to that engine. Both are
reference decisions with conditional integration routes, not acquired
entitlements or verified deployments \cite{exec13_smile_intro,
exec13_smile_license,exec24_smile_choice}.

\subsection{What the retained official documentation establishes}
The retained SMILE introduction declares manual version 2.2.4.R1, built on
27 April 2024; the retained GeNIe identity page declares 5.0.R2, built on
23 November 2024. The primary pages were acquired later and are mutable.
Those declarations identify the inspected manual families; they do not
prove that every byte was served at the 7 October 2026 research cutoff,
or that these are the current installed versions. The previous official
source audits, local bytes and acquisition records remain preserved
\cite{exec13_smile_intro,exec13_genie_readme,exec24_smile_choice}.

The SMILE introduction describes a proprietary C++ library distributed in
compiled form, with Java, Python, R, .NET and COM wrappers. Its C++ manual
expressly leaves most wrapper interoperability to separate documentation.
It describes SMILE as GeNIe's API and relates elementary GUI operations to
engine calls. That relationship supports a shared vendor comparison. It
does not prove exact wrapper-version parity, lossless GUI-to-service export,
or identical interruption, error and state-lifetime behavior across languages
\cite{exec13_smile_intro}.

The inspected licensing page distinguishes academic and commercial
development licenses from server and end-user deployment licenses. It
describes personalized license-key headers and points to the vendor for
terms and pricing. Consequently, an academic evaluation, desktop modeling
session or development license is not evidence of entitlement for a banking
server or redistributed application. The proposal accepts no agreement,
uses no license key and assumes no price. Rights and supported artifact
profiles are inputs to a later controlled integration decision
\cite{exec13_smile_license,exec24_smile_choice}.

\subsection{Discovery output must retain unresolved orientation}
The official SMILE PC interface learns into a \texttt{DSL\_pattern}, with
one node per dataset variable. Its documented controls include a maximum
adjacency, a significance threshold and background knowledge. A successful
call establishes completion under that documented interface; it does not
establish the truth of causal assumptions, the sufficiency of the sample,
or identification of a desired business intervention
\cite{exec13_smile_pc,exec24_smile_choice}.

The inspected pattern reference lists no-edge, undirected and directed edge
types, a conversion to a DAG, and conversion to a network using dataset
variables and outcomes. That conversion assumes matching dataset and
pattern order. The GeNIe pattern editor separately documents graphical
marks and a Create DAG action that randomly chooses directions to produce
an acyclic graph. The GUI description and the narrower inspected API edge
enumeration must not be equated automatically with a standard CPDAG or PAG
representation. Their exact endpoint mapping remains a public conformance
question; an apparent double arrow in a picture is not enough evidence
for a particular latent-confounding interpretation
\cite{exec13_smile_pattern,exec13_genie_pattern,exec24_smile_choice}.

Consider an exact authored binary distribution with
\[
 p(A=0,Y=0)=p(A=1,Y=1)=\frac25,\qquad
 p(A=0,Y=1)=p(A=1,Y=0)=\frac1{10}.
\]
One structural model has a fair action $A$ causing $Y$, with success
probabilities $1/5$ and $4/5$ under actions zero and one. Its intervention
effect is $3/5$. Another has fair $Y$ causing the observed assignment $A$,
with the same conditional agreement probability $4/5$. It generates exactly
the same observed table, but changing $A$ has zero effect on $Y$.
These are two compatible causal explanations, not a claim that they exhaust
the unrestricted identified set. Choosing a DAG orientation selects one
explanation; it does not make the observational evidence distinguish them
\cite{exec24_smile_choice}.

For a hypothetical 2,000-account campaign worth 100 USD per incremental
success and costing 40,000 USD, these two effects imply incremental net
values of 80,000 and minus 40,000 USD. The 120,000 USD difference arises
before any numerical solver error. An agent drafting a diagram must retain
the orientation ambiguity, ask what substantive or experimental information
could resolve it, and record any imposed direction as an assumption.
Generating a visually complete network is not causal validation
\cite{exec24_smile_choice}.

\subsection{Structure conversion and parameter estimation are distinct}
The PC reference says that conversion of its output to a network produces
uniform probability distributions. The GeNIe pattern editor likewise
distinguishes learning parameters from creating only a structure, whose
tables are initially uniform. For a binary outcome, a row $(1/2,1/2)$ can
therefore be an initialization convention rather than an estimated bank
response. A wrapper must carry a parameter-status field and the data or
elicitation provenance for every table. It must refuse a decision-value
claim when a structural scaffold is presented as a fitted model
\cite{exec13_smile_pc,exec13_genie_pattern,exec24_smile_choice}.

This distinction also informs integration with language-model agents.
An agent can propose node labels, information times, candidate edges and
elicitation questions, and can help translate a business objective into a
query. The proposed system must keep those suggestions separate from

\chapter{Variables, diagrams and justified disagreement}
\label{la:diagrams}

The preceding chapter established what definitions and fallible evidence can
contribute. Here those objects enter a reviewable diagram. The argument first
separates graph classes, premises and retrieval outcomes, then develops exact
proxy, collider, clock and disagreement examples. The ontology comparison
connects the diagram to implementable treatment versions and source records.
The final restrictions study follows a premise through both graph and effect
sets, showing why a smaller graph class need not settle the decision.

\section{From vocabulary to measured variables}

A useful causal diagram begins with variables whose meanings can survive
contact with data. A business glossary may contain ``risk,'' ``relationship''
and ``engagement,'' while a dataset contains a risk-score vintage, a set of
linked accounts and an observed click. Those are related concepts, but they
are not interchangeable causal variables. An assistant can propose mappings,
detect inconsistent names and assemble definitions. Each proposed mapping
still needs an operational meaning, a unit and an information clock.

OntoLearner offers relevant modular ideas for ontology loading, typing,
taxonomy and relation-learning tasks. The inspected paper reports
domain-dependent errors and retrieval failures. Its relation-learning
capability is not a guarantee that a relation is causal, or that a concept
has a valid measured proxy in the bank. Ontology alignment should therefore
precede and inform graph construction without being silently promoted into
causal identification. \cite{v12_la_2607_01977}

For example, ``customer owns account'' may describe a legal relation,
``records share an identifier'' an administrative relation, and ``records
have a high linkage score'' a model output. If ownership affects both offer
eligibility and repayment behavior, substituting the linkage score for
ownership leaves a measurement problem. Adding an arrow from the score to
repayment does not resolve it. The diagram should distinguish latent
ownership, observed records, the linkage procedure and sample selection.

Likewise, an ordinal description such as ``high influence'' cannot be used
as an effect size without a scale. An assistant's rating of a proposed edge
may express a preference among textual explanations. It is not automatically
a probability that the edge is present, a posterior over graphs, or a
confidence level. A typed diagram can retain such a rating as explicitly
uncalibrated metadata while refusing to use it as scientific evidence.

\section{What an edge asserts}

An edge proposal should state more than two variable names. The endpoint
marks identify the proposed graphical object. A source and inspected anchor
state what supports the proposal. A scope describes the population, period
and intervention to which that evidence applies. A counterevidence record
states whether contrary evidence was found, absent in the inspected material,
or not successfully searched. A review disposition records acceptance as a
premise, rejection, or unresolved status.

These fields serve different purposes. A source can be authentic but
inapplicable to the current banking action. A study can concern a different
population or a different definition of treatment. A plausible timing argument
can constrain direction without establishing that any causal connection
exists. The assistant should make the supported proposition as narrow as
the evidence warrants and retain the reasons for disagreement.

CausalChat supplies an example of interactive model development: the inspected
paper combines optional CPDAG discovery, model suggestions, graph editing
and structural-equation coefficient updates. Its prompts use ordinal
causal-significance ratings and ask for possible confounders and mediators.
These are useful interaction ideas. The paper's expert feedback also raises
missing citations and uncertainty about the quality of scientific evidence
provided by the model. A coefficient update after adding an edge cannot
establish that the edge itself is true. \cite{v12_la_2410_14146}

The proposed banking workflow retains the interaction but changes the
scientific handoff. An accepted premise is labeled as a premise with a
responsible review, not as a truth certified by the model. A model proposal
alone cannot remove an observationally compatible graph alternative. The
tool responsible for formal identification receives the complete reviewed
graph object and its restrictions, rather than a picture whose uncertainty
has disappeared in editing.

\section{Graph classes and collections of candidate models}

A CPDAG or PAG is a structured representation with its own interpretation.
A list of proposed DAGs is another object. A collection of edges marked
``possible'' is not automatically an enumeration of every combination of
those edges. Confusing these representations can silently exclude models
or include incompatible ones.

The project contract preserves a CPDAG or PAG directly when that is the
appropriate object, including circle endpoints. It also permits explicitly
listed candidate models. An edge marked possible within a candidate describes
the evidence status of that candidate's edge; it does not make all optional
edge combinations an exhaustive graph class. Downstream calculations must
know which interpretation applies.

An exact binary example shows the consequence of retaining alternatives.
In model \(F\), a binary offer \(A\) is Bernoulli with probability one half,
and response \(Y\) equals \(A\) with probability \(0.9\). In model \(R\),
\(Y\) is Bernoulli with probability one half, and \(A\) equals \(Y\) with
probability \(0.9\). Both models produce
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 &Y=0&Y=1\\\hline
A=0&9/20&1/20\\
A=1&1/20&9/20
\end{array}.
\]
In \(F\), setting \(A\) from zero to one changes \(E[Y]\) by \(0.8\).
In \(R\), intervening on the equation for \(A\) leaves \(Y\) unchanged.
The two compatible constructions therefore imply the effect candidates
\(\{0,0.8\}\). A directional suggestion favoring \(F\) does not provide
new identifying information unless its underlying premise is independently
justified. These finite calculations are project constructions, not a
calibrated confidence set for a learned graph.

More generally, for a declared graph class \(\mathcal G\), one relevant
downstream object is
\begin{equation}
 \Theta(P,Q,\mathcal G)=\bigcup_{G\in\mathcal G}\Theta_G(P,Q),
 \label{la:graph-union}
\end{equation}
where \(\Theta_G(P,Q)\) contains effects compatible with distribution \(P\),
question \(Q\) and the model restrictions for \(G\). A nonidentified member
can make the union broad. A list of estimated points is not automatically
the whole union, and graph-selection uncertainty cannot be replaced with
ordinary coefficient uncertainty after selecting one member.

Equation~\eqref{la:graph-union} also clarifies what a disagreement review
should resolve. If two experts differ only on an edge that leaves the target
functional unchanged, that disagreement may be immaterial for the current
decision while still mattering for another target. If their graphs imply
different effect signs or feasibility, the conflict is decision-relevant.
The assistant can identify that consequence and prioritize the required
evidence. It should not average expert preferences into an unexplained graph.

\section{Retrieval failure and scientific disagreement}

An evidence assistant can fail to find a passage because the document is
unavailable, parsing failed, the query was poor, the retriever missed it, or
the passage is absent from the inspected document. These cases support
different statements. ``No passage was retrieved'' cannot by itself become
``the authors ignored the assumption,'' and neither statement establishes
that the assumption is false in the population.

The inspected ARGUS paper makes this distinction especially useful. It
audits reported evidence concerning DiD identifying assumptions and does
not claim to adjudicate causal truth. Its synthetic flaw study exhibits a
retrieval/abstention tradeoff, and its small human-label pilot reports an
in-sample calibration change that was not tested on unseen papers. These
observations motivate a banking evidence state that is separate from a
scientific risk judgment. \cite{v12_la_2609_30867}

The proposed record contains the source bytes, the query or retrieval
configuration, inspected anchors and the resulting narrow claim. If evidence
is missing, it records the missing step. If two sources conflict, it records
their populations, dates and definitions before treating the conflict as
substantive. The analyst can then determine whether the sources concern
different regimes or whether a genuine contradiction remains.

This process does not require pretending that every edge has a published
study behind it. Some causal premises depend on institutional facts: which
system sets a rate, when a policy becomes visible, how an audit was selected,
or which identifier establishes ownership. Those facts need an accountable
owner and authentic records. Literature retrieval can help formulate the
questions, but it cannot supply an institution's missing assignment truth.

\section{A reviewable editing sequence}

The proposed interaction starts with a question and variable definitions,
then records diagram alternatives. Each edit changes a declared object:
add or remove a variable, refine a clock, replace a proxy, propose an endpoint,
or accept a restriction. The edit retains its predecessor identity and
reason. A reviewer can therefore see whether an apparent improvement in
fit came from a new assumption, a different target, or an actual correction
of an error.

Formal checks can reject a directed cycle in a DAG, impossible declared
time order or an explicitly forbidden direction. They can flag mediator,
collider or common-ancestor patterns in the supported representation. Such
checks help maintain a coherent declaration but do not cover every graph
class or establish that an accepted edge is causally true. In particular,
a diagram with no syntax error can still omit an important common cause or
misrepresent the observation process.

The user should be able to retain an unresolved diagram and ask for analyses
conditional on several alternatives. A refusal to pick one graph can be the
scientifically correct output. The later discovery and identification
operations then need to report what changes across those alternatives and
what remains common. This makes uncertainty operational: it directs the
next information request rather than appearing only as a disclaimer after
a single confident answer.

The following constructions make that consequence explicit. They separate
observational equivalence from sampling precision, measured proxies from
confounders, and a graph edit from evidence that warrants it. Their monetary
comparisons then locate the disagreements worth investigating.

tool responsible for formal identification receives the complete reviewed
graph object and its restrictions, rather than a picture whose uncertainty
has disappeared in editing.

\section{Graph classes and collections of candidate models}

A CPDAG or PAG is a structured representation with its own interpretation.
A list of proposed DAGs is another object. A collection of edges marked
``possible'' is not automatically an enumeration of every combination of
those edges. Confusing these representations can silently exclude models
or include incompatible ones.

The project contract preserves a CPDAG or PAG directly when that is the
appropriate object, including circle endpoints. It also permits explicitly
listed candidate models. An edge marked possible within a candidate describes
the evidence status of that candidate's edge; it does not make all optional
edge combinations an exhaustive graph class. Downstream calculations must
know which interpretation applies.

An exact binary example shows the consequence of retaining alternatives.
In model \(F\), a binary offer \(A\) is Bernoulli with probability one half,
and response \(Y\) equals \(A\) with probability \(0.9\). In model \(R\),
\(Y\) is Bernoulli with probability one half, and \(A\) equals \(Y\) with
probability \(0.9\). Both models produce
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 &Y=0&Y=1\\\hline
A=0&9/20&1/20\\
A=1&1/20&9/20
\end{array}.
\]
In \(F\), setting \(A\) from zero to one changes \(E[Y]\) by \(0.8\).
In \(R\), intervening on the equation for \(A\) leaves \(Y\) unchanged.
The two compatible constructions therefore imply the effect candidates
\(\{0,0.8\}\). A directional suggestion favoring \(F\) does not provide
new identifying information unless its underlying premise is independently
justified. These finite calculations are project constructions, not a
calibrated confidence set for a learned graph.

More generally, for a declared graph class \(\mathcal G\), one relevant
downstream object is
\begin{equation}
 \Theta(P,Q,\mathcal G)=\bigcup_{G\in\mathcal G}\Theta_G(P,Q),
 \label{la:graph-union}
\end{equation}
where \(\Theta_G(P,Q)\) contains effects compatible with distribution \(P\),
question \(Q\) and the model restrictions for \(G\). A nonidentified member
can make the union broad. A list of estimated points is not automatically
the whole union, and graph-selection uncertainty cannot be replaced with
ordinary coefficient uncertainty after selecting one member.

Equation~\eqref{la:graph-union} also clarifies what a disagreement review
should resolve. If two experts differ only on an edge that leaves the target
functional unchanged, that disagreement may be immaterial for the current
decision while still mattering for another target. If their graphs imply
different effect signs or feasibility, the conflict is decision-relevant.
The assistant can identify that consequence and prioritize the required
evidence. It should not average expert preferences into an unexplained graph.

\section{Retrieval failure and scientific disagreement}

An evidence assistant can fail to find a passage because the document is
unavailable, parsing failed, the query was poor, the retriever missed it, or
the passage is absent from the inspected document. These cases support
different statements. ``No passage was retrieved'' cannot by itself become
``the authors ignored the assumption,'' and neither statement establishes
that the assumption is false in the population.

The inspected ARGUS paper makes this distinction especially useful. It
audits reported evidence concerning DiD identifying assumptions and does
not claim to adjudicate causal truth. Its synthetic flaw study exhibits a
retrieval/abstention tradeoff, and its small human-label pilot reports an
in-sample calibration change that was not tested on unseen papers. These
observations motivate a banking evidence state that is separate from a
scientific risk judgment. \citep{v12_la_2609_30867}

The proposed record contains the source bytes, the query or retrieval
configuration, inspected anchors and the resulting narrow claim. If evidence
is missing, it records the missing step. If two sources conflict, it records
their populations, dates and definitions before treating the conflict as
substantive. The analyst can then determine whether the sources concern
different regimes or whether a genuine contradiction remains.

This process does not require pretending that every edge has a published
study behind it. Some causal premises depend on institutional facts: which
system sets a rate, when a policy becomes visible, how an audit was selected,
or which identifier establishes ownership. Those facts need an accountable
owner and authentic records. Literature retrieval can help formulate the
questions, but it cannot supply an institution's missing assignment truth.

\section{A reviewable editing sequence}

The proposed interaction starts with a question and variable definitions,
then records diagram alternatives. Each edit changes a declared object:
add or remove a variable, refine a clock, replace a proxy, propose an endpoint,
or accept a restriction. The edit retains its predecessor identity and
reason. A reviewer can therefore see whether an apparent improvement in
fit came from a new assumption, a different target, or an actual correction
of an error.

Formal checks can reject a directed cycle in a DAG, impossible declared
time order or an explicitly forbidden direction. They can flag mediator,
collider or common-ancestor patterns in the supported representation. Such
checks help maintain a coherent declaration but do not cover every graph
class or establish that an accepted edge is causally true. In particular,
a diagram with no syntax error can still omit an important common cause or
misrepresent the observation process.

The user should be able to retain an unresolved diagram and ask for analyses
conditional on several alternatives. A refusal to pick one graph can be the
scientifically correct output. The later discovery and identification
operations then need to report what changes across those alternatives and
what remains common. This makes uncertainty operational: it directs the
next information request rather than appearing only as a disclaimer after
a single confident answer.

The following constructions make that consequence explicit. They separate
observational equivalence from sampling precision, measured proxies from
confounders, and a graph edit from evidence that warrants it. Their monetary
comparisons then locate the disagreements worth investigating.

\chapter{Interference, allocation policies and software adoption}
\label{v13:sw-networks}

The preceding relationship analysis showed why a policy may require joint
graph and action information. This chapter examines the allocation problem
itself. It distinguishes network and grouped targets, develops the two initial
software references, and compares spatial, experimental, learned-policy and
simulation alternatives. The recurring small graphs and cost denominators are
matched comparison devices; each implementation's different assumptions and
failure conditions remain part of the argument.

\section{The unit receiving treatment need not be the independent unit}

A household member's offer can influence another member's borrowing, and an
outreach campaign can affect connected firms. In such settings a potential
outcome depends on more than the individual's own action. Writing only
$Y_i(a_i)$ hides the policy being evaluated. A more explicit representation is
$Y_i(a_i,\mathbf a_{-i})$, often restricted through an exposure mapping of
other units' actions. The mapping and the network are scientific inputs;
neither is established merely by finding matching customer identifiers.

Two broad software constructions appear in the inspected sources. MossSpider
uses a network and exposure summaries in a network-targeted estimation
workflow. Inferference uses grouped formulas, allocation probabilities and
inverse-probability weighting. These constructions have different observation
laws and potentially different targets. Their package names do not establish
interchangeability. \cite{v13_sw_mossspider,v13_sw_inferference}

An allocation policy illustrates the target. Suppose two linked borrowers have
binary outreach actions $A_1,A_2$, independently assigned with probability $p$
under the proposed policy. Stipulate the synthetic financial outcome
\[
 Y_i(a_i,a_j)=100a_i+40a_j-30a_i a_j
\]
in CNY. The first term represents the own-action contribution, the second a
spillover and the last diminishing combined benefit. These are hypothetical
structural values, not bank estimates. Averaging under the allocation gives
\[
 V(p)=140p-30p^2.
\]
For $p=0.2$ the mean is 26.8 CNY; for $p=0.8$ it is 92.8 CNY. The allocation
contrast is 66 CNY per borrower. Exact enumeration of the four assignments
checks the formula. \cite{v13_project_exact}

The direct effect of changing only the individual's own action is instead
$100-30a_j$, or $100-30p$ when the neighbor is independently treated with
probability $p$. This differs from the total allocation contrast. Reporting
one as the other can misprice the campaign even when every arithmetic
calculation is correct. The bank must specify whether it changes one action,
the neighborhood's allocation or an entire branch policy, and which costs
are included in the outcome.

\section{MossSpider: network semantics are part of the estimand}

The inspected \texttt{NetworkTMLE} documentation describes expected incidence
under a treatment plan, with Monte Carlo integration over allocations for
stochastic plans. It states a direct-contact interference assumption. The
constructor rejects self-loops, noninteger node identities and nonbinary
exposure, creates a relabeled network while retaining original identities,
and constructs an unweighted adjacency matrix. \cite{v13_sw_mossspider}

These details matter for bank graphs. A weighted guarantee network is not the
same as an unweighted adjacency graph. Removing weights can turn a small
guarantee into the same exposure contribution as a large one. Relabeling nodes
is harmless only when results can be mapped back to the correct identities.
A linkage error can attach the correct numerical estimate to the wrong firm.
Semantic conformance therefore needs an identity roundtrip and an explicit
policy for unsupported weighted relationships.

Direction requires particular review. The documentation initially describes an
undirected graph but also explains a directed influence convention opposite
the graph arrow, and the selected constructor includes directed handling. This
combination requires a concrete test with an asymmetric small graph. One should
not infer direction from a diagram's appearance or assume that every library
uses source-to-target influence. A two-node one-way example with distinguishable
covariates can determine which neighbor contributes to each exposure summary.
Section~\ref{sec:exec24-interference-reuse} develops the selected mapping,
policy and variance paths. Their inspected direction convention still needs
matched native tests; directed bank-network adoption remains a proposed use. \cite{v13_sw_mossspider}

Degree restrictions also change the target. The documentation treats nodes
outside a requested degree range as background, with their exposures unchanged
by the intervention. This can be scientifically useful, but it is not the
same as deleting those nodes from the graph or intervening on all customers.
The response must state which nodes are in the target population, which remain
background and how their factual exposure affects the intervention outcome.

The source disclaims a missing-data procedure. Missing node attributes,
uncertain links and omitted customers are common in banking, but the existence
of an exposure-mapping function does not solve those observation problems.
One must either supply defensible complete data in the declared regime or
develop a separate missingness/linkage construction. Network-targeted estimation
does not automatically qualify ownership or inclusion truth.

The observed MIT text makes a restricted adapter worth considering. Full adoption
requires qualification of the exposure-model and mapping code, targeting step,
Monte Carlo integration and variance calculation, together with actual
dependency/runtime checks. The developed study retains deterministic-policy
refusals, background-node treatment and a potentially negative variance
quadratic; these restrictions belong in any proposed adapter. A claim of general contagion, dynamic financial-network equilibrium or
arbitrary spillovers would go beyond the selected implementation evidence.

\section{Inferference: grouped allocation and numerical integration}

The inspected \texttt{interference} function uses a formula that identifies
outcome, exposure, optional participation, propensity covariates and a grouping
variable. It accepts allocation probabilities and propensity-model choices
including \texttt{glm}, \texttt{glmer}, \texttt{HLfit} and an oracle route.
Its documented causal-estimation path is IPW with naive or robust variance
options. The selected code sorts records by group and checks group count,
allocation range and the variance option. \cite{v13_sw_inferference}

A group-based model can be appropriate when the scientific design justifies
within-group interference and the required between-group sampling assumptions.
It does not become a model of arbitrary connected borrowers by assigning
everyone a group label. Cross-group guarantees or shared market shocks can
violate the intended observation law. The grouping decision needs domain
evidence and should be subjected to sensitivity analysis where boundaries
are uncertain.

The default logit integrand is restricted to a single random effect in the
documented implementation. The code rejects more than one when that integrand
is selected. Thus a proposal with household and branch random effects needs a
different justified integration path; silently dropping one random effect is
a model change. An oracle propensity option is useful for synthetic reference
calculations, but supplied true parameters cannot be counted as evidence that
an estimated-propensity workflow is calibrated.

There is also a reproducibility issue visible directly in the source. The prose
describes \texttt{integrate\_allocation} as defaulting to false, while the
inspected function signature sets it to true. The proper response is to specify
and record the argument explicitly. Section~\ref{sec:exec24-interference-reuse}
traces the downstream ratio and derivative paths; their flag propagation,
allocation-mass and missing-group restrictions still require matched native
qualification. It is not appropriate to select whichever default gives a more
favorable result after comparing outputs. \cite{v13_sw_inferference}

For large groups, multiplying many probabilities can create numerical problems.
The documentation discusses an allocation-integration option in this context.
Qualification should include large and uneven groups, boundary allocation
probabilities, integration tolerances and variance derivatives. A successful
floating-point result does not prove adequate support; an underflow error does
not prove nonidentification. These are different failure modes and need
different diagnostics.

The observed DESCRIPTION declares GPL version 2 or later and a dated version.
That informs a dependency review but does not establish the license status of
every linked component or distribution arrangement. A candidate grouped-policy
reference should remain distinct from a decision to embed or port it.

\section{A common comparison must distinguish network and group assumptions}

The two packages can be compared on a common small allocation problem only
after their target, exposure mapping and sampling assumptions are aligned.
For the two-borrower example, the exact four-assignment enumeration supplies a
transparent functional reference. A larger benchmark should vary degree,
group size, allocation probability, support, observation errors and dependence.
It should include examples where a direct-contact or group restriction is false.

Metrics should separate the target mean, direct and spillover contrasts,
coverage, finite availability, Monte Carlo integration error and total cost.
Increasing simulated allocations reduces integration error conditional on a
fitted model. It does not create independent groups or validate the graph.
Uncertainty must follow the actual sampling unit; counting nodes as independent
merely because the graph is stored in a table can produce misleading precision.

The implementation contract should retain the original graph, its direction
and weights, the identity map, intervention population, allocation rule,
background nodes and exposure mapping. A result should be rejected as
semantically incompatible if a proposed bridge silently changes any of these.
This requirement is shared by library calls, command-line jobs and agent tools.
An interface can make a scientific restriction visible; it cannot make it true.

\section{Provisional reuse choices and the evidence needed to change them}

The inspected software supports a portfolio of candidate components rather
than a single universal engine. The following choices describe potential uses and qualification conditions,
not accepted integrations or benchmarks. The earlier functional and
longitudinal chapters develop the corresponding source findings
(Chapters~\ref{v13:sw-functional} and~\ref{v13:sw-regimes}); the table retains
the conditions that must survive implementation rather than treating those
studies as still absent.

\begin{longtable}{P{0.18\textwidth}P{0.34\textwidth}P{0.39\textwidth}}
\toprule
Component & Candidate role & Conditions to preserve and qualify\\
\midrule
\endhead
DirectLiNGAM & Functional discovery adapter & Reviewed base-class behavior, prior orientation,
functional assumptions and adverse latent/Gaussian cases\\
y0 & Symbolic ID/IDC adapter & Reviewed recursive paths, conditional-path restriction,
graph validation, expression roundtrip and nonidentification references\\
delicatessen & Equation and numerical reference & Solver, Jacobian, covariance,
sampling unit and complete dependency contract\\
statsmodels & Point-treatment GMM baseline & Matched population, propensity bounds,
actual covariance behavior and dependent-data limits\\
pygformula & Longitudinal-regime adapter & History/event meaning, simulation,
bootstrap unit, diagnostics and policy scope\\
grf & R/native heterogeneous-effect component & Native algorithms, variance,
aggregation measure, ABI and license/distribution review\\
CausalGPS & Continuous-density component & Density/transformation helpers,
counterfactual doses, support and downstream estimation\\
causaldrf & Dose-response reference & Full function, interval procedures,
support, recovered holder notice and dependency terms\\
MossSpider & Restricted network-policy component & Direction, mapping, identity,
targeting, variance and observation restrictions\\
inferference & Grouped-allocation reference & Integrands, numerical defaults,
variance, group law and dependency terms\\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

An integration decision is stronger than identifying a promising function.
Direct adoption needs a stable, compatible dependency and scientific contract.
An adapter needs semantic parity and error preservation. A port needs the right
to reuse the implementation, an upstream behavioral oracle, independent
references, numerical/statistical equivalence criteria and a maintenance owner.
A research reference can be valuable without becoming a product dependency.
Deferral is justified when these prerequisites are missing; rejection should
state a concrete incompatibility and a revisit condition.

Commercial comparison must apply the same discipline. Vendor documentation can
establish a dated documented feature, but not measured agreement or operating
cost without an executed comparison. An inaccessible manual cannot support a
claim that the vendor lacks an operation. Our proposed graph-to-effect or
banking workflow is likewise not a delivered competitive advantage. A sound
build/buy/partner decision compares the vendor's documented and measured state
with our implemented, conditional, proposed or absent state, and makes the
missing evidence explicit.

Licensing is one part of this decision. The selected MIT and BSD texts,
repository GPL text and package license declarations provide traceable starting
points. Dependencies, bundled data, separate notices, native libraries and the
intended distribution arrangement still need review. A subprocess boundary
does not automatically settle licensing obligations, just as a Python wrapper
does not establish that a native operation has been qualified.

The software survey can therefore guide implementation immediately without
claiming premature adoption. It identifies precise operations, preserves their
mathematical meaning and specifies the evidence needed for the next decision.
Runtime, bank validation and independent scientific acceptance remain separate
from these source-grounded provisional choices.
