\section{Policy evaluation software must preserve the decision and its uncertainty}
\label{exec23:scope-rl-scope}
A servicing team may use an offline policy evaluation library to compare a
sequence of reminders, forbearance offers and escalations. The useful output is
the value of a specified feasible policy under an information clock, together
with defensible uncertainty. A function returning a ranking is only one part of
that task. SCOPE-RL provides a particularly useful proposal comparator because
its selected discrete estimators, interval helpers and policy-selection paths
make several boundaries explicit. This review concerns version 0.2.1 at the
immutable 1 December 2023 revision returned by the cutoff query. Eleven
authenticated source and declaration files support the following observations;
the continuous-action, distributional and density-learning families have not
received equivalent inspection. No upstream program was executed.
\cite{exec23_scope_rl_sources}

\subsection{An episode, a propensity and a policy are substantive inputs}
\label{exec23:scope-rl-target}
Let a customer episode have $T$ decisions. At decision $t$, $H_t$ is all
information available before the action, $A_t$ the action, and $R_t$ the
subsequent monetary reward. Write $b_t(a\mid H_t)$ for the actual logging
probability and $\pi_t(a\mid H_t)$ for the policy being evaluated. For a declared
initial population and discount $0<\gamma\leq1$, the proposed target is
\[
 J(\pi)=\mathbb E_\pi\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^tR_t\right],
 \qquad
 W_{it}=\prod_{s=0}^{t}
 \frac{\pi_s(A_{is}\mid H_{is})}{b_s(A_{is}\mid H_{is})}.
\]
The elementary change-of-measure argument needs the logging probabilities to
describe the actual action mechanism, support for every target action-history
pair, and the same conditional transition/reward law under the intervention.
Multiplying the logging trajectory density by $W_{i,T-1}$ then replaces each
action factor by its target counterpart. For a reward observed by time $t$,
future action factors integrate to one, which explains the per-decision form.
An omitted private distress signal or a post-action feature can invalidate this
argument even if every probability row sums to one. The independent-episode
sampling condition used for the simple uncertainty examples below is additional
to this identification argument.

The inspected implementation reshapes flattened records into equal-length
episodes, cumulatively multiplies action probabilities, and either repeats the
final weight or retains the prefix weights. Its two scores therefore correspond
to
\[
 Z_i^{\rm TIS}=W_{i,T-1}\sum_t\gamma^tR_{it},
 \qquad Z_i^{\rm PDIS}=\sum_t\gamma^tW_{it}R_{it}.
\]
The interface checks dimensions, row counts, divisibility by the horizon and
target probability normalization. Such checks cannot establish truthful
logging, temporal ordering or common episode membership. The probability
validator is called with a zero lower limit; the discount expression divides a
cumulative product by $\gamma$ while its scalar check also uses a zero lower
limit. A proposed adapter must enforce finite, strictly positive observed-action
denominators and an explicitly supported discount domain before these calls.
This is a static source finding, not an observed runtime failure.
\cite{exec23_scope_rl_sources}

An exact two-period example clarifies why two estimators can disagree without
targeting different policies. Let both logging actions be independent fair
coins and both target actions have probability $3/4$ of action one. Set
$R_0=2A_0$, $R_1=4+4A_1$ and $\gamma=1/2$. Direct enumeration of all four
trajectories gives $J(\pi)=5$. Both importance scores average to five under the
logging law. On the particular two-episode sample $(1,0),(0,1)$, however, TIS is
$3$ and PDIS is $15/4$. Neither sample result proves bias or superior precision.
The project's rational-arithmetic reference enumerates the complete finite law
and distinguishes this population calculation from the illustrative sample.
\cite{exec23_scope_rl_reference}

The inspected doubly robust score adds a fitted state-value term and subtracts
the fitted action value, with current and previous prefix weights:
\[
 Z_i^{\rm DR}=\sum_t\gamma^t
 \{W_{it}(R_{it}-\widehat Q_t(H_{it},A_{it}))
       +W_{i,t-1}\widehat V_t(H_{it})\},\quad W_{i,-1}=1.
\]
Its source calculation is useful for conversion tests, but the label does not
prove robustness to an arbitrary hidden logging signal, an estimated policy,
or dependent customers. The input builder defaults to one fitted-Q fold; its
multi-fold branch excludes contiguous groups of whole trajectories. It caches
fitted models by policy name. Therefore episode grouping, calendar dependence,
policy identity and changes to training settings must be bound explicitly.
Repeated calls with a reused name are not evidence of a fresh fit. The d3rlpy
delegate and a full frozen environment remain native qualification obligations.
\cite{exec23_scope_rl_sources}

\subsection{Terminal rewards and uncertainty cannot be inferred from names}
\label{exec23:scope-rl-uncertainty}
The high-level evaluator defaults to disabling rewards after a done flag. The
actual mask is the cumulative product of $1-d_t$, including the current row.
If a dataset defines $d_t$ as indicating that the transition just produced the
terminal reward, this removes that terminal reward as well. A different
pre-transition convention could justify the mask; the adapter must state and
test the convention. With undiscounted rewards $(2,8)$ and flags $(0,1)$, the
literal mask leaves value $2$, whereas retaining the terminal receipt gives
$10$. At a stipulated servicing cost of six dollars, the margins are $-4$ and
$4$. These are authored examples, not measured bank returns or observed
package outputs. The dataset documentation separately describes episode end
and maximum-step termination, while the fitted-Q dataset call passes the done
array as its terminal argument. A conversion must resolve both meanings.
\cite{exec23_scope_rl_sources,exec23_scope_rl_reference}

The basic estimator's interval method first calculates one score per trajectory
and delegates the resulting vector to a common interval helper. The bootstrap
helper samples those fixed scores with replacement, takes percentile endpoints,
and reports the mean of bootstrap means. Its signature defaults to 100
replications although its parameter prose says 10,000, and it requires an
explicit random seed. Neither this helper nor the selected call refits the
value model, estimates new logging propensities or repeats policy learning in
each bootstrap sample. Whether conditioning on those fits is scientifically
appropriate needs a separate argument; it is not supplied by the word
bootstrap. \cite{exec23_scope_rl_sources}

This distinction already matters without a learned nuisance. For a
self-normalized weighted mean, let two episode weights be $(1,3)$ and returns
$(0,4)$. Ignoring the implementation's tiny denominator stabilizer solely for
this exact algebraic illustration, the estimate is $3$ and the precomputed
normalized scores are $(0,6)$. The four equally likely size-two bootstrap index
pairs produce means $(0,3,3,6)$ if these scores are fixed, but ratios
$(0,3,3,4)$ if the denominator is recalculated. Their bootstrap variances are
$9/2$ and $9/4$. This is not a coverage assessment of either procedure; it shows
that they are different resampling targets. The selected self-normalized class
inherits the score-based interval path and uses a $10^{-10}$ denominator
stabilizer. A native test must retain that stabilizer, distinguish ratio
recalculation from score resampling, and state which procedure is justified.
\cite{exec23_scope_rl_sources,exec23_scope_rl_reference}

Three analytic interval helpers need particularly careful admission. The
Hoeffding-named helper computes the radius
\[
 \max_i z_i\sqrt{\log(2/\alpha)n/2},
\]
whereas its adjacent displayed formula places $n$ in the denominator. Parsing
the expression as inert syntax confirms multiplication by $n$; at $n=20$ the
source radius is twenty times the expression with the same logarithm and $n$
in the denominator. More fundamentally, an observed sample maximum is not a
known population range. For independent Bernoulli rewards with mean $1/100$,
all twenty observations are zero with probability $(99/100)^{20}>0.8$. The
source Hoeffding and Bernstein expressions then both give zero radius despite
the positive mean. A constant negative sample also makes the first radius
negative and reverses its endpoints. No concentration guarantee follows from
these helper names for unrestricted banking rewards.
\cite{exec23_scope_rl_sources,exec23_scope_rl_reference}

The Bernstein-named helper also differs from its printed variance expression:
the executable expression divides the variance contribution by $n-1$, while
the prose display includes $n(n-1)$, and a supplied sample maximum again replaces
a declared range. These observations warrant explicit comparison of definitions
and sample-variance conventions, not a silent formula patch. The Student helper
uses the $1-\alpha$ quantile and returns symmetric endpoints labelled
$100(1-\alpha)$ percent. Under the exact nondegenerate normal-sample model in
which the usual Student pivot has a symmetric continuous law, those endpoints
have central probability $1-2\alpha$: $90$ percent at $\alpha=0.05$. This
algebra does not establish a distributional approximation for importance
scores. Positive sample sizes, finite values, signed rewards, degenerate
samples, alpha endpoints and valid simultaneous coverage must all be explicit
adapter contracts. \cite{exec23_scope_rl_sources,exec23_scope_rl_reference}

\subsection{A selection benchmark is not an offline safety certificate}
\label{exec23:scope-rl-decision}
The inspected lower-bound selector obtains on-policy selection results before
ranking candidate interval endpoints, even when the requested output omits
evaluation metrics. The called routine rejects a missing on-policy return
array. This is a concrete benchmark-data requirement: a logged-only banking
request generally cannot furnish those counterfactual returns. Missing truth
must lead to a refusal or a separately designed selection path, never fabricated
on-policy values. The selected call forwards the same alpha to each candidate
and estimator; no multiplicity adjustment appears in this path. Even twenty
independent tests with individual false-admission probability $0.05$ have
probability $1-0.95^{20}$, approximately $0.642$, of at least one false admission.
That hypothetical example is not a measured SCOPE-RL error rate. A candidate
policy learned or selected on the evaluation histories requires its own
selection-aware design. \cite{exec23_scope_rl_sources,exec23_scope_rl_reference}

The ground-truth lower-quartile output also needs a name/value fixture. The
source sorts the policy-value array before deriving a lower-quartile name
ordering, then sorts lower-quartile values separately. In input order A, B,
give A returns $(-10,-10,40,40)$ and B returns $(4,4,4,4)$. Their means are
$15,4$, but lower quartiles are $-10,4$. The selected expressions pair the
unchanged name order A, B with descending values $4,-10$, rather than the
correct lower-tail name order B, A. The static witness is sufficient to require
an identity-preserving test; native behavior in a frozen dependency environment
has not been measured. A printed safety or regret column must also preserve the
source's explicit true-safe and estimated-safe denominators instead of relying
on generic type-I/type-II labels. \cite{exec23_scope_rl_sources,exec23_scope_rl_reference}

The proposal disposition is therefore \emph{reference}, with no approved native
adapter. SCOPE-RL's explicit trajectory scores, fitted-value preparation and
evaluation organization inform a narrow design. Whole-package adoption would
admit much more functionality than the inspected contract. A Python worker is
a candidate only after complete artifact and dependency custody, terminal/time
fixtures, interval repair review and fresh native conformance. Porting the
package to R, Java or C++ currently has no demonstrated advantage sufficient to
justify reproducing its preprocessing, model delegates and maintenance burden.
Independent exact references are valuable test oracles; they do not replace the
package or establish empirical policy performance.

The source declares Apache 2.0 and includes the license text, but this does not
clear transitive dependencies, datasets or deployment terms. The requirements
span NumPy, SciPy, pandas, scikit-learn, plotting libraries, torch, d3rlpy,
Gym/Gymnasium and Hydra; most are lower bounds, not a reproducible environment
lock. Named authors and the dated revision establish identity, not a current
support commitment. The maintenance owner must resolve actual dependency
versions and rights; the scientific owner must define target, logging truth,
support and sampling law; the operator must measure resource and recovery cost.
\cite{exec23_scope_rl_sources}

A proposed library/CLI/MCP request should carry immutable episode IDs, decision
times, the information set, reward/termination conventions, action vocabulary,
logging and target probabilities, policy/training identities, horizon, discount,
uncertainty method and random seed. Its response should preserve the target,
score definition, source revision, refusal reason, finite-weight diagnostics and
whether uncertainty is conditional on fitted quantities. An agent must not
convert a schema-valid answer into an identified effect or a safety approval.
Public qualification can begin with finite known-policy trajectory laws and
adversarial permutations, missing propensities, terminal rewards, signed returns,
shared calendar shocks and policy-selection leakage. Fresh native tests and
measured costs follow only in a reviewed environment; bank truth and adoption
remain later independent gates.

\section{How estimated components can change a sequential value}
\label{exec14:l5-remainder}

The exact score moments above assume the true conditional quantities. A
prototype must also make visible what happens when its fitted components are
wrong. This is particularly relevant when an assistant chooses a regression,
uses an estimated assignment model, and presents the resulting augmented
calculation as automatically protected against bias. Double robustness is a
property of a specified construction under specified conditions. It is not a
guarantee that any two imperfect components cancel each other.

Consider the same fixed risk policy, without retention loss or baseline
variation. Let $p_0$ be the observational probability of its first action and
$p_1(l)$ the probability of its required second action at state $l$. These are
probabilities of following the rule: when the rule requests zero, $p_1(l)$ is
the probability of action zero. Let $\widetilde p_0$ and
$\widetilde p_1(l)$ be fixed positive approximations, and define
\[
 \rho_0=\frac{p_0}{\widetilde p_0},\qquad
 \rho_1(l)=\frac{p_1(l)}{\widetilde p_1(l)}.
\]
Write $\widetilde m_g(l)=m_g(l)+d(l)$ and
$\widetilde q=V(g)+\eta$. The last quantity is an approximation to the
first-stage regression; it need not equal the average of
$\widetilde m_g$ under the true transition law. Replace the quantities in
equation~\eqref{eq:exec14-l5-score} by these fixed approximations and add
$V(g)$ to obtain an uncentered augmented value $\widetilde Z$. Conditioning
successively on the action history gives
\begin{align*}
 E[\widetilde Z]
 ={}&-\rho_0E_g[\rho_1(L_1)d(L_1)]\\
 &+\rho_0E_g[m_g(L_1)+d(L_1)-\widetilde q]
   +\widetilde q.
\end{align*}
Here $E_g$ averages over the state law after the regime's first action.
Subtracting $V(g)$ yields the exact identity
\begin{equation}
 E[\widetilde Z]-V(g)
 =(1-\rho_0)\eta
   +\rho_0E_g[(1-\rho_1(L_1))d(L_1)].
 \label{eq:exec14-l5-remainder}
\end{equation}
This is a project derivation for this restricted two-stage law, independently
checked by enumerating the observational histories
\cite{exec14_workflow_remainder}. It does not claim the general sequential
robustness theorem discussed by Luedtke and colleagues
\cite{sequentialdr2018}.

The identity separates two errors with different histories. Correct action
probabilities at both stages make the right side zero. Correct outcome
quantities at both stages also make it zero. Other combinations can make it
zero, but only by satisfying the displayed stage conditions. If $d=0$ while
both $\rho_0\neq1$ and $\eta\neq0$, correctness of the final outcome model
alone does not remove the first-stage product. Conversely, a correct
first-action probability does not remove a second-stage treatment/outcome
product. Fitting two separate models and calling one of them a critic has no
bearing on these conditions.

For a concrete failure, use the servicing law's $p_0=1/2$, approximate it by
$\widetilde p_0=2/5$, and set $\widetilde q=V(g)+3$. In the low-distress
state the rule requires action zero with true and approximated probability
$1/2$. In the distressed state it requires action one with true probability
$3/4$ and approximated probability $1/2$. Let $d(0)=0$ and $d(1)=5$.
Then $\rho_0=5/4$, and the second product averaged under the regime is
$(2/5)(1-3/2)5=-1$. The total bias is
\[
 (1-5/4)3+(5/4)(-1)=-2.
\]
The augmented mean becomes 92.8 instead of 94.8. Enumeration of the weighted
residual, intermediate regression and final scalar separately gives the same
answer. Restoring both assignment probabilities restores 94.8 despite these
outcome errors; restoring both outcome components also restores it despite
the assignment errors. These are population identities with fixed
approximations, not fitted-estimator performance results
\cite{exec14_workflow_remainder}.

There is also a quantitative diagnostic. With square-integrable components
under the regime's state law, Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 |E[\widetilde Z]-V(g)|
 \leq |1-\rho_0|\,|\eta|
 +\rho_0\|1-\rho_1\|_{2,g}\|d\|_{2,g}.
\]
Lower bounds on approximated treatment probabilities are relevant because
they control the ratios; weak support can amplify small absolute propensity
errors. The bound does not supply observable values of the unknown errors.
It explains which approximations must be justified, and why predictive fit
alone need not settle the causal quantity.

For nuisance quantities trained on an independent sample, the fixed-component
calculation can be read conditionally on that training sample. A familiar
route to root-$n$ inference requires the bias products to be
$o_p(n^{-1/2})$, appropriate convergence of the centered score, and a valid
limit law for its sampling unit. Each requirement needs its own argument;
sample splitting alone proves none of them. Under the independent-account,
known-law construction above, the contrast's standard-error scale is
$\sqrt{667.52/n}$. A normal planning multiplier of 1.96 would require at
least 4007 accounts to make its planning half-width no greater than USD 0.8.
This is arithmetic using the known-law variance, not a claimed achieved
confidence interval, a selected trial size, or a bank precision commitment
\cite{exec14_workflow_remainder}. Dependence, estimated components and rare
histories can invalidate that planning scale. Increasing the account count
does not remove the fixed bias of two in the preceding example.

The assistant should therefore keep the causal target, fitted components,
training boundary, covariance unit and approximation status together. It can
flag a mistaken probability of action one when the policy requests zero,
propose checks of each stage, and compare a transparent fixed-regime
calculation. An unavailable rate argument remains an uncertainty limitation
even when the numerical value is finite. A report should explain that
limitation before turning the point estimate into a recommendation.

\section{Conditional panel comparisons must preserve cohort composition}
\label{exec14:l5-composition}

The preceding panel example used identical untreated trends across cohorts.
Conditional parallel trends allow a different situation: branches with the
same baseline covariates have comparable untreated changes, while adopting
and control branches have different covariate compositions. Pooling their
changes without standardization can then answer the wrong question even
though the conditional design is valid. Callaway and Sant'Anna's
identification representations average the conditional comparison over the
adopting group's covariate distribution \cite{callaway2021}.

Here is an independent stipulated two-period example in USD per account
\cite{exec14_workflow_remainder}. Let $X$ distinguish two branch markets,
and suppose three quarters of adopting branches have $X=1$, compared with
one quarter of never-adopting controls. At $X=0$, the untreated change is two
and the adoption effect is four. At $X=1$, those quantities are ten and
eight. Within each market the untreated change is identical for adopting
and control branches; no anticipation and stable composition are stipulated.
The target is the adopting cohort's average treatment effect,
\[
 \operatorname{ATT}=\tfrac14(4)+\tfrac34(8)=7.
\]
The adopting cohort's observed average change is
$\tfrac14(2+4)+\tfrac34(10+8)=15$. The pooled control change is
$\tfrac34(2)+\tfrac14(10)=4$. Their unadjusted difference is eleven,
overstating the target by four. The difference is caused by unequal market
composition, not by a violation of the stipulated conditional trends.

Outcome standardization instead computes the control change under the
adopting composition: $\tfrac14(2)+\tfrac34(10)=8$. Subtracting it from
fifteen restores seven. Weighting supplies a second representation. Suppose
the two cohorts have equal population mass, so the propensity to belong to
the adopting cohort is $e(0)=1/4$ and $e(1)=3/4$. Control weights proportional
to $e(X)/\{1-e(X)\}$ are $1/3$ and three. Their control-group average is
one, and their weighted change is
\[
 \tfrac34\left(\tfrac13\right)2
 +\tfrac14(3)10=8.
\]
The weights reconstruct the adopting covariate distribution. They are
cohort-comparison weights, rather than the probabilities of following a
two-action account policy. The corresponding target and observation clocks
must remain distinct when an assistant selects an API.

If market $X=1$ has no untreated controls, this representation cannot be
evaluated from the stipulated comparison without extrapolation or another
restriction. Dropping that market changes the target from seven to four;
silently describing the retained-market result as the original ATT would
replace the business question. Matching, regression and weighting should
therefore be compared on their supported target, not merely on whether each
returns a coefficient. Adding a covariate measured after platform adoption
can also change the scientific argument; the baseline market variable here
does not justify adjustment for any convenient post-adoption metric.

For an illustrative deployment cost of six per adopting account, the
identified gross effect of seven leaves a net margin of one. The pooled
difference of eleven would suggest five. These are planning values under
stipulated truth and cost, with no fitted uncertainty or bank ROI claim
\cite{exec14_workflow_remainder}. They show why composition and support checks
matter to the investment proposal: a target error can dominate a modest
economic margin even when every arithmetic step and generated explanation
appears convincing.
\label{exec14:l5-depth-end}

\section{How estimated components can change a sequential value}
\label{exec14:l5-remainder}

The exact score moments above assume the true conditional quantities. A
prototype must also make visible what happens when its fitted components are
wrong. This is particularly relevant when an assistant chooses a regression,
uses an estimated assignment model, and presents the resulting augmented
calculation as automatically protected against bias. Double robustness is a
property of a specified construction under specified conditions. It is not a
guarantee that any two imperfect components cancel each other.

Consider the same fixed risk policy, without retention loss or baseline
variation. Let $p_0$ be the observational probability of its first action and
$p_1(l)$ the probability of its required second action at state $l$. These are
probabilities of following the rule: when the rule requests zero, $p_1(l)$ is
the probability of action zero. Let $\widetilde p_0$ and
$\widetilde p_1(l)$ be fixed positive approximations, and define
\[
 \rho_0=\frac{p_0}{\widetilde p_0},\qquad
 \rho_1(l)=\frac{p_1(l)}{\widetilde p_1(l)}.
\]
Write $\widetilde m_g(l)=m_g(l)+d(l)$ and
$\widetilde q=V(g)+\eta$. The last quantity is an approximation to the
first-stage regression; it need not equal the average of
$\widetilde m_g$ under the true transition law. Replace the quantities in
equation~\eqref{eq:exec14-l5-score} by these fixed approximations and add
$V(g)$ to obtain an uncentered augmented value $\widetilde Z$. Conditioning
successively on the action history gives
\begin{align*}
 E[\widetilde Z]
 ={}&-\rho_0E_g[\rho_1(L_1)d(L_1)]\\
 &+\rho_0E_g[m_g(L_1)+d(L_1)-\widetilde q]
   +\widetilde q.
\end{align*}
Here $E_g$ averages over the state law after the regime's first action.
Subtracting $V(g)$ yields the exact identity
\begin{equation}
 E[\widetilde Z]-V(g)
 =(1-\rho_0)\eta
   +\rho_0E_g[(1-\rho_1(L_1))d(L_1)].
 \label{eq:exec14-l5-remainder}
\end{equation}
This is a project derivation for this restricted two-stage law, independently
checked by enumerating the observational histories
\citep{exec14_workflow_remainder}. It does not claim the general sequential
robustness theorem discussed by Luedtke and colleagues
\citep{sequentialdr2018}.

The identity separates two errors with different histories. Correct action
probabilities at both stages make the right side zero. Correct outcome
quantities at both stages also make it zero. Other combinations can make it
zero, but only by satisfying the displayed stage conditions. If $d=0$ while
both $\rho_0\neq1$ and $\eta\neq0$, correctness of the final outcome model
alone does not remove the first-stage product. Conversely, a correct
first-action probability does not remove a second-stage treatment/outcome
product. Fitting two separate models and calling one of them a critic has no
bearing on these conditions.

For a concrete failure, use the servicing law's $p_0=1/2$, approximate it by
$\widetilde p_0=2/5$, and set $\widetilde q=V(g)+3$. In the low-distress
state the rule requires action zero with true and approximated probability
$1/2$. In the distressed state it requires action one with true probability
$3/4$ and approximated probability $1/2$. Let $d(0)=0$ and $d(1)=5$.
Then $\rho_0=5/4$, and the second product averaged under the regime is
$(2/5)(1-3/2)5=-1$. The total bias is
\[
 (1-5/4)3+(5/4)(-1)=-2.
\]
The augmented mean becomes 92.8 instead of 94.8. Enumeration of the weighted
residual, intermediate regression and final scalar separately gives the same
answer. Restoring both assignment probabilities restores 94.8 despite these
outcome errors; restoring both outcome components also restores it despite
the assignment errors. These are population identities with fixed
approximations, not fitted-estimator performance results
\citep{exec14_workflow_remainder}.

 |E[\widetilde Z]-V(g)|
 \leq |1-\rho_0|\,|\eta|
 +\rho_0\|1-\rho_1\|_{2,g}\|d\|_{2,g}.
\]

The assistant should therefore keep the causal target, fitted components,

\section{JMP: treatment targets, selected subgroups and competing events}
\label{sec:exec24-jmp-reuse}

A bank analyst considering a retention campaign may want an overall
treatment effect, a subgroup worth targeting, or a prediction of default
before another event such as prepayment. JMP's retained documentation
provides distinct relevant workflows. Comparing them requires preserving
the estimand and edition rather than treating a causal-treatment report,
an uplift tree and a survival display as interchangeable evidence. The
proposal retains JMP as a commercial reference with conditional analyst
and worker routes; no native capability or entitlement is established
\cite{exec13_ch_jmp_causal,exec13_ch_jmp_uplift,exec14_survival_jmp,
exec24_jmp_choice}.

\subsection{Declared editions and the inspected technical boundary}
The causal-treatment pages are retained from the JMP Pro 19.2 help family
and display 13 January 2026 publication dates. The uplift overview belongs
to 19.0 and is dated 15 July 2025; the more detailed retained Consumer
Research guide is version 16. The supplied-model instrumental-variable
discussion is from the September 2025 version-19 Multivariate Methods
guide, while the selected survival pages are 18.1 and dated 27 June 2024.
Later acquisition of those mutable pages is not proof of exact bytes at
the 7 October 2026 cutoff. Older-guide behavior is not automatically
verified for a newer installed product
\cite{exec13_ch_jmp_causal,exec13_ch_jmp_uplift,exec13_ivrd_jmp,
exec14_survival_jmp}.

The causal help contains equations rendered as images. The retained
inspection uses the surrounding substantive prose, not an invented
transcription of those equations. The finite equations and examples below
are independently authored and identified as such. No additional image
review is claimed. Exact installed edition, supported automation profile,
commercial rights and prices remain separate questions; a help page is
neither a license nor evidence of an executed service
\cite{exec24_jmp_choice}.

\subsection{An average causal effect has a specified target population}
The documented Causal Treatment personality is available in JMP Pro and
supports binary or continuous treatment and outcome. For binary treatment,
the prose distinguishes average treatment effect from average treatment
effect among the treated. It documents IPWR, regression adjustment and
augmented inverse-probability methods using specified logistic propensity
and linear or logistic response models. For continuous treatment, the
reported targets are mean potential outcomes. These are useful concrete
capabilities to compare, but their interpretation depends on positivity,
consistency and conditional exchangeability
\cite{exec13_ch_jmp_causal}.

The assumption page explicitly distinguishes assumptions about the
data-generating process from empirical checks on a sample. A propensity
plot can reveal observed overlap problems; it cannot establish that every
unmeasured cause was included or that a campaign code corresponds to the
same intervention for every account. A business-to-causal assistant should
therefore record treatment versions, assignment information and alternative
causal explanations alongside any generated model specification. A fitted
response surface is not a substitute for that argument
\cite{exec13_ch_jmp_causal,exec24_jmp_choice}.

Targeting also requires preserving treatment-level coding. The version-16
uplift guide says that, with more than two treatment levels, the first
level is compared with a combination of all remaining levels. It also
documents value-order conventions and validation-column roles. These are
important historical contracts to test in the intended version, not
defaults that can be silently carried forward
\cite{exec13_ch_jmp_uplift}.

An authored randomized example has success probabilities $1/5$, $3/5$
and $9/10$ for a baseline and two distinct offers. If the pooled alternative
uses the latter offers with weights $(3/4,1/4)$, its contrast with baseline
is $19/40$. Reversing the mixture weights gives $5/8$. For 1,000
hypothetical accounts worth 100 USD per incremental success, the values
are 47,500 and 62,500 USD before offer costs. Both are valid mixture
contrasts under the stated experiment, but neither is automatically the
effect of a particular offer. The adapter must retain the first level,
pooled levels, their weights and the business action actually proposed
\cite{exec24_jmp_choice}.

\subsection{A selected uplift split needs its own evaluation law}
The retained uplift overview describes partition splits based on
treatment-by-split interactions, using linear models for continuous
responses and logistic models for categorical responses. It documents a
Monte Carlo adjustment intended to address predictor-selection bias from
different numbers of levels or candidate models. The older guide also
describes validation-based split selection. These features should be
acknowledged as documented controls, without inferring a general
post-selection interval or dependent-data guarantee
\cite{exec13_ch_jmp_uplift}.

A simple authored selection example explains the unresolved statistical
question. Suppose four independent candidate scores each equal minus one
or plus one with equal probability and have true mean zero. The selected
maximum is minus one only when all four scores are negative, which has
probability $1/16$. Its expected value is therefore
\[
 E[\max_j S_j]=\frac{15}{16}-\frac1{16}=\frac78.
\]
Selecting the largest score creates optimism even though no candidate
has a positive mean. This calculation does not test JMP's adjustment or
claim that it produces this bias. It specifies why the proposed comparison
needs a held-out or otherwise justified evaluation law for the complete
selection process, including predictor search, tree depth and policy choice
\cite{exec24_jmp_choice}.

In a bank, splits may be selected repeatedly across branches, customer
histories or calendar periods. Public fixtures should separate training,
selection and evaluation units according to the declared dependence regime.
They should retain all attempted splits and policies, treatment allocation,
costs and failure counts. A language-model agent may explain candidate
segments, but should not convert a selected in-sample difference into a
qualified intervention recommendation without the corresponding evidence
\cite{exec24_jmp_choice}.

\subsection{A continuous density model does not create empirical support}
The continuous-treatment prose specifies a normal conditional treatment
density with parameters estimated through linear regression. It describes
a stabilized-weight marginal structural model and a generalized propensity
score response model. These are particular modeling choices, not evidence
of identification for every dose or treatment distribution. A density
model assigning a positive number outside the observed range can conceal
an unsupported policy extrapolation if the wrapper records only that number
\cite{exec13_ch_jmp_causal,exec24_jmp_choice}.

For an authored bounded outcome, suppose treatments are observed only on
$[0,1]$. Two response laws agree there at $\mu(a)=a/2$. Beyond one, let
the first continue to $\mu_1(2)=1$, while the second declines according to
$\mu_2(a)=1-a/2$ and reaches $\mu_2(2)=0$. Both laws fit the same
observed support but imply opposite responses at the proposed dose two.
A parametric continuation chooses a restriction; it does not reveal the
missing response from the observed sample. Public tests can check that a
worker reports the support boundary and the chosen extrapolation model.
Actual off-support bank response requires new information or a justified
restriction \cite{exec24_jmp_choice}.

\subsection{Competing-event displays are not automatically removal interventions}
The inspected competing-causes page describes estimating each cause's
survival distribution by treating other events as censored, under a stated
independent-causes premise. It offers an Omit Causes display that
recalculates survival estimates to illustrate a situation in which selected
causes are no longer hazardous. Those documented operations do not establish
what would happen if a bank changed a prepayment policy or prevented a
particular competing event
\cite{exec14_survival_jmp}.

An authored finite example clarifies the distinction. Half of accounts
have a competing event at time one and latent default at time two; the
other half default at time two before their competing event at time three.
The observed fraction defaulting before a competing event is one half.
Under a specifically defined intervention that removes the competitor
while leaving each latent default time unchanged, all accounts default
by time two. Other intervention mechanisms could also change default
times. The observed competing-event record alone does not select the
unchanged-latent-time intervention. This example is not a native JMP
calculation and does not assume that its display uses this discrete model
\cite{exec24_jmp_choice}.

The proposed product therefore needs distinct labels for observed
cumulative incidence, cause-specific or net survival, and an explicitly
defined counterfactual removal target. Event coding, censoring, risk sets,
time units and dependence assumptions must be preserved. A plotting or
simulation option is a useful analytical interface; it does not supply the
causal intervention mechanism by itself
\cite{exec14_survival_jmp,exec24_jmp_choice}.

\subsection{The supplied-model IV route and remaining scope}
The retained version-19 multivariate guide documents model-implied
instrumental-variable estimation with equation-level diagnostics and
instrument lists. Its instruments follow a supplied structural model;
those declarations do not make invalid exclusion assumptions true or
establish unrestricted graph discovery. This is another conditional
comparison route, separate from causal-treatment regression and uplift
partitioning \cite{exec13_ivrd_jmp}.

The present evidence does not establish complete panel, sequential-treatment,
latent-discovery or agent-service contracts for every JMP product and
extension. That is a coverage limit, not a claim that the vendor lacks all
such features. The next survey should identify the intended edition,
official API or automation interface, supported artifact and entitlement,
then acquire the concrete missing technical pages. Image-only equations
need a fresh permitted visual inspection before claims relying on them
are admitted \cite{exec24_jmp_choice}.

Reference use is retained for the documented analytical workflows.
Conditional integration may use an entitled analyst workflow or isolated
worker after public target, coding, support, selection and event-time
fixtures pass. Direct adoption as the full causal product is deferred.
Porting a proprietary implementation is not an authorized open-source
reuse route; independent implementation of public methods is a separate
proposal. Unsupported causal, off-support or post-selection guarantees
are rejected without rejecting every bounded use of the software
\cite{exec24_jmp_choice}.

Scientific ownership covers intervention, target, assumptions and loss;
statistical ownership covers selection and dependence; adapter ownership
covers treatment order, mixture weights, events and typed refusals; platform
ownership covers supported automation, rights and complete costs. A
hypothetical 21,000 USD over 700 submitted, 525 completed and 350
qualified requests gives 30, 40 and 60 USD respectively. Actual prices,
support and bank value remain unmeasured. Package execution and independent validation remain to be performed
\cite{exec24_jmp_choice}.

segments, but should not convert a selected in-sample difference into a
qualified intervention recommendation without the corresponding evidence
\citep{exec24_jmp_choice}.

\subsection{A continuous density model does not create empirical support}
The continuous-treatment prose specifies a normal conditional treatment
density with parameters estimated through linear regression. It describes
a stabilized-weight marginal structural model and a generalized propensity
score response model. These are particular modeling choices, not evidence
of identification for every dose or treatment distribution. A density
model assigning a positive number outside the observed range can conceal
an unsupported policy extrapolation if the wrapper records only that number
\citep{exec13_ch_jmp_causal,exec24_jmp_choice}.

For an authored bounded outcome, suppose treatments are observed only on
$[0,1]$. Two response laws agree there at $\mu(a)=a/2$. Beyond one, let
the first continue to $\mu_1(2)=1$, while the second declines according to
$\mu_2(a)=1-a/2$ and reaches $\mu_2(2)=0$. Both laws fit the same
observed support but imply opposite responses at the proposed dose two.
A parametric continuation chooses a restriction; it does not reveal the
missing response from the observed sample. Public tests can check that a
worker reports the support boundary and the chosen extrapolation model.
Actual off-support bank response requires new information or a justified
restriction \citep{exec24_jmp_choice}.

\subsection{Competing-event displays are not automatically removal interventions}
The inspected competing-causes page describes estimating each cause's
survival distribution by treating other events as censored, under a stated
independent-causes premise. It offers an Omit Causes display that
recalculates survival estimates to illustrate a situation in which selected
causes are no longer hazardous. Those documented operations do not establish
what would happen if a bank changed a prepayment policy or prevented a
particular competing event
\citep{exec14_survival_jmp}.

An authored finite example clarifies the distinction. Half of accounts
have a competing event at time one and latent default at time two; the
other half default at time two before their competing event at time three.
The observed fraction defaulting before a competing event is one half.
Under a specifically defined intervention that removes the competitor
while leaving each latent default time unchanged, all accounts default
by time two. Other intervention mechanisms could also change default
times. The observed competing-event record alone does not select the
unchanged-latent-time intervention. This example is not a native JMP
calculation and does not assume that its display uses this discrete model
\citep{exec24_jmp_choice}.

The proposed product therefore needs distinct labels for observed
cumulative incidence, cause-specific or net survival, and an explicitly
defined counterfactual removal target. Event coding, censoring, risk sets,
time units and dependence assumptions must be preserved. A plotting or
simulation option is a useful analytical interface; it does not supply the
causal intervention mechanism by itself
\citep{exec14_survival_jmp,exec24_jmp_choice}.

\subsection{The supplied-model IV route and remaining scope}
The retained version-19 multivariate guide documents model-implied
instrumental-variable estimation with equation-level diagnostics and
instrument lists. Its instruments follow a supplied structural model;
those declarations do not make invalid exclusion assumptions true or
establish unrestricted graph discovery. This is another conditional
comparison route, separate from causal-treatment regression and uplift
partitioning \citep{exec13_ivrd_jmp}.

The present evidence does not establish complete panel, sequential-treatment,
latent-discovery or agent-service contracts for every JMP product and
extension. That is a coverage limit, not a claim that the vendor lacks all
such features. The next survey should identify the intended edition,
official API or automation interface, supported artifact and entitlement,
then acquire the concrete missing technical pages. Image-only equations
need a fresh permitted visual inspection before claims relying on them
are admitted \citep{exec24_jmp_choice}.

Reference use is retained for the documented analytical workflows.
Conditional integration may use an entitled analyst workflow or isolated
worker after public target, coding, support, selection and event-time
fixtures pass. Direct adoption as the full causal product is deferred.
Porting a proprietary implementation is not an authorized open-source
reuse route; independent implementation of public methods is a separate
proposal. Unsupported causal, off-support or post-selection guarantees
are rejected without rejecting every bounded use of the software
\citep{exec24_jmp_choice}.

Scientific ownership covers intervention, target, assumptions and loss;
statistical ownership covers selection and dependence; adapter ownership
covers treatment order, mixture weights, events and typed refusals; platform
ownership covers supported automation, rights and complete costs. A
hypothetical 21,000 USD over 700 submitted, 525 completed and 350
qualified requests gives 30, 40 and 60 USD respectively. Actual prices,
support and bank value remain unmeasured. Package execution and independent validation remain to be performed
\citep{exec24_jmp_choice}.

\chapter{Learning funding responses from verified histories}
\label{integrated:linked_funding}

\begin{quote}\small
Correctness counts can leave an individual funding response unidentified when
two candidate histories mix equally. An audit that resolves the actual focal
history supplies a different observation. We derive a sampled-outcome score
for the existing continuous-action, common-calendar funding target, including
its additional audit variance and independent nuisance pilot. A registered
4,800-request comparison finds finite intervals in every linked-outcome
request. At exact identity rank one, the augmented method has median width
about USD 527,000, while the count-based set is whole-line in all 600 requests.
Its coverage there is 559/600, so finite availability is not general
calibration. False exogeneity, incorrect inclusion probabilities and noisy
truth labels produce severe failures. The result identifies useful new
information to seek from a bank; its authenticity, price and acceptable
decision precision remain external requirements.
\end{quote}

\section{The same bank decision, with a richer observation}

A deposit team considers a one-month increase of ten basis points in its
offered rate. Let $F_t=(F_{t0},\ldots,F_{tH})'$ denote the focal portfolio's
balance response history at origin $t$, with $H=6$. Two candidate vectors
$Y_{t1},Y_{t2}$ contain the focal and companion histories in an uncertain
order. An origin's assignment applies to all seven horizons. The two strata
$S_t\in\{0,1\}$ each have fixed target weight one half. If $\beta_{sh}$ is
the focal balance response to the rate intervention, define
\begin{equation}
 \theta_s=\sum_{h=0}^{H}w_h\beta_{sh},\qquad
 V=\tfrac12(\theta_0+\theta_1)-C.\label{integrated:linked_funding:eq:value}
\end{equation}
The inherited synthetic account has 48 branches, USD one million per balance
unit, monthly margin .002 and discount .99. Its weights are
$w_h=48\times10^6\{.002(.99)^h-(.001/12)1\{h=0\}\}$ and
$C=48\times100\times10^6(.001/12)=400{,}000$ USD. The immediate induced
balance also pays the increased rate; future margins are discounted once.
With focal response $2(.82)^h$, the target is USD 375,149, or USD 751,749
when persistence is .96. These are reproducible synthetic accounts, not
measured bank profits.

Chapters~\ref{integrated:weak_audit_projection} and~\ref{integrated:weak_audit_sharpening} infer $V$ from candidate responses and independent correctness counts. If the probability $p_s$ of the first candidate being
focal equals one half, the mean mixing equations cannot separate focal and
companion effects. Better interval algebra retains that ambiguity. Consider
instead an audit indicator $R_t$ with known probability $q_t>0$ that, when
selected, reveals \emph{which stored candidate history is focal}. The bank
must provide this information in both evaluation and independent pilot
histories. One audit resolves an origin's vector, not seven independent
audits. Unselected labels are unavailable to the estimator.

This is an extension of the monograph's independent-pair audit argument to
the selected dependent funding calendar. It does not identify persistent
maps across arbitrary customer pairs, arbitrary shared audit errors or
many-to-many ownership. Here the inherited candidate swaps are independent
by origin and the new audit draws are conditionally independent across
origins given the complete histories and their supplied probabilities.

\section{Identification from sampled linked outcomes}

Let $B_t=(Y_{t1}+Y_{t2})/2$ be the observed candidate average and let
$\mathcal H$ contain all complete focal/companion histories, assignments and
actions before audit randomization. Define the vector pseudo-outcome
\begin{equation}
 Z_t=B_t+\frac{R_t}{q_t}(F_t-B_t),\qquad
 \E[R_t\mid\mathcal H]=q_t.\label{integrated:linked_funding:eq:pseudo}
\end{equation}
Only the selected term requires the focal identity. Conditional expectation
gives $\E[Z_t\mid\mathcal H]=F_t$ exactly. No inverse $1/(2p_s-1)$ appears;
indeed swapping the candidate names and complementing the selected audit
labels leaves $Z_t$ unchanged. The alternative $Z_t^{I}=R_tF_t/q_t$ has the
same conditional expectation, but uses no observed average as augmentation.
There is no unconditional theorem that either has lower variance for every
possible outcome law.

The variance comparison follows from the audit randomization. Write
$f_t=w'F_t$ and $b_t=w'B_t$ for the focal and candidate-average monetary
outcomes before taking the action score. Conditional on the complete history,
the two scalar pseudo-outcomes have the same mean and audit variances
\begin{equation}\label{rel81:audit-augmentation}
 \operatorname{Var}(w'Z_t\mid\mathcal H)
   =(q_t^{-1}-1)(f_t-b_t)^2,\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(w'Z_t^I\mid\mathcal H)
   =(q_t^{-1}-1)f_t^2.
\end{equation}
For an incomplete audit, augmentation reduces this conditional contribution
exactly when the candidate average is closer to the focal outcome than zero
is. Multiplying by the squared oracle action-score coefficient and averaging
gives the corresponding comparison of added audit variance. Both constructions
retain the same latent focal score; estimated nuisance functions introduce
further finite-sample differences, so this calculation does not order every
fitted interval.

For a dimensionless illustration, stipulate a focal monetary outcome of two
and audit probability one quarter. A candidate average of 1.25 gives audit
variance 1.6875, compared with 12 under pure inverse weighting. If the candidate
average is instead five, the augmented variance is 27 and exceeds 12. These
values illustrate the conditional identity, not a new empirical funding case.
With complete auditing both additional variances vanish. The candidate average
can therefore be useful information without being a uniformly beneficial
augmentation under every outcome law.


Write $A_t=m_s(X_t)+v_t$ for the observed action, where $X_t$ contains the
fixed driver dictionary and stratum. Let
$\ell_s(X_t)=\E[w'Z_t\mid X_t,S_t=s]$.
Under the inherited exogenous-innovation response law,
\begin{equation}
 \E\!\left[1\{S_t=s\}v_t
   \{w'Z_t-\ell_s(X_t)-\theta_sv_t\}\right]=0,
 \qquad Q_s=\E[1\{S_t=s\}v_t^2]>0.\label{integrated:linked_funding:eq:score}
\end{equation}
Equation~\eqref{integrated:linked_funding:eq:pseudo} reduces this observed moment to the corresponding
focal-outcome moment. Thus the same intervention target is identified even
at $p_s=1/2$, provided the new audit law and the causal action restriction
are true. The conditional expectation identity does not establish exogeneity.

An independent 4,800-origin pilot selects among the fixed penalties
$0,1,10,100$ using first-half fitting and second-half standardized prediction
loss, then refits on its whole history. Its outcomes are the same audited
pseudo-outcomes, so its labels are part of the information bill. On the
1,200 evaluation origins, set $\widehat v_t=A_t-\widehat m_s(X_t)$ and
$\widehat u_t=w'Z_t-\widehat\ell_s(X_t)$. The estimator is
\begin{equation}
 \widehat\theta_s=
 \frac{\sum_t1\{S_t=s\}\widehat v_t\widehat u_t}
      {\sum_t1\{S_t=s\}\widehat v_t^2},\qquad
 \widehat V=\tfrac12(\widehat\theta_0+\widehat\theta_1)-C.
 \label{integrated:linked_funding:eq:estimate}
\end{equation}
The partialling-out orthogonality and joint nuisance-product/action-square
rate premise appear in the inspected DML original \cite{dml2018}.
That paper's iid result does not by itself prove the dependent result here.
For this fixed stable Gaussian dictionary, fixed $q\ge q_{\min}>0$ and
independent invariant pilot, coefficient errors of order $M^{-1/2}$ give
product remainders $O_p(M^{-1})=o_p(T^{-1/2})$ when $M=4T$. This is a
pointwise growing-history statement, not a uniform guarantee when audit
probability tends to zero or persistence tends to one. A falsely supplied
probability changes the population moment before any rate argument applies.

\section{Audit variance on a shared calendar}

Define the oracle scalar influence for $V$ using focal outcomes as $\psi_t^F$.
With $c_t=\tfrac12\sum_s1\{S_t=s\}v_t/Q_s$, the pseudo-outcome influence is
\begin{equation}
 \psi_t^Z=\psi_t^F+a_t,
 \qquad a_t=c_t(R_t/q_t-1)w'(F_t-B_t).\label{integrated:linked_funding:eq:decompose}
\end{equation}
Conditionally on $\mathcal H$, $\E a_t=0$. Independent audit randomization
also gives $\E[a_ta_u\mid\mathcal H]=0$ for $u\ne t$, and every $a_t$ is
uncorrelated with any complete-history score $\psi_u^F$. Its variance is
\begin{equation}
 \E a_t^2=\E\!\left[c_t^2(1/q_t-1)\{w'(F_t-B_t)\}^2\right].
 \label{integrated:linked_funding:eq:auditvar}
\end{equation}
The added audit term therefore changes lag zero only. This conclusion uses
independent audit draws \emph{conditional on the complete histories}; a
persistent audit mechanism or correlated label errors needs a new argument.

For the latent focal score, the monograph's innovation filtration condition
averages the current exogenous action innovation and shocks through $t+H$
to zero, conditional on the full exogenous driver path and shocks before $t$.
The score is measurable through $t+H$. A later score more than $H$ dates away
has conditional mean zero given the earlier one, giving zero covariance
beyond $H$. The scores need not be $H$-dependent. Stable roots, finite higher
moments and stationary mixing supply the score CLT; the finite horizon by
itself is insufficient. This condition fails under the deliberately endogenous
innovation law.

Using the fitted scalar score
\begin{equation}
 \widehat\psi_t=\frac{T}{2}
 \sum_s\frac{1\{S_t=s\}\widehat v_t
   (\widehat u_t-\widehat\theta_s\widehat v_t)}
  {\sum_j1\{S_j=s\}\widehat v_j^2},
\end{equation}
center it by its sample mean and write the centered scores as $d_t$.
The selected variance estimate and normal interval are
\begin{equation}
 \widehat s^2=T^{-2}\!\left\{\sum_t d_t^2+
       2\sum_{k=1}^{H}\sum_{t=k+1}^{T}d_td_{t-k}\right\},
 \qquad \widehat V\pm z_{.975}\widehat s.\label{integrated:linked_funding:eq:variance}
\end{equation}
The empirical scores include audit noise, so adding a second independent
``audit variance'' would double count it. We refuse nonpositive/nonfinite
variance, absent sampled strata and deterministic scores at the numerical
roundoff floor. We do not clip a negative estimate into an interval.
The inspected Newey--West original proves positive semidefiniteness for its
Bartlett weighting \cite{newey1986}; this untapered, fixed-horizon scalar
construction is different and inherits no such guarantee. Its advantage
within the stated filtration law is avoiding attenuation of nonzero short-lag
covariances.

\section{Fresh comparison and retained adverse evidence}

The eight designs and three procedures were fixed before their final draws.
Each design has 600 independent requests, the same evaluation/pilot histories
across methods, and distinct random streams for count audits and outcome-linked
audits. The count method uses 1,600 correctness labels per stratum and the
previous half-sum/half-difference rectangular projection. The linked methods
use $q=.25$ in both histories, except the $q=.10$ low-audit cell. Near rank
means $(p_0,p_1)=(.55,.515)$; exact rank means $(.5,.5)$; the baseline is
$(.9,.85)$. The persistent cell changes the balance root from .82 to .96.
Three adverse cells separately violate exogeneity, actual inclusion or
label truth. Neither the reported probabilities nor the declarations test
their own truth.

All 4,800 requests produced computed sets for all three procedures. The
linked intervals were finite in every request. Table~\ref{integrated:linked_funding:tab:coverage}
reports all-request coverage and availability, and
Table~\ref{integrated:linked_funding:tab:diagnostics} retains bias, empirical dispersion and labels.
Exact-binomial Monte Carlo intervals are saved for each coverage frequency,
with Bonferroni simultaneous control across all 24 design/method combinations.
They describe Monte Carlo uncertainty under these selected laws only.

\begin{table}[htbp]\centering\small
\caption{Fresh 600-request cells. C uses count-audit transformed sets; A uses augmented linked outcomes; I uses inverse audit weighting. Widths are conditional finite medians in thousands of USD.}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrrr}\toprule
Design & C cover & A cover & I cover & C finite & A finite & A width & I width\\\midrule
Baseline & 600 & 564 & 572 & 600 & 600 & 524 & 1091\\
Near rank & 600 & 572 & 575 & 48 & 600 & 529 & 1110\\
Exact rank & 600 & 559 & 553 & 0 & 600 & 527 & 1105\\
Low linked audit & 600 & 572 & 568 & 51 & 600 & 599 & 1762\\
Persistent & 600 & 571 & 562 & 55 & 600 & 1413 & 2731\\
False exogeneity & 600 & 148 & 464 & 45 & 600 & 591 & 1203\\
Wrong inclusion & 600 & 378 & 159 & 53 & 600 & 450 & 698\\
Noisy labels & 600 & 528 & 549 & 38 & 600 & 508 & 1054\\
\bottomrule\end{tabular}\label{integrated:linked_funding:tab:coverage}\end{table}
\begin{table}[htbp]\centering\small
\caption{Augmented-estimator diagnostics. Bias and empirical SD are thousands of USD, conditional on computed intervals. Labels count evaluation plus independent-pilot origin histories; each resolves all seven response dates.}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}\toprule
Design & Bias & Empirical SD & Mean SE / SD & Mean linked labels\\\midrule
Baseline & -12.7 & 135.0 & 1.002 & 1499.2\\
Near rank & -0.8 & 130.4 & 1.048 & 1498.6\\
Exact rank & 9.1 & 144.4 & 0.943 & 1502.0\\
Low linked audit & -3.2 & 155.0 & 1.008 & 600.7\\
Persistent & 7.9 & 368.3 & 0.989 & 1498.3\\
False exogeneity & 388.1 & 158.5 & 0.955 & 1500.5\\
Wrong inclusion & -179.2 & 112.5 & 1.034 & 598.7\\
Noisy labels & -84.7 & 132.9 & 0.986 & 1501.7\\
\bottomrule\end{tabular}\label{integrated:linked_funding:tab:diagnostics}\end{table}

\FloatBarrier

In the near-rank cell, the count set was whole-line in 552/600 requests;
its 48 finite sets had median width USD 17.396 million. The augmented
interval was finite in all 600 with median width USD 528,513 and coverage
572/600. In all 48 paired finite requests it was narrower. At exact rank,
the count set was whole-line in all 600 requests, while the augmented median
width was USD 526,663. This is new outcome information resolving an old
mean ambiguity; it is not an improvement obtained from the old count data
alone. There is no paired finite width ratio at exact rank because the
baseline has no finite set there.

Finite precision does not establish 95\% calibration. Exact-rank augmented
coverage is $559/600=.9317$, with mean SE/empirical SD .943. Its individual
Monte Carlo interval is approximately $[.9084,.9505]$ and simultaneous
interval $[.8942,.9593]$. Baseline augmented coverage is \mbox{$564/600=.94$}.
These finite samples neither prove a general failure nor qualify uniform
nominal coverage. Under the persistent law, augmented median width is USD
1.413 million against synthetic value USD .752 million. The low-audit
design uses about 601 linked labels across both histories and has median
width USD 599,027. The ordinary $q=.25$ designs use about 1,500 labels.
Neither label count is an observed market price.

The augmented interval was narrower than inverse weighting in 4,793 of
4,800 matched requests and wider in seven wrong-inclusion requests. This
descriptive result includes invalid-law cells and has no universal ordering
interpretation. Even on the valid laws, reducing the augmented width relative
to the count box trades the box's strong conservatism for a normal-approximation
interval; one must assess coverage and precision together.

\section{Why truthful audits and exogeneity remain essential}

The false-exogeneity cell has innovation correlation .5 with a balance shock
of scale 2. The inherited observational-equivalence argument shifts the
observed action coefficient by one. The financial shift is therefore
$\sum_h w_h(.82)^h=387{,}575$ USD. The observed augmented bias is USD 388,119,
and coverage is only 148/600. Resolving focal identity does not resolve action
confounding; the wide count set's 600/600 coverage in this cell supplies no
causal validation.

If actual inclusion is $q_a$ but the caller supplies $q_d$, then
\begin{equation}
 \E[Z_t\mid\mathcal H]
  =B_t+\frac{q_a}{q_d}(F_t-B_t).\label{integrated:linked_funding:eq:wrongq}
\end{equation}
With $q_a=.10$, $q_d=.25$, focal coefficient 2 and companion .5, the
augmented coefficient is 1.55, not 2. Its population monetary bias is about
USD $-174{,}409$, compared with the saved bias USD $-179{,}157$. Coverage
is 378/600. Pure inverse weighting instead targets coefficient .8, explaining
its larger negative bias and 159/600 coverage. This failure happens even
with independent selection; more complicated unknown selection laws add
further obligations.

If selected labels independently flip with probability $e$, the apparent
focal mean becomes $(1-e)F_t+eG_t$, where $G_t$ is the companion. For $e=.15$
the coefficient shifts by $.15(.5-2)=-.225$, producing population monetary
bias about USD $-87{,}204$. The augmented observed bias is USD $-84{,}726$
and coverage 528/600. Label-error correction would need external gold truth
and its sampling uncertainty; pretending that the label is exact has not
performed such a correction. These population identities and the numerical
audit-variance decomposition are project checks, not source-derived bank
guarantees.

\section{A design calculation before buying labels}

For a constant, truthful $q$, write
$K=\E[c_t^2\{w'(F_t-B_t)\}^2]$ and let $\Omega_F$ be the latent focal
long-run variance. Equation~\eqref{integrated:linked_funding:eq:auditvar} gives
$\Omega_Z=\Omega_F+(1/q-1)K$. If an external bank decision specifies a
maximum interval width $w_\star$, its first-order planning inequality is
\begin{equation}
 \Omega_F+(1/q-1)K\le
 L,\qquad L=T\left(\frac{w_\star}{2z_{.975}}\right)^2.
\end{equation}
When $K>0$ and $L\ge\Omega_F$, this gives
$q\ge K/(L-\Omega_F+K)$; if $L<\Omega_F$, even complete audit cannot meet
the width target at that calendar size. If $K=0$, audits add no variance in
this specific moment, but the caller still needs a valid information law.
This algebra is a planning approximation, not a finite-sample coverage
certificate. Values of $K$ and $\Omega_F$ used for a new design must come from
an independent design pilot and include their estimation uncertainty.

For the registered $M=4T$ pilot, expected linked-label demand is $q(T+M)=5qT$.
An economic comparison also needs history acquisition, truthful resolution,
pilot fitting, complete evaluation and review costs. Count labels and linked
histories are different services; 1,500 linked histories cannot be declared
cheaper than 3,200 correctness labels without actual prices. The bank has
supplied neither those prices nor $w_\star$. A fixed precision target and
authentic audit design are the next inputs required to turn this construction
into an investment or deployment decision.

\section*{Evidence, scope and continuation}

Independent enumeration checks the audit expectation and added diagonal
variance. Dense fitting and direct lag products agree with the implementation
across chunk boundaries to about $1.9\times10^{-14}$ relative error. Complete
audits reduce to observed focal histories; unsampled labels, invalid
probabilities and degenerate variance are rejected. The first 600 raw requests
were preserved as unqualified after an interval-serialization mismatch stopped
summary generation. The shared-format repair and round-trip check preceded a
fresh registered seed; none of those first requests is part of the 4,800 final
comparison. The saved journal reconstructs every summary and interval; eight
fixed requests were separately regenerated. These are author checks, not an
independent scientific review.

Resolving the actual customer history supplies information that
correctness counts alone can miss. Finite intervals at exact identity rank
one are demonstrated for the specified funding model; their calibration and
useful precision for a bank remain uncertain. Valid assignment, known audit
inclusion and accurate labels are essential. Independent origin audits do
not establish inference under arbitrary persistence of customer identity and
calendar shocks. Nonlinear policies, temporal graphs and other learners
require their own arguments. Bank adoption also needs independent review,
relevant operating trials and measured costs. The following comparison asks what stronger assignment and sampling information can achieve across funding, servicing, discovery and learning. It retains this chapter's distinction between finite availability, calibrated uncertainty and worthwhile financial precision; the stronger information has its own acquisition and feasibility costs.

The experiment preserves its specification, code, completed results
and the failed partial run. These records distinguish the reported evidence
from unperformed work. The literature cutoff remains 7 October 2026. No new exhaustive source search
was performed; the two inherited primary copies were reinspected for the
limited roles cited above.

\section{Identification from sampled linked outcomes}

Let $B_t=(Y_{t1}+Y_{t2})/2$ be the observed candidate average and let
$\mathcal H$ contain all complete focal/companion histories, assignments and
actions before audit randomization. Define the vector pseudo-outcome
\begin{equation}
 Z_t=B_t+\frac{R_t}{q_t}(F_t-B_t),\qquad
 \E[R_t\mid\mathcal H]=q_t.\label{integrated:linked_funding:eq:pseudo}
\end{equation}
Only the selected term requires the focal identity. Conditional expectation
gives $\E[Z_t\mid\mathcal H]=F_t$ exactly. No inverse $1/(2p_s-1)$ appears;
indeed swapping the candidate names and complementing the selected audit
labels leaves $Z_t$ unchanged. The alternative $Z_t^{I}=R_tF_t/q_t$ has the
same conditional expectation, but uses no observed average as augmentation.
There is no unconditional theorem that either has lower variance for every
possible outcome law.

The variance comparison follows from the audit randomization. Write
$f_t=w'F_t$ and $b_t=w'B_t$ for the focal and candidate-average monetary
outcomes before taking the action score. Conditional on the complete history,
the two scalar pseudo-outcomes have the same mean and audit variances
\begin{equation}\label{rel81:audit-augmentation}
 \operatorname{Var}(w'Z_t\mid\mathcal H)
   =(q_t^{-1}-1)(f_t-b_t)^2,\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(w'Z_t^I\mid\mathcal H)
   =(q_t^{-1}-1)f_t^2.
\end{equation}
For an incomplete audit, augmentation reduces this conditional contribution
exactly when the candidate average is closer to the focal outcome than zero
is. Multiplying by the squared oracle action-score coefficient and averaging
gives the corresponding comparison of added audit variance. Both constructions
retain the same latent focal score; estimated nuisance functions introduce
further finite-sample differences, so this calculation does not order every
fitted interval.

For a dimensionless illustration, stipulate a focal monetary outcome of two
and audit probability one quarter. A candidate average of 1.25 gives audit
variance 1.6875, compared with 12 under pure inverse weighting. If the candidate
average is instead five, the augmented variance is 27 and exceeds 12. These
values illustrate the conditional identity, not a new empirical funding case.
With complete auditing both additional variances vanish. The candidate average
can therefore be useful information without being a uniformly beneficial
augmentation under every outcome law.


Write $A_t=m_s(X_t)+v_t$ for the observed action, where $X_t$ contains the
fixed driver dictionary and stratum. Let
$\ell_s(X_t)=\E[w'Z_t\mid X_t,S_t=s]$.
Under the inherited exogenous-innovation response law,
\begin{equation}
 \E\!\left[1\{S_t=s\}v_t
   \{w'Z_t-\ell_s(X_t)-\theta_sv_t\}\right]=0,
 \qquad Q_s=\E[1\{S_t=s\}v_t^2]>0.\label{integrated:linked_funding:eq:score}
\end{equation}
Equation~\eqref{integrated:linked_funding:eq:pseudo} reduces this observed moment to the corresponding
focal-outcome moment. Thus the same intervention target is identified even
at $p_s=1/2$, provided the new audit law and the causal action restriction
are true. The conditional expectation identity does not establish exogeneity.

An independent 4,800-origin pilot selects among the fixed penalties
$0,1,10,100$ using first-half fitting and second-half standardized prediction
loss, then refits on its whole history. Its outcomes are the same audited
pseudo-outcomes, so its labels are part of the information bill. On the
1,200 evaluation origins, set $\widehat v_t=A_t-\widehat m_s(X_t)$ and
$\widehat u_t=w'Z_t-\widehat\ell_s(X_t)$. The estimator is
\begin{equation}
 \widehat\theta_s=
 \frac{\sum_t1\{S_t=s\}\widehat v_t\widehat u_t}
      {\sum_t1\{S_t=s\}\widehat v_t^2},\qquad
 \widehat V=\tfrac12(\widehat\theta_0+\widehat\theta_1)-C.
 \label{integrated:linked_funding:eq:estimate}
\end{equation}
The partialling-out orthogonality and joint nuisance-product/action-square
rate premise appear in the inspected DML original \citep{dml2018}.
That paper's iid result does not by itself prove the dependent result here.
For this fixed stable Gaussian dictionary, fixed $q\ge q_{\min}>0$ and
independent invariant pilot, coefficient errors of order $M^{-1/2}$ give
product remainders $O_p(M^{-1})=o_p(T^{-1/2})$ when $M=4T$. This is a
pointwise growing-history statement, not a uniform guarantee when audit
probability tends to zero or persistence tends to one. A falsely supplied
probability changes the population moment before any rate argument applies.

\section{Audit variance on a shared calendar}

Define the oracle scalar influence for $V$ using focal outcomes as $\psi_t^F$.
With $c_t=\tfrac12\sum_s1\{S_t=s\}v_t/Q_s$, the pseudo-outcome influence is
\begin{equation}
 \psi_t^Z=\psi_t^F+a_t,
 \qquad a_t=c_t(R_t/q_t-1)w'(F_t-B_t).\label{integrated:linked_funding:eq:decompose}
\end{equation}
Conditionally on $\mathcal H$, $\E a_t=0$. Independent audit randomization
also gives $\E[a_ta_u\mid\mathcal H]=0$ for $u\ne t$, and every $a_t$ is
uncorrelated with any complete-history score $\psi_u^F$. Its variance is
\begin{equation}
 \E a_t^2=\E\!\left[c_t^2(1/q_t-1)\{w'(F_t-B_t)\}^2\right].
 \label{integrated:linked_funding:eq:auditvar}
\end{equation}
The added audit term therefore changes lag zero only. This conclusion uses
independent audit draws \emph{conditional on the complete histories}; a
persistent audit mechanism or correlated label errors needs a new argument.

For the latent focal score, the monograph's innovation filtration condition
averages the current exogenous action innovation and shocks through $t+H$
to zero, conditional on the full exogenous driver path and shocks before $t$.
The score is measurable through $t+H$. A later score more than $H$ dates away
has conditional mean zero given the earlier one, giving zero covariance
beyond $H$. The scores need not be $H$-dependent. Stable roots, finite higher
moments and stationary mixing supply the score CLT; the finite horizon by
itself is insufficient. This condition fails under the deliberately endogenous
innovation law.

Using the fitted scalar score
\begin{equation}
 \widehat\psi_t=\frac{T}{2}
 \sum_s\frac{1\{S_t=s\}\widehat v_t
   (\widehat u_t-\widehat\theta_s\widehat v_t)}
  {\sum_j1\{S_j=s\}\widehat v_j^2},
\end{equation}
center it by its sample mean and write the centered scores as $d_t$.
The selected variance estimate and normal interval are
\begin{equation}
 \widehat s^2=T^{-2}\!\left\{\sum_t d_t^2+
       2\sum_{k=1}^{H}\sum_{t=k+1}^{T}d_td_{t-k}\right\},
 \qquad \widehat V\pm z_{.975}\widehat s.\label{integrated:linked_funding:eq:variance}
\end{equation}
The empirical scores include audit noise, so adding a second independent
``audit variance'' would double count it. We refuse nonpositive/nonfinite
variance, absent sampled strata and deterministic scores at the numerical
roundoff floor. We do not clip a negative estimate into an interval.
The inspected Newey--West original proves positive semidefiniteness for its
Bartlett weighting \citep{newey1986}; this untapered, fixed-horizon scalar
construction is different and inherits no such guarantee. Its advantage
within the stated filtration law is avoiding attenuation of nonzero short-lag
covariances.

\section{Fresh comparison and retained adverse evidence}

The eight designs and three procedures were fixed before their final draws.
Each design has 600 independent requests, the same evaluation/pilot histories
across methods, and distinct random streams for count audits and outcome-linked
audits. The count method uses 1,600 correctness labels per stratum and the
previous half-sum/half-difference rectangular projection. The linked methods
use $q=.25$ in both histories, except the $q=.10$ low-audit cell. Near rank
means $(p_0,p_1)=(.55,.515)$; exact rank means $(.5,.5)$; the baseline is
$(.9,.85)$. The persistent cell changes the balance root from .82 to .96.
Three adverse cells separately violate exogeneity, actual inclusion or
label truth. Neither the reported probabilities nor the declarations test
their own truth.

All 4,800 requests produced computed sets for all three procedures. The
linked intervals were finite in every request. Table~\ref{integrated:linked_funding:tab:coverage}
reports all-request coverage and availability, and
Table~\ref{integrated:linked_funding:tab:diagnostics} retains bias, empirical dispersion and labels.
Exact-binomial Monte Carlo intervals are saved for each coverage frequency,
with Bonferroni simultaneous control across all 24 design/method combinations.
They describe Monte Carlo uncertainty under these selected laws only.

\begin{table}[htbp]\centering\small
\caption{Fresh 600-request cells. C uses count-audit transformed sets; A uses augmented linked outcomes; I uses inverse audit weighting. Widths are conditional finite medians in thousands of USD.}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrrr}\toprule
Design & C cover & A cover & I cover & C finite & A finite & A width & I width\\\midrule
Baseline & 600 & 564 & 572 & 600 & 600 & 524 & 1091\\
Near rank & 600 & 572 & 575 & 48 & 600 & 529 & 1110\\
Exact rank & 600 & 559 & 553 & 0 & 600 & 527 & 1105\\
Low linked audit & 600 & 572 & 568 & 51 & 600 & 599 & 1762\\
Persistent & 600 & 571 & 562 & 55 & 600 & 1413 & 2731\\
False exogeneity & 600 & 148 & 464 & 45 & 600 & 591 & 1203\\
Wrong inclusion & 600 & 378 & 159 & 53 & 600 & 450 & 698\\
Noisy labels & 600 & 528 & 549 & 38 & 600 & 508 & 1054\\
\bottomrule\end{tabular}\label{integrated:linked_funding:tab:coverage}\end{table}
\begin{table}[htbp]\centering\small
\caption{Augmented-estimator diagnostics. Bias and empirical SD are thousands of USD, conditional on computed intervals. Labels count evaluation plus independent-pilot origin histories; each resolves all seven response dates.}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}\toprule
Design & Bias & Empirical SD & Mean SE / SD & Mean linked labels\\\midrule
Baseline & -12.7 & 135.0 & 1.002 & 1499.2\\
Near rank & -0.8 & 130.4 & 1.048 & 1498.6\\
Exact rank & 9.1 & 144.4 & 0.943 & 1502.0\\
Low linked audit & -3.2 & 155.0 & 1.008 & 600.7\\
Persistent & 7.9 & 368.3 & 0.989 & 1498.3\\
False exogeneity & 388.1 & 158.5 & 0.955 & 1500.5\\
Wrong inclusion & -179.2 & 112.5 & 1.034 & 598.7\\
