\FloatBarrier

In the near-rank cell, the count set was whole-line in 552/600 requests;
its 48 finite sets had median width USD 17.396 million. The augmented
interval was finite in all 600 with median width USD 528,513 and coverage
572/600. In all 48 paired finite requests it was narrower. At exact rank,
the count set was whole-line in all 600 requests, while the augmented median
width was USD 526,663. This is new outcome information resolving an old
mean ambiguity; it is not an improvement obtained from the old count data
alone. There is no paired finite width ratio at exact rank because the
baseline has no finite set there.

Finite precision does not establish 95\% calibration. Exact-rank augmented
coverage is $559/600=.9317$, with mean SE/empirical SD .943. Its individual
Monte Carlo interval is approximately $[.9084,.9505]$ and simultaneous
interval $[.8942,.9593]$. Baseline augmented coverage is \mbox{$564/600=.94$}.
These finite samples neither prove a general failure nor qualify uniform
nominal coverage. Under the persistent law, augmented median width is USD
1.413 million against synthetic value USD .752 million. The low-audit
design uses about 601 linked labels across both histories and has median
width USD 599,027. The ordinary $q=.25$ designs use about 1,500 labels.
Neither label count is an observed market price.

The augmented interval was narrower than inverse weighting in 4,793 of
4,800 matched requests and wider in seven wrong-inclusion requests. This
descriptive result includes invalid-law cells and has no universal ordering
interpretation. Even on the valid laws, reducing the augmented width relative
to the count box trades the box's strong conservatism for a normal-approximation
interval; one must assess coverage and precision together.

\section{Why truthful audits and exogeneity remain essential}

The false-exogeneity cell has innovation correlation .5 with a balance shock
of scale 2. The inherited observational-equivalence argument shifts the
observed action coefficient by one. The financial shift is therefore
$\sum_h w_h(.82)^h=387{,}575$ USD. The observed augmented bias is USD 388,119,
and coverage is only 148/600. Resolving focal identity does not resolve action
confounding; the wide count set's 600/600 coverage in this cell supplies no
causal validation.

If actual inclusion is $q_a$ but the caller supplies $q_d$, then
\begin{equation}
 \E[Z_t\mid\mathcal H]
  =B_t+\frac{q_a}{q_d}(F_t-B_t).\label{integrated:linked_funding:eq:wrongq}
\end{equation}
With $q_a=.10$, $q_d=.25$, focal coefficient 2 and companion .5, the
augmented coefficient is 1.55, not 2. Its population monetary bias is about
USD $-174{,}409$, compared with the saved bias USD $-179{,}157$. Coverage
is 378/600. Pure inverse weighting instead targets coefficient .8, explaining
its larger negative bias and 159/600 coverage. This failure happens even
with independent selection; more complicated unknown selection laws add
further obligations.

If selected labels independently flip with probability $e$, the apparent
focal mean becomes $(1-e)F_t+eG_t$, where $G_t$ is the companion. For $e=.15$
the coefficient shifts by $.15(.5-2)=-.225$, producing population monetary
bias about USD $-87{,}204$. The augmented observed bias is USD $-84{,}726$
and coverage 528/600. Label-error correction would need external gold truth
and its sampling uncertainty; pretending that the label is exact has not
performed such a correction. These population identities and the numerical
audit-variance decomposition are project checks, not source-derived bank
guarantees.

\section{A design calculation before buying labels}

For a constant, truthful $q$, write
$K=\E[c_t^2\{w'(F_t-B_t)\}^2]$ and let $\Omega_F$ be the latent focal
long-run variance. Equation~\eqref{integrated:linked_funding:eq:auditvar} gives
$\Omega_Z=\Omega_F+(1/q-1)K$. If an external bank decision specifies a
maximum interval width $w_\star$, its first-order planning inequality is
\begin{equation}
 \Omega_F+(1/q-1)K\le
 L,\qquad L=T\left(\frac{w_\star}{2z_{.975}}\right)^2.
\end{equation}
When $K>0$ and $L\ge\Omega_F$, this gives
$q\ge K/(L-\Omega_F+K)$; if $L<\Omega_F$, even complete audit cannot meet
the width target at that calendar size. If $K=0$, audits add no variance in
this specific moment, but the caller still needs a valid information law.
This algebra is a planning approximation, not a finite-sample coverage
certificate. Values of $K$ and $\Omega_F$ used for a new design must come from
an independent design pilot and include their estimation uncertainty.

For the registered $M=4T$ pilot, expected linked-label demand is $q(T+M)=5qT$.
An economic comparison also needs history acquisition, truthful resolution,
pilot fitting, complete evaluation and review costs. Count labels and linked
histories are different services; 1,500 linked histories cannot be declared
cheaper than 3,200 correctness labels without actual prices. The bank has
supplied neither those prices nor $w_\star$. A fixed precision target and
authentic audit design are the next inputs required to turn this construction
into an investment or deployment decision.

\section*{Evidence, scope and continuation}

Independent enumeration checks the audit expectation and added diagonal
variance. Dense fitting and direct lag products agree with the implementation
across chunk boundaries to about $1.9\times10^{-14}$ relative error. Complete
audits reduce to observed focal histories; unsampled labels, invalid
probabilities and degenerate variance are rejected. The first 600 raw requests
were preserved as unqualified after an interval-serialization mismatch stopped
summary generation. The shared-format repair and round-trip check preceded a
fresh registered seed; none of those first requests is part of the 4,800 final
comparison. The saved journal reconstructs every summary and interval; eight
fixed requests were separately regenerated. These are author checks, not an
independent scientific review.

Resolving the actual customer history supplies information that
correctness counts alone can miss. Finite intervals at exact identity rank
one are demonstrated for the specified funding model; their calibration and
useful precision for a bank remain uncertain. Valid assignment, known audit
inclusion and accurate labels are essential. Independent origin audits do
not establish inference under arbitrary persistence of customer identity and
calendar shocks. Nonlinear policies, temporal graphs and other learners
require their own arguments. Bank adoption also needs independent review,
relevant operating trials and measured costs. The following comparison asks what stronger assignment and sampling information can achieve across funding, servicing, discovery and learning. It retains this chapter's distinction between finite availability, calibrated uncertainty and worthwhile financial precision; the stronger information has its own acquisition and feasibility costs.

The experiment preserves its specification, code, completed results
and the failed partial run. These records distinguish the reported evidence
from unperformed work. The literature cutoff remains 7 October 2026. No new exhaustive source search
was performed; the two inherited primary copies were reinspected for the
limited roles cited above.

\chapter{Comparing methods by what they estimate}
\label{sw:interfaces}

\section{The decision determines the comparison}

A bank does not need an abstract winner among causal libraries. It needs to
know whether a particular computation answers its particular question. A
funding desk might ask how changing a quoted rate affects twelve-month retained
balances. A servicing team might ask when to contact an account whose financial
condition changes after earlier contacts. A model-risk team might ask whether
two plausible causal diagrams imply different intervention decisions. These
questions require different information, estimands and outputs, even when the
software accepts the same rectangular dataset.

The useful comparison therefore starts with a scientific interface. Let
\(q=(\mathcal P,A,Y,h,s)\) denote a target population \(\mathcal P\), an intervention
\(A\), an outcome \(Y\), a horizon \(h\), and a scale \(s\). A request also supplies
an information history, a causal model or model class, a sampling design and
explicit assumptions. An implementation may identify a functional of the
observed distribution, estimate that functional, characterize uncertainty, or
report that its method does not support the request. These are different
operations. A scalar with a standard error is inadequate if the scientifically
appropriate answer is an equivalence class of graphs, a disconnected set of
effects, or a symbolic expression for which no numerical estimator has been
provided.

This distinction organizes the selected software comparisons developed here.
The evidence is package-authored documentation and selected implementation
paths at explicitly recorded revisions. A documented option is compared with
the relevant source where available. These inspections establish what was
read and what interfaces expose; they do not establish installation success,
numerical parity, statistical calibration or suitability for confidential bank
data. The banking calculations are project examples with specified mechanisms,
not measurements from those packages or from a bank.

The language of a package matters because it constrains integration, but it is
not a scientific ranking. R offers several specialized design and longitudinal
interfaces. Python offers graph, discovery and orchestration interfaces.
Tetrad supplies a Java implementation family. aGrUM exposes C++ causal-model
and identification interfaces with a related Python wrapper. A wrapper can
reduce deployment effort while changing exception behavior or result types;
a port can make deployment more uniform while introducing a second numerical
implementation to validate. These tradeoffs are assessed at the operation and
result boundary, rather than by counting languages or API names.

\section{An observed relationship can leave its causal direction unresolved}

Consider a deliberately simple project example involving a standardized quoted
rate \(X\) and a standardized balance response \(Y\). Two linear Gaussian
structural models are
\begin{align}
 \mathcal M_1 &: X=U_X,\qquad Y=0.4X+U_Y,
    &\operatorname{var}(U_X)&=1,&\operatorname{var}(U_Y)&=0.84,\\
 \mathcal M_2 &: Y=V_Y,\qquad X=0.4Y+V_X,
    &\operatorname{var}(V_Y)&=1,&\operatorname{var}(V_X)&=0.84.
\end{align}
All disturbances are centered and independent within their model. Both models
generate a bivariate normal distribution with unit marginal variances and
covariance \(0.4\). Under \(\mathcal M_1\), increasing \(X\) by one standardized
unit through an intervention changes the mean of \(Y\) by \(0.4\). Under
\(\mathcal M_2\), replacing the equation for \(X\) leaves \(Y\) unchanged. The
observational covariance does not choose between these answers. The example
is an algebraic construction, not an assertion that either model describes
actual funding behavior.

A graph interface should therefore preserve the distinction between an
asserted causal DAG and a class learned from observations. The inspected
Tetrad PC documentation states causal sufficiency, acyclicity and faithfulness,
uses an externally supplied conditional-independence test, and describes CPDAG
output. Its FCI search path contains circle endpoints, possible-d-separation
processing and PAG-oriented logic. An inconsistent class-level description
calling that output a CPDAG cannot serve as the interchange specification.
The algorithm path and the actual endpoint representation must be checked
together. \cite{v12_sw_tetrad}

The inspected causal-learn PC interface makes the dependence on procedural
choices explicit: it accepts a conditional-independence test, a test level,
a stabilized skeleton option, collider-orientation rules, conflict priorities
and background knowledge. Its graph matrix can encode two arrowheads, and
one documented conflict priority deliberately permits that outcome. Thus a
bidirected mark produced during a PC conflict must not automatically be
translated into an FCI-style statement about latent confounding. The FCI
interface separately documents tails, arrowheads and circles and marks its
result as a PAG. Both endpoint values and the method that produced them
belong in the result. \cite{v12_sw_causallearn}

Search bounds also belong in that result. causal-learn exposes a conditioning
bound for PC and adjacency-depth and discriminating-path bounds for FCI. These
can change the computation being performed. A time limit or restricted search
is not merely a performance annotation if it changes which separating sets or
orientation rules can be examined. The proposed adapter must retain these
settings and distinguish completed bounded search from interrupted search.
The conditional-independence test level is a setting of that test; no whole-graph
confidence level follows from the presence of a single parameter named alpha.

For a banking application, background knowledge should specify the proposition
being added and its provenance. An accounting identity, a verified temporal
ordering and a language model's directional suggestion carry different
evidentiary weight. A useful graph object retains alternatives until additional
information resolves them. Exporting the first available DAG would convert
computational convenience into an unrecorded identifying assumption.

The detailed Java and Python comparisons now follow that distinction through
specific implementations. The Java cases show how numerical failure,
classifier objectives and matrix conventions can change the interpretation.
The Python cases extend the comparison to weighted and partially directed
outputs, continuous acyclicity conditions and learned structural models.
Their separate examples test different ways an effect interpretation can be
lost; they do not rank engines on unmatched default outputs.

\section{Symbolic identification and numerical evaluation}

The graph comparisons establish what an output can mean before it enters an
intervention calculation. The next distinction concerns that calculation
itself: a graph can support an identifying expression even when the supplied
data or implementation cannot evaluate it. Conversely, an implementation
failure supplies no proof that the effect is unidentified.

aGrUM's inspected \texttt{CausalModel} documentation permits a causal DAG with
an optional observational Bayesian network. Structural operations, including
backdoor/frontdoor queries and construction of do-calculus expressions, can
be available when conditional probability tables are absent. Operations that
read those tables then raise an unavailable-operation exception. This is a
useful separation: a funding query can be identified relative to a supplied
graph before a distribution has been fitted. It does not follow that the
effect can already be reported numerically. \cite{v12_sw_agrum}

The selected \texttt{CausalImpact} implementation first attempts appropriate
backdoor and frontdoor paths, then invokes a do-calculus routine. The inspected
dispatch supports a comparison of these routes; it is not a verification of
the full ID or IDC algorithm. A particularly consequential detail is the
handling of failures. A not-yet-implemented method and a hedge exception are
caught in different branches, but each produces a formula with no expression
tree. Their explanation strings differ. An adapter that reads only the boolean
\texttt{isIdentified} would erase the distinction between an unavailable
implementation and a causal nonidentification result. \cite{v12_sw_agrum}

These outputs should instead be represented as separate states:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{p{.29\textwidth}p{.60\textwidth}}
\toprule
State & Required scientific meaning\\
\midrule
Identified expression & A functional has been obtained under the declared graph and assumptions.\\
Numerical result unavailable & The expression may exist, but distributions, estimators or numerical prerequisites are absent.\\
Method unsupported & This implementation cannot perform the requested method or graph operation.\\
Nonidentified in the model & The supplied causal model and information do not determine the requested functional, with the relevant reason retained.\\
Computational failure & The attempted operation failed; the failure supplies no causal conclusion.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

pgmpy's guide also separates identification from estimation and uses annotated
graph roles. Its adjustment interface returns a graph or collection of graphs
and a success indicator. Source inspection narrows what the guide alone would
suggest: the \texttt{minimal\_variance} branch raises
\texttt{NotImplementedError}, despite the guide's description of variance-optimal
adjustment. The minimal branch rejects multiple exposures or outcomes. The
selected implementation contains a graph-type TODO, so the broad graph-type
docstring does not by itself qualify every graph class. \cite{v12_sw_pgmpy}

An unsuccessful adjustment search is also narrower than failure of general
causal identification. The package guide discusses a frontdoor route as a
distinct alternative. The proposed product should retain the method attempted
and its applicability rather than mapping every false adjustment indicator to
``causal effect impossible.'' For a bank analyst, that distinction determines
whether the next action is to consider another identifying functional, obtain
additional information, or correct an unsupported request.

\section{Effect candidates, hulls and confidence sets}

Tetrad's inspected IDA constructor requires a legal partially directed acyclic
graph and continuous data. Its total-effect routine produces regression-based
candidates across eligible parent configurations. Candidate-specific exceptions
are caught and logged without a typed failed-candidate object in the returned
list. Consequently, the downstream interface needs enough information to
distinguish a genuinely small candidate set from a larger intended calculation
whose members partly failed. \cite{v12_sw_tetrad}

Three numerical objects must remain distinct. A candidate multiset records
effects attached to graph alternatives. Its convex hull fills all values
between the smallest and largest candidate. A confidence set is a random set
with a stated coverage interpretation under a sampling law. Neither the
candidate list nor its hull becomes a confidence set merely because it has
endpoints.

The inspected IDA distance helper illustrates the distinction. For project
values \(S=\{0,0.8\}\) and hypothetical truth \(\theta=0.4\),
\[
 d(\theta,S)=\min_{s\in S}|\theta-s|=0.4,
 \qquad d(\theta,\operatorname{hull}(S))=0.
\]
The selected helper uses the minimum--maximum interval, so it computes the
second quantity. Its empty-list branch returns the supplied true effect, which
could even be negative. These are static observations about that helper,
accompanied by project arithmetic; no Tetrad execution is claimed. They imply
that evaluation and transport must define their set object before choosing a
distance metric. An empty set of available estimates requires an explicit
unavailable or failed state, not an arbitrary scalar score. \cite{v12_sw_tetrad}

The initial adoption preference is therefore to evaluate the existing Java
engine through a narrow process boundary, with endpoint roundtrips and typed
failure handling. Porting an isolated helper would omit the graph semantics
that make its output meaningful. For aGrUM, the existing C++ core and Python
wrapper deserve comparison before any reimplementation. Its saved build files
declare version 3.2.0 and C++20; these are environment requirements to test,
not evidence that the proposed binary or wrapper already works.

## Edit 281
docs/release/2026-10-29/source/docs/writing-repair/2026-10-29/src/f50f32c01b8a03ec.tex

Use parenthetical supporting citations at the individually inspected non-subject occurrences; bare cite renders author names as stray prose.

Substantive destination: All substantive text remains at the same position. The only replacement is the citation command name cite→citep. Every equation, numeric input, citation key, label, assumption, negative result and alternative survives in order.

Before:
~~~text
\chapter{Evaluating causal assistance without changing the question}
\label{la:evaluation}

The question throughout this chapter is whether assistance preserves a banking decision while improving its resolution at an acceptable cost. The opening defines the comparison; the coverage screen and prospective experiment then show what a finite evaluation could establish. The source studies test the reference answers, exposure history, adjudication and scoring rules on which that experiment would rely. Finally, the evaluator, memory and toolkit comparisons follow those requirements into a working interface. Their different failure mechanisms cannot be reduced to a single accuracy score.

\section{The benchmark unit is a causal problem}

An agent can produce a plausible report, execute valid code and still answer
the wrong causal question. Evaluation must follow the entire chain from
business meaning through assumptions and identification to uncertainty,
availability and decision loss. A benchmark of text fluency, graph edit
distance or successful tool calls measures only part of that chain.

CLadder demonstrates the value of formal questions with varied verbalizations,
including commonsense and deliberately unfamiliar or conflicting stories.
The inspected paper also identifies language-to-formal-tool formulation as
a continuing challenge. Its historical binary-answer accuracy is evidence
about those tasks and models; it is not a measurement of effect coverage,
decision loss or banking readiness. \cite{v12_la_2312_04350}

CausalDS expands the evaluation object to narrated synthetic mechanisms,
data and a separate observation model. Its inspected results show why
symbolic success, uncertainty quality, abstention and cost should be reported
separately. Its author-reported exam and repeated runs are useful design
evidence, not model evaluations conducted in this project. A generated world
with known truth also remains different from authentic bank data whose
semantic and assignment mechanisms must be established externally.
\cite{v12_la_2607_08093}

The proposed experimental unit is therefore an independently generated or
independently adjudicated causal mechanism and question. Several phrasings,
label conditions or stochastic model calls can be nested within that unit.
They do not create new independent worlds. Repeating one problem fifty times
can measure response variation for that problem; it does not provide fifty
independent demonstrations of general causal competence.

\section{Matched information and meaningful alternatives}

The prospective design compares a fixed numerical workflow, a language-only
workflow, retrieval assistance, a hybrid of numerical tools and typed model
proposals, and structured expert workflows with and without assistance.
Each arm needs a declared information budget. If one receives the true
causal graph and another must discover it, their effect-estimation scores
do not isolate the value of language assistance. If retrieval adds a valid
institutional fact, that information gain should be distinguished from a
better inference algorithm.

Eight strata are proposed: independent sufficient DAGs; latent-variable
graph classes; temporal data with known clocks; treatment-confounder
feedback; panel or quasi-experimental assignment; proxies, linkage and
selection; weak or nonidentifying effects; and ambiguous business targets
or monetary loss. Label and evidence conditions cross ordinary descriptions,
unfamiliar labels, misleading or irrelevant material, and conflict between
numerical evidence and text. These strata test different failure mechanisms
rather than treating all causal questions as interchangeable.

The current planning allocation is 400 mechanisms, with 50 per stratum and
three stochastic repetitions nested within each mechanism. This is an
allocation for developing the design, not a frozen final sample size or a
power calculation. For orientation, the worst-case normal approximation for
one Bernoulli proportion at 400 independent observations has half-width
\(1.96\sqrt{0.25/400}\), approximately 0.049. Paired differences, stratified
outcomes and rare severe errors require their own precision design. A
development pilot would inform that design and must be excluded from the
final test. The six task families developed in Section~\ref{exec13:live-design} describe workflow functions, whereas the eight strata here describe scientific conditions; they are different design dimensions. That later section uses additional sample sizes to illustrate error control, power and cost. Those calculations refine the choice of a trial rather than combine into an approved allocation.

Both natural-workflow and matched-budget comparisons can be useful. The
first asks what an analyst can achieve with a realistic workflow, including
review. The second asks what changes when information or computation is
controlled. Neither should hide extra expert time, repeated retrieval or
retry costs. The comparison must state which question it answers.

\section{A target error can survive perfect arithmetic}

An exact project IV construction illustrates a benchmark-label hazard.
Let a randomized binary instrument \(Z\) affect treatment for half the
population, the compliers; the other half never receives treatment. Set
\(Y(0)=0\) for everyone, \(Y(1)=1\) for compliers and \(Y(1)=3\) for
never-takers. Treatment equals \(Z\) for compliers and zero otherwise.
Randomization, exclusion and monotonicity hold in this construction.

The observed outcome difference across instrument values is \(0.5\) and
the treatment-probability difference is \(0.5\), so the Wald ratio is one.
The population ATE is two. Changing the never-takers' unobserved treated
outcome changes the population ATE without changing the observed law. A
scorer that calls the unrestricted Wald ratio the population ATE would
reward a target substitution. This is a finite counterexample supporting
review of generator assumptions, not a claim that every IV question in a
named benchmark uses this construction.

The same concern applies to trimming, overlap weighting and selected
populations. A language answer can reproduce the right formula for a
different target. Evaluation should therefore compare the population,
measure, action, comparator, horizon and units before comparing the numeric
answer. Critical semantic errors deserve their own count, even when a
numeric discrepancy happens to be small in the test mechanism.

\section{Graphs, sets and refusals need separate scores}

Graph evaluation should compare adjacency and endpoint statements against
the appropriate identifiable class. A justified circle or undirected edge
should not be penalized merely because a simulator internally selected one
fully directed graph. Orientation informativeness can be reported alongside
validity. This makes a method that preserves genuine ambiguity distinguishable
from one that returns little information and from one that confidently
overorients the graph.

Identification outcomes also need separate labels. Scientific
nonidentification, unsupported implementation, malformed output, explicit
abstention, timeout and missing input are not the same event. A well-designed
agent can correctly identify a missing premise without successfully computing
an effect. A backend can be unable to implement a valid functional. Combining
these into one ``incorrect'' or ``no answer'' category would obscure the
remedy.

For identified scalar targets, bias and error can be meaningful. For reported
sets, evaluate coverage, topology, finite availability and size. Whole-line
answers can have high coverage and little decision value. A method that
returns short intervals on a selected easy subset needs an all-request
availability denominator. Unbounded and disconnected sets must remain in the
evaluation rather than being replaced by finite plotting limits.

For an eligible finite interval \([l,u]\), one prospective score at nominal
level \(1-\alpha\) is
\[
 (u-l)+\frac{2}{\alpha}(l-\theta)1\{\theta<l\}
       +\frac{2}{\alpha}(\theta-u)1\{\theta>u\}.
\]
The formula balances length with penalties for missing the target. It is
not an instruction to compress a union of intervals into one interval. For
unions, coverage and total Lebesgue length can be reported while retaining
infinite lengths. Raw losses should not be capped simply to make a plot or
ranking convenient. The eligible target type must be stated before the
score is selected.

\section{Contamination, adaptation and selective reporting}

An exposed demonstration cannot become a held-out evaluation merely because
its variables are renamed. The local problem fixtures and replay examples
have already been used to develop and debug the prototype. They can continue
to test conformance, but they cannot provide independent estimates of a
language model's causal accuracy.

The final design needs a frozen development/test split, mechanism identities,
prompts, model/provider revisions, retrieval corpus and ranking rules, numerical
baselines, stopping rules and analysis code. Mechanism families should be
separated where family reuse would reveal the answer. Label novelty and
mechanism novelty should be varied independently. An unfamiliar name attached
to a memorized mechanism is not the same test as an unfamiliar mechanism.

Test outcomes cannot be used to tune prompt templates, choose the best
retriever, strengthen selected priors or discard difficult cells while
retaining a final-test interpretation. A changed method requires a new
reviewed evaluation revision. Failed and unavailable requests remain in the
record. Reporting only the critic-approved subset would confound answer
quality with selection by the critic.

The inspected OCI paper provides a useful refusal example: its critic
declines many replications when overlap is poor. That can be preferable
to an unsupported estimate, but it makes the denominator essential.
The reported successful answers, refused requests, review effort and
remaining target population must all be visible. The external results
are author reports, not a validation of this project's critic.
\cite{v12_la_2607_22443}

\section{Decision value and cost}

The ultimate question is whether assistance improves feasible decisions at
an acceptable total cost. In a known synthetic mechanism, a policy's expected
loss can be calculated under the mechanism and compared with the chosen
baseline. In a bank, the feasible policy, valuation model, risk limits,
operating costs and outcome truth need authentic inputs. Synthetic decision
loss does not establish institutional return on investment.

The prospective cost record includes model calls, input/output/cache tokens,
retrieval, numerical CPU time, wall time, memory, retries and human review
and rework. Actual dated prices are needed to turn these quantities into a
currency total. Unknown prices remain missing; zero live calls in an offline
prototype do not imply a free live workflow. A fast answer that requires
substantial correction can have a worse total cost than a slower transparent
analysis.

No final live-model experiment is reported by this chapter. Five prerequisite
classes remain: an exact live backend and custody terms; actual prices and
a bounded budget; independent held-out mechanisms and original benchmark
bytes; named business/diagram adjudicators and a rubric; and qualified
numerical baselines. These are missing program inputs. No credentials were
read and no provider endpoint was probed to infer that a service is unavailable.
The design provides a route to evaluation once those inputs are supplied;
it provides no current empirical model-performance claim. The remaining studies turn these requirements into inspectable tests: first the probability of passing a coverage rule, then a prospective comparison, and finally the reliability of its references, evaluators and numerical handoffs.

~~~

\section{Servicing decisions: intervention histories and net value}
\label{exec14:l5-servicing}

The policy functional in equation~\eqref{eq:la04-policy} becomes operationally
useful only when its histories have a banking interpretation. Consider an
initial servicing contact $A_0$, a subsequent distress indicator $L_1$, and a
second contact $A_1$. An initial contact can prevent distress; distress can
prompt a second contact; and both contacts incur costs. A request to compare
``contacted and uncontacted customers'' conceals all three relations. It also
conceals whether the analyst wants the value of a fixed history, a rule that
responds to distress, or a policy learned from the same observations. These are
different inferential requests. An assistant can make the alternatives explicit
and translate the selected request into a rule. Its interpretation remains
reviewable against the business decision.

The following mechanism is stipulated for an independent exact reference; its
numbers are illustrative USD per account, not observations from a bank
\cite{exec14_workflow_oracle}. There is no baseline covariate in this small law.
The first action has probability $1/2$, and the state transitions satisfy
\[
 P(L_1=1\mid A_0=0)=\frac45,\qquad
 P(L_1=1\mid A_0=1)=\frac25.
\]
The observational second-action probabilities are
\[
 e_1(l)=P(A_1=1\mid A_0,L_1=l)
 =\begin{cases}1/2,&l=0,\\3/4,&l=1.\end{cases}
\]
Gross recovery is $100-40L_1+10A_0+30L_1A_1$. Each contact costs eight, so the
outcome to be compared is
\[
 Y=100-40L_1+2A_0+(30L_1-8)A_1.
 \label{eq:exec14-l5-net}
\]
The stipulated mechanism has independent assignment noise at each action,
conditional on the displayed history, and a deterministic final outcome.
This supplies the exchangeability needed for its illustrative intervention
interpretation. An observed bank table with the same conditional means would
still require an assignment argument; numerical resemblance would not supply
that premise. Treatment-confounder feedback and the causal conditions of the
g-formula are developed by Hern\'an and Robins \cite{hernan2020}.

Compare three fixed, feasible policies. The no-contact policy sets both
actions to zero. The treat-all policy sets both to one. The risk-responsive
policy sets $A_0=1$ and $A_1=L_1$. Its second contact is affordable and available
only after the distress state is delivered. The policy does not use a future
outcome or a revised state unavailable at that decision. Under the risk policy,
net recovery is 102 when $L_1=0$ and 84 when $L_1=1$. Averaging under its own
post-first-action state law gives
\[
 V(g_{\mathrm{risk}})=\frac35(102)+\frac25(84)
 =\frac{474}{5}=94.8.
\]
The corresponding values are $V(g_{\mathrm{none}})=68$ and
$V(g_{\mathrm{all}})=90$. The risk-responsive policy gains
$134/5=26.8$ over no contact and 4.8 over contacting everyone. The first contrast
decomposes into two from the first contact's direct net contribution, sixteen
from the reduction in distress probability, and $44/5=8.8$ from the second
contact's net contribution under the changed state distribution. This
decomposition explains why a recovery lift alone is insufficient for the
business decision. A contact can improve gross recovery while its marginal
net contribution is negative in a low-risk state.

Two plausible shortcuts answer different questions. Restricting the observed
data to histories that happen to follow the risk policy gives mean 93, because
the two retained states have equal conditional frequency. Restricting to
histories with both actions zero gives $220/3$, because distress changes the
chance of avoiding the second contact. The unweighted difference is therefore
$59/3$, rather than $134/5$. Alternatively, averaging the risk-policy outcome
under the pooled distress frequency $3/5$ yields 91.2. That calculation holds
the mediator distribution at its observational mixture, rather than allowing
the first intervention to change it. Neither error is repaired by producing
an explanation of a correctly computed mean. The assistant's most valuable
intervention is to detect the target substitution before numerical execution.

For a general baseline $L_0$, write
$H_1=(L_0,A_0,L_1)$ and
$m(H_1,a_1)=E[Y\mid H_1,A_1=a_1]$. With a fixed regime $g$, define
\begin{align*}
 m_g(H_1)&=m\{H_1,g_1(H_1)\},\\
 Q_0(L_0)&=E[m_g(H_1)\mid L_0,A_0=g_0(L_0)].
\end{align*}
Then $V(g)=E[Q_0(L_0)]$ under the stated longitudinal identification
conditions. Backward outcome regression implements these successive
conditional expectations. Forward g-computation models the state transition
and outcome, then propagates the regime through both. Inverse-probability
weighting instead uses
\[
 w_0=\frac{\mathbf1\{A_0=g_0(L_0)\}}
 {P\{A_0=g_0(L_0)\mid L_0\}},\qquad
 w_1=\frac{\mathbf1\{A_1=g_1(H_1)\}}
 {P\{A_1=g_1(H_1)\mid H_1\}},
\]
for which $E[w_0w_1Y]=V(g)$. All three representations use the intervention's
history. They differ in which nuisance quantities must be estimated and in
their behavior when data are sparse, weights are variable, or a regression
extrapolates. The choice should follow the declared target and its supported
histories, rather than the name of a preferred package.

\section{Retention, recursive augmentation and uncertainty}
\label{exec14:l5-retention}

The outcome may become unavailable when an account moves to another servicing
system or its case is unresolved. Let $R$ indicate that $Y$ is observed at the
final horizon. To identify the same full-population value, suppose
$R\perp Y\mid H_1,A_1$, with
$r(H_1,A_1)=P(R=1\mid H_1,A_1)>0$ on the regime's support. This is a final-outcome
missingness law. If earlier histories also disappear, their observation
mechanisms require additional nodes and weights; the single $R$ does not
silently represent them. Nor does administrative censoring justify this
conditional independence merely because its date is recorded
\cite{hernan2020}.

In the stipulated servicing law, let retention be one for $L_1=0$ and one half
for $L_1=1$, independently of the outcome given history. Among retained accounts
under the risk intervention, the mean becomes
\[
 \frac{(3/5)102+(2/5)(1/2)84}{3/5+(2/5)(1/2)}=97.5.
\]
Inverse retention weights restore the intervention value 94.8. Multiplying
$w_0w_1$ by $R/r$ also restores it in the observational enumeration. The
complete-case mean is higher because distressed accounts are less often
retained, not because servicing became more effective. A fluent report that
describes 97.5 as a population policy value would obscure an observation-law
error. Conversely, if loss depends on an unobserved recovery component even
after conditioning, these weights have no such causal justification. The
appropriate output is a sensitivity analysis or unresolved population value,
not a fabricated retention probability.

An augmented representation shows where the pieces enter. With the true
nuisance quantities, a centered score for this two-action, final-retention
problem is
\begin{align}
 \phi_g(O)={}&w_0w_1\frac{R}{r(H_1,A_1)}
          \{Y-m(H_1,A_1)\}\nonumber\\
 &+w_0\{m_g(H_1)-Q_0(L_0)\}+Q_0(L_0)-V(g).
 \label{eq:exec14-l5-score}
\end{align}
The first residual has conditional mean zero under the observation law. The
second has mean zero conditional on $L_0$ after first-action reweighting.
The last term centers the baseline regression. Where $R=0$, the first term
is defined as zero; it does not require an unavailable value of $Y$. This
mean-zero argument is a population identity. A fitted estimator needs control
of nuisance errors and remainder terms, a valid sampling law, and the
appropriate handling of sample splitting. The display does not establish
coverage simply by being called an influence function.

The exact law isolates one aspect of precision. Its outcome is deterministic
given history and it has no varying $L_0$. The first and last components in
equation~\eqref{eq:exec14-l5-score} vanish, leaving variation from the intermediate
state. Under independent accounts, the risk-policy score has variance
$3888/25=155.52$; the no-contact score has variance 512. Their covariance is
zero here because their nonzero first-action indicators are disjoint and both
scores are centered. The variance of their difference is consequently
$16688/25=667.52$. A normalized policy-IPW estimator with true weights has
asymptotic centered score $w_0w_1\{Y-V(g)\}$ when there is no retention loss.
Its variance is 248.832 for the risk policy and 1228.8 for no contact.
These are exact moments under the declared law
\cite{exec14_workflow_oracle}. They explain how recursive adjustment can remove
second-action sampling variation in this example. They do not rank fitted
procedures under arbitrary bank dependence or qualify any confidence interval.

Robustness requires equally precise terminology. Luedtke and colleagues
distinguish conventional longitudinal double robustness, requiring all outcome
components or all treatment components to be correct in the relevant sense,
from sequential double robustness, allowing the appropriate component to be
correct at each stage \cite{sequentialdr2018}. Their definitions distinguish
outcome-regression specification from treatment-mechanism consistency. A
point-treatment AIPW function placed inside a loop does not inherit their
recursive construction or its theorem. An assistant recommending a
``doubly robust longitudinal estimator'' should therefore identify the actual
algorithm and its conditions, rather than treating robustness as a universal
package property. The safe comparison includes a transparent fixed-regime
g-formula, an IP-weighted representation, and an estimator whose longitudinal
construction is genuinely supported by primary text.

Support is a property of the policy's histories, not only a histogram of the
first propensity. An initially supported contact can lead to a distressed
state where the requested later action is never taken. Product probabilities
can also become very small although each decision separately looks tolerable.
Weight truncation may improve numerical behavior while changing bias and the
effective comparison. Diagnostics should show where weights concentrate,
which histories disappear, and how the result changes under a declared
sensitivity choice. A regime that requires a forbidden or unavailable contact
should be returned for redesign. A new policy learned after inspecting the
same outcomes introduces selection and policy-learning questions beyond the
fixed-policy arithmetic above. Its apparent best value cannot be reported
with a fixed-regime interval without a separate argument.

\section{Branch adoption is a panel question with a different target}
\label{exec14:l5-panel}

Suppose branches adopt a servicing platform at different dates and the bank
asks whether the platform improves recovery. This differs from evaluating the
account-level dynamic contact rule. Let $G_i$ be branch $i$'s first adoption
time, $Y_{it}(g)$ its outcome at time $t$ if adoption begins at $g$, and
$Y_{it}(\infty)$ the outcome without adoption. A useful target is
\[
 \operatorname{ATT}(g,t)
 =E[Y_{it}(g)-Y_{it}(\infty)\mid G_i=g],\qquad t\geq g.
\]
The unit, adoption event, composition of branch accounts, and monetary outcome
must be fixed before estimation. A decline in average loss among remaining
accounts could arise from account transfers rather than an improvement for
the original cohort. A repeated cross-section and a stable account panel
therefore need different observation arguments. Arkhangelsky and Imbens
organize panel methods by data configuration, relative numbers of units and
periods, and treatment assignment patterns; this organization helps avoid
selecting a method solely because the table has a date column
\cite{panelreview2024}.

With no anticipation and an appropriate never-treated comparison group $C$,
unconditional parallel untreated trends over the relevant periods identify
\begin{align*}
 \operatorname{ATT}(g,t)
 ={}&E[Y_{it}-Y_{i,g-1}\mid G_i=g]\\
 &-E[Y_{it}-Y_{i,g-1}\mid C_i=1].
\end{align*}
Conditional parallel trends instead require comparing changes at the relevant
baseline covariates $X$ and averaging over the adopting cohort's covariate
distribution, with overlap for that comparison. Callaway and Sant'Anna also
develop not-yet-treated comparisons and explicit anticipation windows
\cite{callaway2021}. For an anticipation horizon $\delta$, the baseline must
precede $g-\delta$, and a comparison group must still be unaffected at the
relevant later time including its anticipation window. A branch preparing for
rollout can change staffing before formal adoption; the recorded software
installation date alone does not establish no anticipation.

The comparison choice carries substantive assumptions. Never-treated branches
may operate in different markets. Not-yet-treated branches may be more similar
but supply no untreated comparison after the last adoption, and their rollout
plans may already affect behavior. Both designs require an argument about
untreated changes, rather than the stronger sequential exchangeability of an
account-level dynamic policy. The analyst must state which argument is being
used. An assistant can locate adoption notices, reconstruct candidate dates,
and propose competing controls. It cannot establish the unobserved untreated
trend from a satisfactory regression fit.

A small stipulated panel makes these distinctions visible
\cite{exec14_workflow_oracle}. There are three equal-sized cohorts, early
adopters $E$, late adopters $L$, and never adopters $N$. Their observed means are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Cohort & Time 0 & Time 1 & Time 2\\
\midrule
Early &100&107&119\\
Late &100&102&108\\
Never &100&102&104\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The stipulated untreated means are 100, 102, and 104 for every cohort.
Early adoption has effects five at time 1 and fifteen at time 2; late adoption
has effect four at time 2. Comparing early and never cohorts from time 0 to
time 1 gives five; from time 0 to time 2 gives fifteen. Comparing late and
never cohorts from time 1 to time 2 gives four. In contrast, comparing the
late cohort's change to the already-treated early cohort's change gives
\[
 (108-102)-(119-107)=-6.
\]
The early cohort's treatment effect increases by ten during that comparison.
The negative difference therefore subtracts another group's changing effect
from the late cohort's benefit. It is not evidence that the platform harms
late adopters.

Aggregation also changes the question. Equal weighting of the three treated
cohort-time cells gives $(5+15+4)/3=8$. Equal weighting of the two cohorts at
their first exposure gives $(5+4)/2=4.5$. The first includes a later-exposure
effect for early adopters; the second compares a common event horizon. Other
bank questions may weight cohort sizes, account exposure, or the distribution
of dates in a proposed rollout. These weights must be stated. In this particular
balanced fixture, residualizing the adoption indicator against cohort and
calendar effects produces a two-way fixed-effects coefficient of 4.5: the
early time-2 cell has zero residual weight and the other treated cells have
equal positive weights. It happens to equal the first-exposure target here.
The contaminated two-group comparison does not imply that every fixed-effects
coefficient is negative or scientifically useless. The exact residualization
and the survey's qualified discussion both argue for inspecting the target and
weights, rather than adopting a universal rejection of fixed effects
\cite{panelreview2024,exec14_workflow_oracle}.

Observational ambiguity remains even after this algebra is correct. Suppose
the early cohort's untreated outcome at time 2 is 107 because it receives a
cohort-specific favorable shock of three, and its actual treatment effect
is twelve. The observed value remains 119, and every other displayed value is
unchanged. The first law's effect fifteen and the alternative law's effect
twelve are compatible with the same observed panel. The alternative violates
the relevant post-adoption parallel untreated trend. Additional common
pre-adoption periods can be appended to both laws without distinguishing
them. Good pre-adoption agreement is a useful diagnostic; it does not exclude
every later counterfactual shock. A bank may need a rollout assignment design,
a defensible control, or explicit sensitivity to such shocks before attaching
a causal interpretation to the contrast.

Synthetic control and factor-based alternatives are substantive when the
bank has few treated units, rich histories, and a credible structure for
untreated outcomes. They do not automatically solve an unsupported
counterfactual: donor contamination, a new factor after rollout, or a change
in measurement can defeat their argument. The panel survey motivates these
alternatives without asserting a particular bank guarantee
\cite{panelreview2024}. The assistant's proposal should connect each candidate
to the data dimensions and assignment pattern, identify which restriction
supplies its counterfactual, and retain uncertainty about that restriction.
A dynamic servicing value should not be silently substituted for a branch
adoption ATT merely because both methods return a monetary number.

\section{Observation construction can determine the answer}
\label{exec14:l5-observations}

The preceding values assume that accounts and outcomes have been correctly
assembled. A causal workflow should instead begin with the population frame,
inclusion mechanism, ownership relation, and label meaning. An assistant
extracting ``recovery'' from notes may confuse gross recovery with net value,
or a revised figure with the figure available at the decision. Linking two
accounts to a customer may change the unit, create duplicated outcomes, and
alter dependence at once. These changes belong to the scientific observation
model. A schema that accepts the resulting rows does not establish their truth.

Consider a frame containing two equally frequent strata with values zero and
100. Suppose every zero-value unit is included but each 100-value unit is
included independently with probability $1/4$. Writing $S$ for inclusion,
the mean among observed records is
\[
 \frac{E[SY]}{E[S]}=
 \frac{(1/2)(1/4)100}{(1/2)1+(1/2)(1/4)}=20.
\]
The population mean is 50. If the frame size $N$ and truthful inclusion
probabilities $\pi_i$ are known, the Horvitz--Thompson form
\[
 \widehat\mu_{\mathrm{HT}}=
 \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{S_iY_i}{\pi_i}
\]
has expectation 50 under the stipulated sampling law. This uses the known
frame denominator; a ratio estimator with an estimated denominator is a
different construction. For independently generated framed units, the
per-unit weighted contribution is zero or 400. Its variance is
$20000-50^2=17500$, so the mean's variance is $17500/N$
\cite{exec14_workflow_oracle}. Correcting selection can therefore increase
uncertainty even while restoring the target. A narrow unweighted interval
around 20 does not constitute a more precise estimate of 50.

The correction requires knowledge that an LLM cannot manufacture. If inclusion
probabilities are estimated from an incomplete frame, depend on an unknown
outcome component, or are zero for a relevant group, the displayed equality
need not apply. Retrieving a description of the sampling system can identify
a candidate probability model; an actual audit must establish that it was
followed. When the target is an intervention mean, treatment, retention,
sampling, and linkage cannot simply be handled as unrelated cleaning steps.
Their joint chronology determines which histories and outcomes are observed
and which probabilities can be conditioned on. The longitudinal observation
intervention discussed by Hern\'an and Robins supplies a model-based way to
formulate that joint problem \cite{hernan2020}.

Noisy labels pose a separate problem. Let $T$ be a true binary ownership or
distress label, $Z$ its observed classifier label, $p=P(T=1)$, sensitivity
$s=P(Z=1\mid T=1)$ and specificity $c=P(Z=0\mid T=0)$. If these error rates are
known for the target population, then
\[
 P(Z=1)=sp+(1-c)(1-p),\qquad
 p=\frac{P(Z=1)+c-1}{s+c-1}.
\]
With $p=0.4$, $s=0.8$ and $c=0.9$, the positive-label frequency is 0.38 and
the inversion returns 0.4. If $s+c=1$, the observed label frequency contains
no information about prevalence through this model. Close to that boundary,
sampling noise is amplified by the denominator. With known rates and $n$
independent labels in this example, the inverted proportion has variance
$(589/1225)/n$ before any probability-bound handling
\cite{exec14_workflow_oracle}. Estimating the error rates from a gold-label
sample adds uncertainty. Reusing one error-rate estimate across many account
records also introduces shared estimation error; multiplying the number of
rows does not make that component disappear.

This inversion concerns a marginal prevalence, not a causal effect or an
individual ownership map. Errors can differ by treatment, history, market or
time, and two competing customer mappings can have the same correctness
count. A prevalence correction does not reconstruct which record belongs to
which economic owner. For causal use, the workflow must retain the candidate
mapping and how its uncertainty affects exposure, outcome and unit formation.
An LLM can propose label rules and flag contradictory notes; the proposal
should compare that assistance with deterministic rules and human adjudication
on genuinely reviewed examples. Agreement between two assistants exposed to
the same notes is not an independent gold label. Missing truth is an evidence
limitation, rather than a reason to replace adjudication with confidence in
generated prose.

Dependence can survive correct inclusion and label handling. Let $B$ independent
branches each have a centered shock $\varepsilon_b$ of variance one, shared
by two account records. Their overall account mean is
$B^{-1}\sum_b\varepsilon_b$, with variance $1/B$. Treating the $2B$ rows as
independent instead gives $1/(2B)$. Now add a centered calendar shock $C$ of
variance four shared by every branch, independently of their shocks. The
mean's variance is $4+1/B$. More accounts or branches reduce only the second
component. This is an exact covariance construction
\cite{exec14_workflow_oracle}, not a universal banking variance model. It
shows why account counts alone cannot justify precision and why a common
calendar component needs replicated dates or additional restrictions.
Splitting nuisance training and evaluation by independent branch can protect
one dependence boundary; it cannot remove the shared calendar shock. The
sampling and covariance argument must follow the intended deployment and
observation law.

\section{What assistance and software reuse can responsibly achieve}
\label{exec14:l5-handoffs}

These three pathways suggest distinct roles for an assistant. In sequential
servicing, it can translate a verbal rule into a decision-time history, locate
post-action variables, and ask why assignment and retention are conditionally
ignorable. In a branch rollout, it can distinguish cohort time from event time,
construct candidate comparison groups, and expose anticipation or account
composition changes. In observation construction, it can extract candidate
definitions and mappings while retaining conflicting evidence and unavailable
truth. A generic request to ``run causal inference'' is insufficient for all
three. The proposed product should make the pathway and its resulting target
visible to the analyst before selecting an estimator.

The point-in-time OCI workflow demonstrates a narrower literature precedent:
an accountable human principal, actor/critic assistance, reproducible notebooks,
cross-fitted AIPW and overlap diagnostics under supplied unconfoundedness
\cite{exec13_data_oci}. It supports discussion of human oversight and
point-treatment workflow. It does not establish sequential exchangeability,
identify a rollout counterfactual, or qualify ownership reconstruction. These
are candidate extensions requiring the corresponding scientific and numerical
arguments. A reviewer should be able to see whether the assistant asks for
the missing premise, changes the target explicitly, or refuses the requested
interpretation. An apparently complete notebook can still be wrong if its
target differs from the business question.

The inspected R package \texttt{ltmle} offers a relevant longitudinal
component. It estimates means specific to treatment and censoring, supports
dynamic treatment rules, and returns outcome-regression and weighting
outputs \citep{sw_ltmle}. Its interface
uses column order to encode model chronology and binary treatment nodes.
An adapter would need to validate the actual event and availability clocks
before constructing that order. A continuous contact dose cannot be passed
as though it were binary without an explicit intervention redesign.
Absorbing event coding is appropriate for a one-time event only when its
semantics are actually absorbing. Automatically truncating net outcomes at a
declared range can alter the quantity being averaged, whereas a known affine
scaling can be reversed for an intervention mean. These interface choices
have scientific consequences, rather than merely formatting consequences.
The saved source inspection motivates restricted reuse; it is not an execution
or qualification of the package in a bank setting.

A matched baseline is an analyst using explicit decision interviews, a graph
editor, and deterministic estimation software with the same sources and
information budget. Assistance should be assessed on preserved targets,
unsupported assumptions, actual tool completion, accurate uncertainty, and
review effort. Comparisons should include unavailable histories, unsupported
actions, contaminated controls, missing frames, and labels without gold truth.
An appropriate unresolved answer may be more valuable than a confidently
generated estimate. Genuine improvement would mean reducing analyst effort
while preserving those decisions and making more errors detectable, rather
than increasing the number of successful-looking reports.

The immediate prototype can use the finite mechanisms above and suitable
public panels to test those transformations economically. Known synthetic
truth tests target preservation and numerical arithmetic; a public observed
panel tests the discipline of stating a counterfactual without supplying its
truth by construction. A later bank experiment must resolve the actual
assignment, observation, operating-cost and acceptance questions. The proposal
can justify that experiment through its scoped comparisons and explicit
failure modes. It cannot replace the experiment's missing evidence with the
existence of an agent architecture.
\label{exec14:l5-development-end}
